Washington has been developing new wildfire safety regulations for several years, including building codes for homes constructed in risky areas and rules for managing plants and vegetation. But restrictions that affect people's homes and gardens can be unpopular. After public pushback, state legislators backtracked and repealed some of the requirements.

Other Western states have also struggled to pass wildfire regulations affecting homeowners' properties. While flood risk is managed by the federal government, wildfire regulations are up to state and local governments. The result is a patchwork of rules.

"It's up to the political will of a community to adopt a building code to address wildfire," says Ryan Maye Handy, who works on community wildfire planning at Headwaters Economics, a land use think tank. "What we're increasingly seeing is many different interpretations of how to reduce that risk. It is literally all over the map."

Loading...

Washington rewrites its wildfire rules

In Spokane, dry conditions and extreme weather set the stage for the explosive wildfires in August. Like much of the Western U.S., eastern Washington is in drought after a winter with low precipitation. In the days leading up to the fires, forecasters warned of a dangerous mix of conditions: gusty winds, low humidity and high temperatures. More than 800 homes and structures were destroyed.

"This was a huge part of our city and a lot of people in the city thought: We're never going to have a fire here, it's never going to come to us and we don't have to worry about this," Kokot says.

Understanding wildfire risk can be challenging in many Western states. For floods, the federal government releases national maps showing which places are at risk of inundation. Wildfire mapping is left to the states, which involves using complex computer models to determine the chances of a fire based on vegetation, terrain and fire behavior.

Sponsor Message

In 2023, Washington building code officials gathered public feedback on the state's new wildfire hazard maps and regulations. In areas mapped as at-risk, newly constructed homes would be required to have fire-resistant roofs, siding and other measures. Homeowners would also be required to manage flammable vegetation to create defensible space, like making sure tree branches are 10 feet from a house or structure.

In a series of public hearings, some conservation groups pushed back, saying the vegetation rules would go against regional goals to increase the urban tree canopy and provide shade that would cool buildings during heat waves. Others said the wildfire maps were overly broad and didn't accurately reflect the real risk.

"Our greatest concern at Audubon is preserving bird habitat," testified Eric Seibel on behalf of the Tahoma Audubon Society, a wildlife conservation group now known as the Tahoma Bird Alliance. "I'm concerned that trees, which are our best defense against climate change, will be destroyed en masse if the provisions of the code pass."

In 2024, Washington passed a bill ordering state regulators to produce new wildfire hazard maps, with fewer rules that would be enforced. New construction would still be required to have fire-resistant roofs and siding, but no vegetation management would be required by homeowners.

"That got the fire service pretty concerned, because that's our primary protection," Kokot says. It's safer for firefighters to defend a burning structure when there's less vegetation directly next to it.

Washington state officials say the new wildfire maps will be released in December. The maps will now account for past wildfire history, which they say will more accurately show which areas are most at risk.

"It's trying to make sure that people are smart, building in those areas," says Angie Lane, assistant division manager with Washington's Department of Natural Resources, who is working on the new wildfire maps. "When you're starting fresh, it's easier to go ahead and prepare for all of that while you're building."

A patchwork of Western wildfire regulations

Oregon faced similar pushback while developing its wildfire regulations. Some residents were concerned that if their home was designated as high risk by the state, insurance companies would cancel their policies. Misinformation about the extent of vegetation restrictions also spread online.

Sponsor Message

Home insurance cancellations have increased rapidly in the Western U.S. as wildfires have become increasingly expensive. But insurance companies base decisions on their own maps, developed with much more granular and comprehensive data. Oregon even passed a law in 2023 banning insurance companies from using state wildfire maps.

"Insurers have their own proprietary maps that are quite sophisticated," Handy of Headwaters Economics says. "We know insurers are mapping wildfire risk already and the state maps are in some senses just catching up to that."

As a result of public pushback, Oregon repealed its wildfire rules last year.

Building codes for housing in wildfire-prone areas were pioneered by California. For almost 20 years, the state has required fire-resistant construction standards. Fire agencies conduct home inspections for vegetation and defensible space in many high-risk areas. The state is currently considering even more stringent vegetation rules, limiting how much greenery can be within five feet of a structure — what's known as "zone zero."

In Colorado, an effort to develop wildfire building codes was defeated more than a decade ago, after pushback from the local building and real estate industry. That changed after the destructive Marshall Fire in 2021. The state now has new rules on building codes and vegetation. Utah also recently passed its own rules.

Still, a number of Western states don't have statewide wildfire rules and codes, or even maps identifying high risk areas. Handy says that leaves many areas vulnerable, given that wildfires are becoming increasingly destructive as the climate gets hotter.

"One of the best ways to get everyone on the same playing field is a wildfire building code," Handy says. "We know now, more so than we knew 10 years ago, that regulating what we call the 'built environment' to reduce wildfire risk is extremely effective."

In Spokane, Kokot feels lucky that the fires were contained before they reached his house. The damage in his community, he says, shows how wildfires have changed, becoming larger and more frequent.

Sponsor Message

"We can't be complacent about the fires," Kokot says. "We have to predict that there's a possibility it could happen. We have to plan for it."

World.title: Elon Musk's Starbase wants to expand in south Texas
World.content:
Elon Musk's Starbase wants to expand in south Texas

toggle caption Reynaldo Leaños Jr./For NPR

STARBASE, Texas — On a scorching August afternoon in south Texas, Bekah Hinojosa, the co-founder of the South Texas Environmental Justice Center, blasts the A/C in her car.

As she drives down Highway 4 towards Boca Chica Beach, large 18-wheelers and silver glistening Cybertrucks zoom past her on the opposite lane.

"This road is always under construction," said Hinojosa. "SpaceX is rapidly colonizing and changing the entire landscape of Boca Chica."

Very soon the newly created city of Starbase, and Elon Musk's SpaceX, could change this area by the Gulf of Mexico, even more. This city was established in 2025 and is now asking its residents to consider annexing around 7,100 acres of surrounding land, including state and private property.

Sponsor Message

The city was created, in part, as a way to help grow its SpaceX workforce and increase its capacity for developing, and the manufacturing needed for more rocket launches.

In April of 2025 the Federal Aviation Administration approved SpaceX's request to increase launches from its Boca Chica Launch Site.

These operations include, "up to 25 annual Starship/Super Heavy orbital launches, up to 25 annual landings of Starship, up to 25 annual landings of Super Heavy, and vehicle upgrades," according to the FAA document.

All this is part of Musk's stated plan to build a complex from where SpaceX could launch humans back to the moon and eventually to Mars.

The current SpaceX complex is home to launch pads, manufacturing and test sites. Starbase controls road access to a nearby beach, and a nature reserve during launches.

According to documents that Starbase provided to neighboring landowners, and has posted on their website, the city said part of what a possible annexation would allow for is, "more efficient coordination with federal and state partners including the Texas Department of Public Safety, Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, U.S. Customs and Border Patrol, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Services and others."

toggle caption Reynaldo Leaños Jr./For NPR

Concerns about the environment

Hinojosa grabs her steering wheel and veers off the highway onto a dirt road with vegetation all around.

Sponsor Message

"We're on beautiful pristine land owned by a property owner who doesn't wanna get sucked up into Elon Musk's city of Starbase," she said.

Activists like Hinojosa and several private land owners are concerned about the impact that the Starbase expansion will have in their community. She's been in touch with several impacted landowners, like 56-year-old Barbara Buckner.

Buckner's grandmother was a Holocaust survivor who fled Poland, lived in Chicago and purchased property in south Texas. She is opposed to the proposed annexation. She asks: Who will Starbase prioritize? Residents? Or SpaceX?

"How can you be supporting residents when you work for SpaceX?" Buckner asks.

Currently, the mayor of Starbase, Robert "Bobby" Peden, and one of the two city commissioners, work for SpaceX. Peden did not respond to several requests for an interview.

Buckner believes that the proposed annexation is just the beginning. " I think they'll keep trying to expand," she said.

toggle caption Reynaldo Leaños Jr./For NPR

Gerold Podraza, an 83-year-old landowner, said he's also opposed to the proposed annexation.

" It just represents that the people who have money are able to do things that they, shouldn't be allowed to do," he said. "The only reason why that's happening is because they have leverage with politicians, and they can influence politicians to make judgments that are not good for the community that they represent."

In 2024, NPR reported that the Environmental Protection Agency found that SpaceX had violated the Clean Water Act after tens of thousands of gallons of industrial wastewater were discharged into the surrounding area. It's this kind of environmental concern that Hinojosa fears could increase with more rocket launches.

"I've come out here several times after a SpaceX launch to document all of the debris," Hinojosa said. "I have photos of metal shrapnel blown up into this area that we're on."

SpaceX did not respond to NPR's questions about the environmental impact of its rocket launches.

Sponsor Message

Sofia Benavides, a Cameron County Commissioner representing the area where Starbase is located, said the law clearly allows Starbase to expand.

"There's nothing that we can do to stop it," Benavides said.

Starbase has until August 18 to hear back from potentially impacted landowners about the annexation plan and determine if they have the necessary signatures needed to move forward. The city then is required to hold two public hearings before voting in September on whether to annex, or not.

Hinojosa's organization is looking into possible legal action to prevent the annexation.

"They call it Starbase. You pull the curtain back, it's the SpaceX annexation," Hinojosa said. "SpaceX threatens the Rio Grande Valley. And that's why we'll continue to resist."

World.title: Where do Canada-U.S. trade negotiations stand? Here's a sector-by-sector breakdown
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is continuing to negotiate a trade deal with the United States that will allow it to both avoid U.S. President Donald Trump's crippling tariff threat — set to come into effect on Wednesday — and get some additional relief on existing tariffs in key sectors.

But after a flurry of meetings between top Canadian and American negotiators over the last three weeks, the two countries remain at an impasse heading into the home stretch.

Sources have told CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear there may be no way to avert Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods, as Washington digs in on its demands while Ottawa tries to persuade provinces to lift restrictions on American alcohol.

The U.S. claims it's imposing the tariffs because of Canadian discrimination toward its automobile, dairy and alcohol sectors.

With two days left to negotiate, here's what sources have told CBC News about where Canada-U.S. trade talks stand on Monday morning, broken down by each key sector.

WATCH | Canadian negotiators worried U.S. tariffs will be imposed: Negotiators fear U.S. tariffs will be imposed as sides dig in | Duration 3:09 Canadian negotiators fear there may be no way to avert new U.S. tariffs from taking effect Wednesday, as Ottawa struggles to win relief from Washington on existing sectoral tariffs while also trying to persuade provinces to lift restrictions on American alcohol.

Automobiles

According to sources, the U.S. is proposing to reduce its existing auto tariffs from the current 25 per cent down to 12.5 per cent, an offer the Canadian side believes is not good enough.

The U.S. has cited issues with Canada's auto trade as one reason why it intends to impose its 50 per cent tariffs. The White House argues Canada imposes tariffs and quotas on vehicles imported to Canada from the U.S. — but not other countries.

Lana Payne, national president of Unifor and a member of Prime Minister Mark Carney's advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations, said on Friday that Trump is missing the fact that his auto tariffs hurt U.S. companies.

"We can't afford to give any more concessions here, and we need a good deal. And that means we've got to grind it out until the very end," Payne said.

An autoworker at the General Motors assembly plant is shown in the body shop producing the Chevrolet Silverado, in Oshawa, Ont., in February 2022. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

Payne has previously warned that agreeing to the levies in writing now could give Washington a path to seeking permanent auto tariffs as part of a renegotiated Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).

Sources say, however, that Canada will need to concede some ground in any sort of deal.

Dairy

Trump has long lambasted Canada's supply management system , which allows a certain amount of U.S. dairy to enter Canada tariff-free before steep duties are applied.

In announcing its 50 per cent tariff threat, the White House said Canada established tariff-rate quotas on cheese from the U.S. that are "much more restrictive" than the quotas applied on similar imports of cheese from the European Union.

On Friday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reiterated that argument and said that "we have an uneven dairy treatment."

Sources have told CBC News that Canada will need to concede on dairy in any new deal. It's unclear what Canada has offered on the matter.

But concessions on this front could be politically dangerous for the Carney government.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said on Friday that supply management is a red line for her province and that several thousand farms and jobs depend on Canada's dairy industry.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette speaks to reporters at a news conference with fellow premiers closing the Council of the Federation meetings, in Charlottetown on July 22. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

Alcohol

The federal government has told provinces to be ready as soon as possible to put U.S. alcohol back on store shelves in case a tariff deal is reached, sources have told CBC News. That irritant is another reason behind Trump's 50 per cent tariff threat.

Only Alberta and Saskatchewan, which have privatized alcohol retail systems, have resumed the sale of U.S. booze. Other provinces have maintained their bans, although there has been division among them for months over whether to relent.

Sources have told CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear this is a significant obstacle in avoiding Trump's tariff threat. The bans are entirely provincially controlled, but some provinces have said they'll only relent if they get relief for their sectors.

A Toronto LCBO employee removes U.S. alcohol from store shelves in March 2025. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

On Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he will end the province's boycott only if negotiators secure what he describes as a "fair deal" that addresses tariffs on key sectors.

"If we get a fair deal that will protect our steel sector, our auto sector, our forestry sector, agriculture sector, manufacturing sector, then we'd be more than happy to bring booze back on the shelves," Ford said.

Similarly, Fréchette has said she's open to allowing U.S. wine to return to store shelves, but she'll need to see reductions in tariffs on key sectors like aluminum and manufacturing.

Sources have also said the federal government has asked provinces and territories to be prepared to drop retaliatory procurement rules that favour Canadian suppliers in case a deal is made.

Steel and aluminum

Canada is pushing to have the Trump administration lower its existing tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper — which range from 10 to 50 per cent.

The Carney government has announced various measures over the last few months to prop up the sectors, including establishing a $1-billion loan program through the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) so companies most affected by tariffs can get the money they need to stay in business.

Last week, the federal government announced it would pump an additional $100 million into Canada's steel industry with a new program that will pay for half the costs of transporting Canadian-made steel by ship or rail within the country.

The program is slated to operate for one year, or until the $100-million funding envelope runs dry, with a single producer eligible for a maximum rebate of $50 million.

When asked what will happen to the program if it runs out of money before the end of its one-year timeline, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon hinted that an extension may be considered.

A worker tags a roll of steel at Cascadia Metals in Delta, B.C., on Friday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Softwood lumber

According to sources, Canada is pushing for relief on tariffs the U.S. has slapped on Canadian softwood lumber, but Washington is not interested in discussions on this front. The existing total tariff rate is 45 per cent.

The Canada-U.S. fight over softwood lumber predates the Trump administration by decades and was also a point of concern when former U.S. president Joe Biden was in office .

Sources say the Trump administration's view is that the softwood issue should be negotiated separately from the other sectoral tariffs.

Trump's looming 50 per cent tariffs are planned to hit items like charcoal, plywood, wooden doors, wooden fixtures and various lumber products. It's expected to be especially challenging for British Columbia.

Ashlee Cribb, CEO of Gorman Bros. Lumber Ltd. in West Kelowna, told CBC's The House last week lumber tariffs need to be resolved quickly and that it will be difficult for the company to respond to the additional tariffs.

On Friday, B.C. Premier David Eby said U.S. lumber tariffs need to be addressed and that Ottawa is "well aware" they are one of B.C.'s biggest concerns.

B.C. Premier David Eby listens to a speaker at a closing news conference following a meeting of western premiers, in Kananaskis, Alta., on May 26. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Critical minerals, energy and security

The Americans are seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and cover security and energy.

Canada has several projects located across the country that mine and develop many critical minerals the U.S. desires , such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper. Ottawa is also working to advance production through its national strategy, released in 2022.

Earlier this month, Trump announced the U.S. government will invest $3 billion in critical minerals and battery projects to increase domestic production and boost national security and industry policy.

Cameco employees walk down a tunnel to a jet boring system (JBS) machine at the company's Cigar Lake uranium mine in northern Saskatchewan on June 15. (Liam Richards/The Canadian Press)

The White House needs critical minerals to replenish weapons stockpiles depleted during its ongoing war with Iran and reduce U.S. dependence on Chinese supply chains.

There's also the question of Canada reviewing its F-35 fighter jet purchase from the United States. Carney launched the review in March 2025 in response to diplomatic and trade tensions with the Trump administration.

Last week, National Defence Minister David McGuinty acknowledged the F-35s are "being examined by our negotiating team."

"The question of what is part and parcel of that negotiation continues. And I am hopeful we will come to a successful outcome in due course," he said.

World.title: Demand for Canadian citizenship certificates soaring, fuelled by Americans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Applications from people around the world seeking Canadian citizenship certificates have been rising rapidly in recent months, fuelled by thousands of applications from the United States, CBC News has learned.

The number of people who have already received certificates as a result of Parliament’s adoption of “Lost Canadian” legislation late last year rose nearly 50 per cent between April 1 and May 31, according to new data obtained by CBC.

Bill C-3 allows citizenship for those who can prove they're descended from a Canadian ancestor, even if that ancestor left the country several generations back. It was adopted after the courts ruled that limiting citizenship to the first generation born outside of Canada was too restrictive.

Between mid-December — when Bill C-3 went into effect — and May 31, some 6,100 citizenship certificates were granted by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to those who now qualify.

That is up from 4,075 certificates issued as a result of Bill C-3 from mid-December until March 31.

Another 17,390 people have received certificates as a result of having a Canadian parent. Prior to the bill's adoption, those who were born outside Canada had to have a Canadian parent to qualify for citizenship.

Tip of the iceberg

The certificates allow the 23,490 newly recognized Canadian citizens to apply for Canadian passports and live and work in Canada.

Elections Canada, however, says they can't vote in federal elections unless they've lived in Canada at some point in their life.

People born in the U.S. account for nearly half of those recognized between mid-December and the end of May. According to the data from IRCC, 3,110 Americans have qualified for Canadian citizenship certificates as a result of Bill C-3, while another 8,125 Americans have been granted certificates because one of their parents was born in Canada.

However, that’s just the tip of a very big iceberg.

The number of citizenship certificate applications waiting for a decision has exploded. In April, around 56,000 applications were waiting to be processed. That climbed to 70,400 in May.

Now, the IRCC’s website says 121,800 people are waiting for a decision. Those applications could be for anything from seeking recognition as a citizen under Bill C-3 to requesting a routine replacement of a lost or stolen certificate.

At the same time, the estimated wait time for a decision has doubled from 12 months in May to 25 months as of Aug. 10.

Estimates of just how many people could qualify for Canadian citizenship as a result of Bill C-3 vary widely.

Some point to a span of over 100 years in the 1800s and 1900s when hundreds of thousands of Canadians — particularly from Quebec — flowed over the border to jobs in the U.S.

The parliamentary budget officer has estimated that 115,000 people could be affected by the change in the law.

Last October, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab told the House of Commons immigration committee that she didn’t expect a flood of applications for citizenship certificates once Bill C-3 went into effect.

“We anticipate volumes in the tens of thousands over time," she said. "We do not expect any surge.”

Taous Ait, spokesperson for Metlege Diab, said IRCC took steps beforehand to prepare for the implementation of Bill C-3 and is working to process applications as quickly as possible while protecting the integrity of the citizenship program.

"We’re closely monitoring application volumes and trends and will adjust our operations as needed to manage demand as efficiently as possible," Ait said.

IRCC has not changed its requirements for documents, she added, but has taken steps to make the requirements clearer on its website and in other information for the public.

Demand soars for genealogical records

Meanwhile, Canada’s archivists are reporting a sharp rise in the number of requests for the genealogical records needed to prove someone seeking a Canadian citizenship certificate under Bill C-3 has an unbroken line of descent from a Canadian ancestor.

Alyssa Hyduk, president of the Association of Canadian Archivists, says her members are swamped, with some institutions seeing requests jump by 100 to 300 per cent.

Some are for documents that go back hundreds of years, she added.

“I think across the board there is this overwhelming feeling of just, of overwhelm and burnout …it’s really having an impact,” Hyduk explained.

“These requests are taking up so much of archivists' time that other reference requests — the [ones from the] rest of the public that we’re trying to still serve and do all our jobs — those are being set back too.”

Hyduk said the requests, most of which appear to be coming from the United States, are often complicated, as the records pre-date Confederation or are located in small church archives.

“We are at the point where [we're] going through boxes and boxes of material to find a single document sometimes,” she said. “You are going through reels of microfilm to find ship manifests with one name.”

“And these aren’t searchable documents,” she added. “We can’t go to Ctrl+F and find a last name. We have to read the handwriting. We have to figure it out.”

Archivists need more funding, says group

Mab Coates-Davies, executive director of the association, says the requests can also take an emotional toll on archivists.

“It is personal, it’s emotionally charged, it’s about family history,” she said. “There’s so many reasons that people, you know, might be looking to leave the States right now or planning for future moves.

“And so, there is that human element to it that archivists are feeling and experiencing, and frankly, IRCC isn’t on that front line in terms of the documentation.”

Another problem archivists are facing is the list of documents that IRCC will accept keeps evolving, said Hyduk. When the association met recently with the department, IRCC didn’t want to provide a definitive list of documents, saying it was likely to change.

The association is calling for more funding for archives across the country to keep up with the demand for records created by Bill C-3.

Coates-Davies said the flood of requests also began just as the Carney government’s budget cuts ended Library and Archives Canada’s $1.5-million-a-year Documentary Heritage Communities program, one that many small-and-medium-sized archives across the country have counted on for funding help.

“This funding package was just cut and then our workload skyrocketed," Coates-Davies said.

Last October, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said she didn’t expect a flood of applications for citizenship certificates once Bill C-3 went into effect. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Another wave looms?

During an association meeting last week, some archivists were also bracing for a new wave of requests for genealogical records.

In June, IRCC suddenly suspended an estimated 100 certificates that had already been issued after flagging problems with the documents submitted with the applications. The concern from archivists is that some people who've already applied to IRCC will be sent back to archives to find more genealogical records.

The IRCC says 83 of the suspensions have been resolved and the certificates restored. It has sent procedural fairness letters to another 17 people whose certificates were suspended and given them 60 days to submit the documents necessary to prove their Canadian ancestry.

If they fail to provide acceptable proof, their citizenship certificates could be revoked.

New Democrat immigration critic Jenny Kwan said she has been getting letters and inquiries from people affected by the suspension letters and has written to Metlege Diab, calling for answers.

“It really makes no sense whatsoever, what’s going on," Kwan said. "And the minister is completely ignoring that reality right now.”

World.title: Push for co-operation among European shipbuilders could have Canadian ripple effect
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of the German company in line to build Canada's new submarines is pushing for more co-operation among European shipbuilders — an effort that could have spillover effects in this country as the navy considers adding corvettes to the fleet.

In an interview with CBC News, Oliver Burkhard, the CEO of ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), made a point of highlighting his company's recent co-operation agreement with the Spanish government-owned Navantia S.A.

The two companies are exploring teaming up on ‌naval projects, including the potential production of TKMS submarine designs at Navantia's shipyards in Spain.

Burkhard said he believes there needs to be collaboration among shipbuilders.

Increasing demand for warships

"The pattern which I always observe in this market is [that] everybody in the past had time but no money. Now everybody has money but no time," Burkhard said in an interview with CBC News, referring to the steady, increasing demand for warship construction.

A recent report by the research and strategy company Imarc pegged that increase at more than five per cent over the next decade.

WATCH | Irving shipyard building Canada's River Class destroyers: Halifax shipyard celebrates keel-laying for Canada's 1st River-class destroyer | Duration 2:16 The ceremony at Irving Shipyard marked the official start of construction on what will become HMCS Fraser. The CBC's Ben Dornan was there for the centuries-old tradition.

In addition to submarines, the Canadian navy has begun construction of its long awaited River-Class destroyers and has suggested there's a military need for smaller, less expensive, ice-capable corvettes.

The destroyers are being built by Irving Shipbuilding in Halifax under the National Shipbuilding Program, which is in the process of wrapping up construction of the lightly-armed Arctic and Offshore Patrol Ships.

Since Canada has no modern submarine building expertise, the 12 boats being planned will be built in Germany.

Burkhard spoke ahead of his trip this week to Ottawa, where he's meeting with companies that have partnered with TKMS to supply Canada's submarine program.

Last month, the Carney government named TKMS as the preferred supplier of the navy's submarines and hopes to have the German shipbuilder under full contract by the end of 2027. Burkhard said, given the speed at which the government has moved, he expects a signed deal will likely happen faster.

Burkhard said he doesn't foresee any of the work on the Canadian boats being transferred to Navantia.

Prime Minister Mark Carney greets sailors in July at HMC Dockyard in Halifax, following an announcement that TKMS will build the Canadian navy's new fleet of submarines. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

'It can be built in Canada with our design'

In the run up to the TKMS selection, German officials behind the scenes floated the idea of how the company could possibly supply its MEKO A-100 corvette design to a Canadian shipyard — helping boost Canada's defence-industrial base.

The notion did not make its way into the submarine bid, but Burkhard confirmed it was under consideration.

He said there's been no pitch to Canadian officials about possibly exporting the MEKO A-100 package.

"Export also means that it can be built in Canada with our design," Burkhard said. "We don't want to build them in Germany. We can build them elsewhere together with partners and maybe they are the general contractor. And we are just delivering, let's say, the material package."

While it remains only a concept, Burkhard added: "Let's say, we're ready if you are. Then we can talk about that."

The MEKO A-1000, a corvette warship designed by TKMS. Burkhard, the German company's CEO, says that though there's been no pitch to Canadian officials about exporting the package to be built in Canada, it could be an option. (TKMS)

Navy identified need for corvettes last year

The Canadian navy identified the need for corvettes last year and has been engaged in an options analysis on what role such a warship could fill and what capabilities it would need.

While he was still commander of the navy, Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee, who has been appointed the vice chief of the defence, defended the need for a smaller warship that packs a punch by saying the country has a quarter million kilometres of coast to defend.

University of Calgary defence expert Rob Huebert said the starting point for any discussion about defence procurement needs to be military necessity, not economic benefit.

He said the navy needs corvettes and he's pleased to see Burkhard recognizes that nations, including Canada need to rapidly rearm.

WATCH | Navy commander discusses defending Canada's Arctic: Defending distant, unsurveyed Arctic 'more complicated,' top naval commander says | Duration 3:53 The navy's top commander, Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee, spoke to CBC's Murray Brewster about challenges that come with Arctic defence. 'It's always a difficult and dangerous environment because it's distant, it's not very well surveyed,' Topshee said.

"I think anything that will facilitate the construction of extra ships for the navy is a good one," Huebert said.

"If we find ourselves in conflict, which I'm very terrified we're going to in the near future, we need to get as many ships as possible and we need the ability to replace losses," he said. "So, if the Canadian government is open to that, I think it would be an excellent idea to go with."

Conditions similar to those that created Airbus

Huebert also said it's good to see closer co-operation among European shipyards — especially in submarine construction.

He said it's necessary when there are some companies, like TKMS, at more than 100 per cent capacity in terms of what their yards can sustain, while others are barely operating.

Burkhard compared the market conditions in shipbuilding to the 1960s when empty aircraft order books pushed European aerospace companies to create Airbus.

Back then, the principal competition was from the U.S. defence contractors, Boeing, Lockheed Martin and McDonnell Douglas.

WATCH | What Canada gets out of its submarine deal with German company: Canada to receive 'tens of billions in investments' as part of sub deal, Carney says | Duration 1:31 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is set to receive 'tens of billions in investment' as part of a deal with Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, the German shipbuilding company that won Canada's bid for new submarines. Carney said the investments 'will impact every region of the country.'

While acknowledging a maritime version of Airbus would be a complex undertaking, Burkhard said perhaps industry could take the lead.

"Politicians have to get re-elected and politicians in France will always take care about French shipyards, and politicians in Spain will always take care of Spanish shipyards," Burkhard said.

"But if the industry comes to an idea and say, 'Well, let's join forces like Airbus did in the '70s.' "

The need for closer partnerships among European defence companies was highlighted three years ago by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), which noted in a landmark study that European countries were spending more on defence but co-operating less. The study framed this issue as a deeply entrenched problem.

World.title: Thunder Bay, Ont., health unit takes owner of seniors' apartment to court
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Thunder Bay District Health Unit (TBDHU) is taking the owner of a seniors’ apartment building to court "as a last resort", saying he failed to address dozens of health code violations.

Abby Mackie, a public health inspector with the TBDHU, said the health unit issued compliance orders to SMS Property Trust Inc. on July 8 and July 29 after receiving complaints about excessive heat, overflowing garbage, and bed bugs at Vickers Manor.

“An order is kind of a last resort for us. We prefer to use education and co-operating with ownership to resolve or mitigate any kind of health hazards,” Mackie said. “In this case, we just weren't getting a response.”

Vickers Manor, formerly known as McKellar Place, offers independent living facilities for seniors, as well as a dozen assisted living units managed by Brain Injury Services of Northern Ontario.

The property, located on 325 Archibald St. S. on the city’s south side, is currently for sale for $1 after being listed for $18.9 million earlier this year.

In addition to health code violations, the owner faces dozens of fire code violations. Earlier this summer, several unpaid bills nearly resulted in utilities being shut off , and after hot meals stopped being served, volunteers started a crowdfunding campaign to bring provide food to the residents.

Garbage is seen on the ground surrounding the waste disposal bins outside Vickers Manor in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Friday afternoon. (Sarah Law/CBC)

SMS Property Trust Inc., owned by Ongrasothy Masillamany of Markham, faces 36 offences under the Health Protection and Promotion Act related to excessive heat in the building, according to documents CBC News obtained from the Ontario Court of Justice through Thunder Bay’s Provincial Offences Office.

“We did issue a summons for the owner to appear in court on the July 8 order, and a second summons will be forthcoming next week on the July 29 order,” said Mackie.

A justice of the peace will make a ruling and assign a fine if Masillamany is found guilty, he explained.

Masillamany is scheduled to appear in the Provincial Offences Court by video conference on Nov. 25.

Vickers Manor in Thunder Bay, Ont. The six-storey building at 325 Archibald St. S. on the city's south side includes 109 residential units and 10 commercial units. (Sarah Law/CBC)

CBC News reached out to the management of Vickers Manor by phone and email multiple times and did not receive a response.

Mackie said it’s “very rare” for the health unit to go through the courts to seek compliance.

“Unfortunately with this ownership, it's been very difficult because they're just not responding,” he said.

“I guess if I had any hope, it would be that maybe new ownership comes in, someone that's committed to providing a safe living environment for these tenants.”

MPP calls on province to investigate

A spokesperson for the City of Thunder Bay provided an emailed statement Friday, saying the Municipal Emergency Control Group is continuing to monitor the situation at Vickers Manor, in case service disruptions put tenants at risk.

It’s also engaging with community partners “ to help connect residents with available services and supports,” and is sharing information with tenants about alternative housing options in town.

Lise Vaugeois is NDP MPP of Thunder Bay—Superior North. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

Thunder Bay—Superior North NDP MPP Lise Vaugeois says conditions at Vickers Manor are unacceptable. She wrote a letter to Ontario's Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack on Aug. 4 and says she hasn’t heard back from him.

Among other things, she’s advocating for Ontario’s Rental Housing Enforcement Unit to investigate the owner’s compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act.

“They ought to be there seeing what's going on and putting the squeeze on the owners to fulfil their obligations,” Vaugeois said.

“Now, does that put people at more risk of being pushed out if they start getting more fines? You know, that's a strategic question that has to be asked, but those authorities need to be there.”

CBC News has reached out to Flack’s office and is awaiting a reply. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Thunder Bay—Atikokan PC MPP Kevin Holland says his office is drafting a response.

Vaugeois said she also wants the province to “ensure that no resident is displaced without an individualized and properly funded plan providing appropriate, accessible and affordable housing.”

‘We don't wanna go anywhere’

Sharon Zoschke moved to Thunder Bay from Ottawa four years ago and quickly became enamoured with the city’s south side, known as Fort William.

“I would see Mount McKay and it was calling me home and I just loved it,” she said.

Sharon Zoschke, a resident at Vickers Manor in Thunder Bay, Ont., says she wants to keep living at the building because of the strong sense of community there. She says she has also grown fond of the Fort William neighbourhood and its rich history. (Sarah Law/CBC)

She’s lived at Vickers Manor for 16 months. Earlier this summer temperatures in her unit reached 32 C, she said, adding that she does not have a window that opens.

Still, she loves the building and learning about its history, being the former McKellar General Hospital, and has made many friends there.

“Having faith really matters, even when things look bleak” - Sharon Zoschke, resident at Vickers Manor

That sense of community has kept her in place, despite the fact that many tenants have left over fears of eviction or utility disconnections.

“We don't wanna go anywhere. We're hoping it'll all work out,” she said.

She said she wants more information provided to tenants about service changes and the building’s potential sale.

“I think if we had been kept informed, fewer people would have moved out,” Zoschke said.

In the meantime, Zoschke is keeping her spirits up, and said she wants the community to respect the tenants at Vickers Manor rather than pity them.

“Having faith really matters, even when things look bleak.”

World.title: Russian enriched uranium shipped to Canadian-owned Westinghouse in U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While Russian President Vladimir Putin’s military occupies Ukraine’s largest nuclear plant and attacks the country's power infrastructure, Europe and the United States still depend on Russian nuclear fuel to power their own electricity grids.

Canadian-owned Westinghouse Electric is among the companies that receive l ow enriched uranium (LEU) from Russia to fuel commercial nuclear reactors in the U.S., shipping data analyzed by CBC’s the fifth estate shows.

The U.S. banned the import of Russian enriched uranium in August 2024 in order “to sever U.S. dependence on Russian material and secure a strong domestic fuel supply,” according to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE).

But the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act allows the DOE to waive the ban if “no alternative viable source of LEU is available” or the “import of the LEU is in the national interest.”

The waivers are scheduled to end by Jan. 1, 2028.

The Bellona Environmental Transparency Center in Vilnius, Lithuania, reported in June that the U.S. imported 400 tonnes of low enriched uranium from Russia in 2025 alone worth around $1 billion US, and that the major recipients included subsidiaries of the French-owned nuclear company Framatome (more than 127 tonnes), U.S. nuclear fuel supplier Global Nuclear Fuel Americas (more than 110 tonnes) and Westinghouse (around 27 tonnes).

Gas centrifuges at a uranium enrichment plant in Seversk, Russia, in December 2025. (Rosatom)

The European Union has no ban on the import of Russian enriched uranium and Canada has not sanctioned doing business with Russia’s state atomiс energy corporation Rosatom or its export arm, Tenex.

“We are against these exports while there is this situation of war [and a] direct threat to Ukraine,” said Dmitry Gorchakov, nuclear adviser at Bellona and co-author of the June report on Russia’s nuclear industry and the war in Ukraine.

“All countries should try to lower their dependence on Russia and cancel all possible co-operation.”

The fifth estate analyzed shipping data between Westinghouse and Tenex from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, collected by the commercial search engine ImportYeti. Over the four-year period of the war in Ukraine, Moscow-based Tenex exported various amounts of uranium from Russia to the address of Westinghouse’s sprawling fuel fabrication plant outside Columbia, S.C.

In one shipment in March of this year, Tenex reportedly delivered 50,612 kilograms of uranium to Westinghouse in four containers, departing Russia from the port of St. Petersburg and arriving in the U.S. at the port of Baltimore.

Enriched uranium shipped to Westinghouse’s South Carolina facility is processed into fuel pellets and then put into fuel rod assemblies that are sent to commercial nuclear power reactors.

“The way that it works is that usually a utility purchases uranium from a source and then the uranium is transported,” said Curtis Roberts, vice-president of communications at Orano USA, a subsidiary of the French nuclear fuel provider that also manages shipment of uranium to the U.S.

“The customer, the utility, is the one then who has a contract with the fuel fabricator. They purchase their uranium, their uranium is transferred to the fuel fabricator, the fuel fabricator then turns it into whatever fuel form is requested by the customer. And then the customer receives the fuel assembly to put into their reactor.”

Westinghouse Electric is 51 per cent owned by Brookfield Renewable Partners, a subsidiary of the Toronto-based investment management firm Brookfield Corporation. The other 49 per cent of Westinghouse is held by Saskatchewan-based Cameco Corporation, one of the world’s largest uranium miners and nuclear fuel suppliers.

Westinghouse and Brookfield did not respond to questions for this story.

Canadian nuclear reactors, like those at the Bruce Nuclear Generating Station on Lake Huron, do not require enriched uranium for fuel. (Bruce Power)

U.S. lobbyist disclosures show that Cameco reported lobbying on the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act in Washington earlier this year, but in responding to emails from the fifth estate the company did not say why. Cameco said it “doesn't handle enriched uranium” and directed us to speak to individual U.S. utilities.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration, a government agency within the DOE, does not publish the total amount of uranium purchased from Russia, citing “data protections designed for privacy” in an email to the fifth estate. But the administration's latest uranium marketing annual report on July 29 did report that in 2025, Russia was the largest foreign provider to the U.S. of uranium enrichment services.

“It is a way for Russia and Rosatom and for Russian propaganda to say that you are dependent on us, that you can't do anything without us,” said Gorchakov. “It's important for them to be the supplier of the United States — it's good money for them.”

Decades-long dependence

The U.S. and Europe have had a decades-long dependence on Russian enriched uranium that Western governments and industry are trying to replace by ramping up domestic production.

Russia supplies approximately 44 per cent of global enriched uranium and 20 to 30 per cent of enriched uranium used in the U.S. and Europe, according to a U.S. Department of Energy estimate from November 2025.

Russia has “been the major supplier of low-enriched uranium for many years and it takes a long time to make changes in the global infrastructure,” said Jeremy Whitlock, a Canadian nuclear scientist and adjunct professor at McMaster University in Hamilton.

Whitlock, who is also a nuclear safety consultant, said there can be an intent to make such a change, but if it’s a commodity that’s “desperately needed,” accommodations are required.

“You have simultaneously the intent to build up infrastructure elsewhere and domestic infrastructure or other suppliers while having to maintain the connection to the Russian supply in the meantime.”

Westinghouse is a major player in the U.S. nuclear industry. Brookfield Corporation CEO Bruce Flatt attended a ceremony last October in Tokyo, where he posed with U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who announced that Westinghouse was going to “invest up to $100 billion in U.S. nuclear reactors to restore U.S. energy dominance.”

U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass, left, Brookfield CEO Bruce Flatt, U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at the U.S. ambassador's residence in Tokyo on Oct. 28, 2025. (Getty Images)

On its website last month, Westinghouse spotlighted a New York Times story that reported the company could also benefit from Trump’s recent announcement of a civil nuclear co-operation agreement with Saudi Arabia to build new reactors.

Although Cameco has two operating uranium mines in northern Saskatchewan, Canada doesn't need enrichment facilities because its 16 operating CANDU reactors (15 in Ontario and one in New Brunswick) are fuelled by natural uranium.

WATCH | Selling uranium to India: Sask. bags $2.6B uranium deal from India trade mission | Duration 1:59 Prime Minister Mark Carney's trade mission to India has produced a multi-billion-dollar deal for Saskatchewan-based mining company Cameco. The uranium giant is expected to sell $2.6 billion worth of uranium to India over nine years. The province says the deal is nearly 10 times larger than a previous deal signed in 2015.

But proposed new reactors, including small modular reactors being considered by several provinces, would require enriched uranium. In 2024, the federal government announced it intended to “backstop” up to $500 million in enriched nuclear fuel purchase contracts from allied countries.

While Canada has imposed Russian sanctions against 875 entities and 1,739 individuals, Global Affairs confirmed to the fifth estate that Rosatom and its export arm, Tenex, are not listed.

“The government of Canada has not imposed sanctions on the state atomiс energy corporation Rosatom or Techsnabexport (Tenex),” the federal department said in an email. “However, a number of subsidiaries and individuals related to Rosatom have been sanctioned.”

The European Union has imposed 21 packages of sanctions against Russia targeting nearly 3,000 individuals and entities, but the bloc of 27 countries has not banned the importation of Russian enriched uranium.

According to Bellona, EU countries imported 583.4 tonnes of enriched uranium from Russia worth 251.8 million euros ($407 million Cdn) in 2025.

The European Commission did not respond to emails from the fifth estate.

“Canada and its allies must do everything possible to prevent Western companies, including Canadian firms, from knowingly or otherwise engaging with Russian state nuclear entities,” said Marcus Kolga, a senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, an Ottawa-based think tank.

“Every dollar that flows into Rosatom or its subsidiaries risks strengthening a Russian state enterprise that is directly tied to Moscow’s war against Ukraine and its broader campaign of coercion,” said Kolga, who has advocated for tough sanctions against Russia.

Dan Lipman, Westinghouse president of energy systems, left; Aziz Dag, Westinghouse senior vice-president; German Galuschenko, Ukraine’s former minister of energy and Petro Kotin, former CEO of Energoatom, announce a fuel agreement in Italy in July 2025. (Westinghouse)

Supporting Ukraine

In its email to the fifth estate, Cameco also highlighted its support for Ukraine. The company signed a long-term agreement in 2023 with the state-owned nuclear energy company Energoatom to supply uranium hexafluoride, which is used to produce enriched uranium.

Westinghouse has also entered into agreements with Ukraine’s Energoatom to supply fuel and build new reactors, replacing Russia as the source of the country's nuclear fuel.

Following a corruption scandal allegedly involving kickbacks for contracts at Energoatom last year, former Westinghouse CEO Patrick Fragman and the former chief of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, Rumina Velshi, were appointed to Energoatom’s new supervisory board this past January.

World.title: '42-year-old Canadian musical cold case' may have Kitchener-Waterloo ties, say online sleuths
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than 40 years ago, someone recorded a song from the radio onto a cassette tape.

It wasn't an unusual thing to do in the 1980s, but all information related to the song is now gone, creating what online sleuths call a lostwave — a tune with no information attached to it. No one knows who sang it, where it was recorded or even its real title.

For now, it's known as CIA.

People online have been looking into its origin story for years, and that search has expanded to Waterloo region in southern Ontario, with some hoping people here may have answers.

Joe Gaschler is one of the moderators of a forum dedicated to searching for the information behind lostwave songs on the website Reddit.

"One of the key songs we've been trying to look into, it's something we've given a placeholder title CIA because that's one of the words in the song," he said.

"It's a 42-year-old Canadian musical cold case."

Gaschler said there are "literally thousands of people who've played some part to try to find out who on earth this band is" either by listening to the song to try to pick up on a clue or answering questions from the amateur musical detectives.

"There's quite a large online community now," he said.

Here's what they know:

The song was played on CFNY-FM, now known as 102.1 The Edge.

They believe it was recorded onto tape in the mid-1980s, perhaps specifically in 1984.

That's it. That's all they know.

Typical 1980s vibe

The song sounds typical of the mid-1980s, with a vibe that may remind listeners of bands like A Flock of Seagulls, Platinum Blonde, The Cure, The Romantics or Duran Duran.

Gaschler said "pretty much everyone in Toronto" with knowledge of the 1980s music scene has been asked about the song.

"The search has now moved on to possibly the Kitchener-Waterloo area," he said, with people believing the band is "possibly from somewhere a little bit outside of the Greater Toronto Area."

WATCH | Listen to the song CIA:

Mystery's gone on for years

The song was first uploaded to YouTube by user DJFormaldehyde on July 20, 2020, after it had been put on Reddit by a user named datafreq in February the same year.

In a post to Reddit in 2024, DJFormaldehyde detailed how they have talked to many people who worked at CFNY-FM and a number of musicians.

"I feel like we are still miles away from solving this," DJFormaldehyde wrote in that post.

One of the people DJFormaldehyde spoke to is Alan Cross, a longtime broadcaster, music writer and a former music director at CFNY-FM.

At first, Cross thought it could be a different song, a lostwave from the 1980s dubbed the most mysterious song on the internet. That song was identified in 2024 as Subways of Your Mind by the German band Fex.

WATCH | Subways of Your Mind was a lostwave identified in 2024:

Cross has posted about CIA to his own website, asking for people to help identify the song.

He told CBC News he's also talked to people who worked at the station at the time, including Liz Janick, who hosted the show Streets of Ontario, and Ivor Hamilton of The Original Import Show.

Neither has any knowledge of the track.

"There is no record of it anywhere. Trust me," Cross said, noting the radio station's archives are in his house.

"The people that would have most likely played it don't know anything about it. It could be that everything has been misremembered and the whole thing has taken on a life of its own."

The search continues

The people who are searching for the truth behind CIA have spent hundreds of hours chasing leads.

They're encouraged by other lostwave mysteries that have been solved, like Subways of Your Mind and a similar discovery in 2023 for How Long Will It Take, which Reddit users discovered was actually by Vancouver musician Paula Toledo.

The Reddit subforum includes people analyzing the vocals, which musical instruments were used, whether they can hear people talking on the track itself and asking questions about contests run at the time, including the Great Ontario Talent Search.

So far, nothing has helped them figure out who is singing or playing on the track.

'Interesting paradox' to the song

Kate Galloway is an assistant professor of popular music at Wilfrid Laurier University in Waterloo.

She said that with the "forensic listening" being done by fans of the song, it's unusual no information has turned up.

"[It's] this kind of interesting paradox of the internet because we're often hearing about how the internet makes music easier to distribute than ever, it's easier to make than ever, it's easier to identify than ever," she said.

"It actually can be surprisingly difficult sometimes to identify who created certain recordings depending on how they came to be online, but it is also very hard for musicians to remain permanently anonymous."

In today's world, people can ask their smart speakers to identify a song or use apps like Shazam to help track down who sang what.

Gaschler said if it was that easy, they wouldn't still be searching.

"You'll come up with people who've sampled the song, people have claimed the song, but you won't find the actual band behind the song."

Search for song's origin can create community

Galloway said some of the joy in the hunt for a lostwave artist is the community that forms online as people follow the breadcrumbs to, hopefully, reveal the musicians.

"There's definitely this kind of retro nostalgia to this type of case," she said.

"As long as it remains a mystery, that kind of social interaction is retained. And that's why a lot of communities of kind of popular music, forensic listening and forensic fandom are sustained and cherished by the communities.

"That kind of communal coming together online would be lost because they would have solved the mystery."

Alan Cross, Toronto broadcaster and music historian, says he's asked around about the song CIA and has written about it on his A Journal of Musical Things website, but hasn't had any luck figuring out who the band is behind the song. (Rachel Houlihan/CBC )

Cross said he's not sure if this musical mystery will ever be solved.

"In an era where everybody knows everything about everything, and information is just a couple of pokes away at your phone, it's kind of cool to have everything a little mysterious once in a while."

Asked if he would be OK never knowing the band behind CIA, Gaschler laughed.

"The mystery is just incredible," he said.

"The great thing about searching in this area of lostwave is when you come across a whole bunch of other obscure bands that probably never got the attention they deserve. And I've come across some amazing music. My playlist now has got a whole bunch of really obscure bands that are just fantastic. It's part of the joy of the search."

He said that ultimately, he wants the band to be revealed so it can understand just how many fans it has gained over the years.

"Whoever did this song did an amazing job. It's a great song. People love it. I think they deserve the attention that they'll get if we do finally find out who the band is," he said.

"Someone pressed record back in, we think, about 1984. They preserved what's a great song … and I think they really deserve the credit."

Do you have information about this song?

You can log onto the sub-Reddit CIAlostwave or email CBC K-W at yournewskw@cbc.ca with information.

World.title: Uncovered texts reveal alleged gun-for-hire network tied to attempted Project South hit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The alleged hit on a jail official that triggered the police corruption and organized crime case known as Project South was organized by suspects contracting out the job using aliases on an encrypted messaging platform, according to court documents.

Days before the alleged attempted murder, suspects are accused of using the Signal app to share personal information and photos about the target, a senior corrections officer at Toronto South Detention Centre whose identity is protected by a publication ban.

The allegations are contained in a factum filed by Crown prosecutors last month in Ontario Superior Court. Based on chats uncovered on seized cellphones, the document paints a picture of how an alleged gun-for-hire network is accused of being behind the alleged attempted murder.

The Project South investigation began in June 2025 after York Regional Police thwarted the alleged attempted hit after the suspect vehicle collided with a police car that was stationed outside the jail official's home.

Initially, nearly 30 people were charged in Project South including seven Toronto police officers and one retired constable. One of the officers, who has since retired, pleaded guilty last month and one civilian's charge was stayed .

'Need the hit squad'

On June 16, 2025, four days before police foiled the alleged attempted murder, Dequon Lemonious, who prosecutors allege went by "Danny Phantom" on Signal, told Median Jackson, who allegedly went by "Lebron James," that he needs someone to drive by an address and confirm whether a vehicle is there.

WATCH | Surveillance footage of alleged attempted hit: Surveillance footage captures alleged conspiracy to commit murder | Duration 0:22 Security footage released by York Regional Police on Thursday captures the moment an alleged conspiracy unfolded to murder a member of corrections management working at an Ontario detention centre. Police say a number of suspects attended the person’s home over a 36-hour period in York Region. UPDATE (Feb. 25, 2026): Some content has been blurred to remove potentially identifying information.

The factum states Lemonious then messaged Jackson a picture of the jail official's address and vehicle that came from a search of the Ministry of Transportation's (MTO) secure database, believed to have been unlawfully accessed by a Toronto police officer.

"If the car there need the hit squad," Lemonious wrote to Jackson, according to the record.

Amid planning the alleged hit on the jail official, prosecutors allege the two were discussing other "jobs."

According to the factum, Lemonious would provide information to Jackson who would subcontract the jobs to others to commit offences for money.

"They discussed recruiting other individuals, as well as the prices for each job and how the money would be split," the court record reads.

The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

Others also offered the job

Police recovered Signal messages from the cellphone of another person accused of conspiring to murder the jail guard just two days before police stopped the alleged planned hit.

Devonte Barker-Campbell, alleged to have gone by "Dwayne Casey," sent a message to a Signal user named "Thunder" that included a headshot of the jail official, a photo of a map showing his address and the same photo of the official's vehicle and home address from the same MTO search result, according to the court filing.

Thunder ultimately declined the job. Hours later, Barker-Campbell offered the same job to a different person going by "Reality" on Signal.

"Bro, everything ready. The Same Play, we can run that today. My Hitters Ready. When can we do this?" Reality wrote to Barker-Campbell two days before the alleged attempted hit, according to the court record.

Over the next 36 hours, the two arranged for a team of "hitters" to attend the jail official's home, according to the factum.

York Regional Police say the suspect vehicle rammed into a police cruiser that was stationed outside the jail official's home. (York Regional Police)

Reality's hitters had difficulties with what the factum describes as their stolen vehicle and sent a video of it to Barker-Campbell. Prosecutors allege it's the same blue Acura that was ultimately intercepted by police at the official's home during the takedown on June 20.

Inside the vehicle was Almar Heath, two young people who can't be identified, a loaded handgun, surgical masks and gloves, and Heath's phone, which was open to GPS directions to the corrections officer's home, according to the factum.

Heath, Jackson, Lemonious, Barker-Campbell and two youths are charged with conspiracy to murder the jail official. None of the allegations have been tested in court.

Lawyers for Health and Barker-Campbell declined to comment. Counsel for Jackson did not provide a comment after CBC News reached out to her office.

Lemonious is not currently represented by a lawyer. CBC News reached out to his previous lawyer, but did not receive a response.

Const. Timothy Barnhardt is accused of accessing and sharing confidential information about the senior corrections officer that was eventually provided to those charged in the alleged murder plot. (@10rcop/X)

While investigating the alleged murder plot, York police discovered Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt was allegedly the person who conducted the illegal search of the jail official's information on the MTO database.

Barnhardt's lawyer previously told CBC his legal team plans to defend him in court, not in the media.

Suspect vehicle cased home

The first time the blue Acura was seen near the corrections officer's home was two days before the takedown, according to the factum.

Just minutes after the jail official arrived home from work that evening, his grandfather opened the door to a masked male pointing a gun, demanding to know who owned a vehicle in the driveway.

The court filing says his grandfather managed to close the door and a group of suspects fled in the blue Acura, which police spotted near the home again around the same time the next evening.

The following day, the car once again went to the house, this time under police surveillance, which led to the early-morning takedown and arrests.

The factum also alleges a video of the same blue Acura was found on Jackson's phone in a conversation showing Jackson and Lemonious directing an unidentified person in relation to a shooting at a restaurant the week earlier.

The person sent a video of the blue Acura complaining something was wrong with it and so another vehicle was used in the restaurant shooting, according to the court filing.

World.title: Everything about WNBA star Caitlin Clark is outsized, from financial influence to impact on U.S. culture wars
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. If you wanted a moment that distilled Caitlin Clark’s current fame in the United States, you could not do better than a basketball practice last month during the WNBA’s All-Star weekend in Chicago. Clark is the most famous women’s basketball player in America — and often at the epicentre of debates about the positives and negatives of the league — and during a practice session for All-Star players on July 24 at the Obama Presidential Center, a familiar man approached the Indiana Fever point guard to offer some sage advice. The man’s name was Barack Obama — and a flurry of cameras allowed us to hear a conversation between the former U.S. president and the Fever point guard. "You're great. You're fantastic,” said Obama. “Don't let all this nonsense get you down. I always say one of the things that was luckiest for me was I didn't get famous 'til I was like 45. So I was an old-ass man. I mean, you're my daughter's age. They've not had that much immersion, nonsense. So don't lose that joy. The game's like the game. And you're a hooper.” “I try,” said Clark. “No, you’re always a hooper,” responded Obama. “And you're on a nice little run right now." Former President Obama to Caitlin Clark: “You’re great. You’re fantastic. Don’t let all this nonsense get you down” pic.twitter.com/KjbW5fuZMs —caitlinclarksty It was an outsized moment, but everything about Clark has been outsized since she entered the WNBA in 2024 — her fame, her otherworldly shooting from distance, her preternatural passing wizardly, her ability to draw television viewers, her being targeted by opposing players, her over-the-top reactions to foul calls, and her consistently being used as an avatar for others to express their politics including elected U.S. politicians. The noise, or nonsense as Obama described it, is never-ending. If you are not familiar with Caitlin Clark, this would be a good week to get acclimated. The 24-year-old makes her debut on Canadian soil Tuesday night against the struggling 10-23 Toronto Tempo at a nearly sold-out Scotiabank Arena. Why has Clark found such cultural relevancy in the U.S.? “First and most importantly, she plays a different style of basketball than any women's player before her,” said Rebecca Lobo, the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Famer who will call the game for U.S.-based ESPN. “We'd never seen anyone consistently take and make 30+ footers in the women's game. Like Steph Curry, she has unmatched range and starting in her college career had the freedom to take them consistently. Her passing is also unique and exciting. She makes people feel excited when watching her in a way that is different.” Clark signs autographs prior to a game in July. (Michael Reaves/Getty Image) Basketball beginnings Clark was a top high school prospect out of West Des Moines, Iowa who drew attention from most major U.S. college programs before choosing the University of Iowa. As a junior at Iowa in 2023, she led her school to its first NCAA women's basketball championship game. Though Iowa lost in a now-famous title game against Angel Reese’s LSU team, Clark’s play attracted significant interest from those who had never watched women’s basketball before. The title game averaged 9.9 million television viewers , shattering the old record by nearly two million viewers. Clark’s fame truly exploded the following year. With cameras and reporters following her every move, she once again led Iowa to the national championship game. While she did not get her storybook ending, women’s college basketball did when the viewership figures came in. South Carolina’s win over Iowa in the 2024 NCAA women’s basketball final was seen by an astonishing 18.9 million viewers in the U.S. and peaked at 24.1 million viewers. Clark finished her college career as the NCAA’s all-time leading scorer and was drafted by the Fever with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2024 WNBA draft, winning Rookie of the Year in her debut pro season. She has battled injuries over the last two seasons — including missing 28 games last year– but looks healthy at the moment, averaging 22 points and 8.3 assists per game for the 23-12 Fever. This season she became the fastest player in WNBA history to reach 1,500 points and 500 assists. Probably the biggest criticism of her game focuses on her on-court comportment and interaction with officials. But to be fair to Clark, WNBA officiating has needed an upgrade for years. “She's a top-five player in the game, and still has plenty of room to grow,” Lobo said. “She is more comfortable driving into the lane and initiating contact and also more comfortable getting to her midrange game. She is also an improved defender, although she can still have lapses occasionally on that end.” Clark with NBA commissioner Adam Silver at the 2025 NBA Finals. (Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) Business impact No singular player has impacted the economics of the WNBA more than Clark. Sportico reported that the 13 WNBA franchises that competed in 2025 are worth an estimated $427 million (all figures US) on average. That’s up 59 per cent over 2024 and 180 per cent over 2023. The expansion fees for the next three franchises to enter the league — Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia — went for $250 million in 2025. Just a year previous, the Tempo paid a $50-million franchise fee — now a relative bargain. The WNBA’s record-setting media deals — totalling $3.1 billion over 11 years — have all occurred over the last three years, matching the Clark era. The league has U.S. media partnerships with Amazon’s Prime Video, Disney’s ABC/ESPN, NBCUniversal’s NBC and Peacock, Paramount’s CBS, Scripps’s ION, USA Sports’ USA Network, and NBA TV while TSN owns the rights in Canada. All 44 games of the Fever’s games this season are nationally televised in the U.S. which makes everything Clark and her teammates akin to the NFL’s Dallas Cowboys. Per Sports Media Watch: WNBA regular season games were averaging 756,000 viewers through Aug 5, up 15 per cent over last year. The league had 29 games averaging over one million viewers prior to the All-Star break, setting a new record. The eight most-watched WNBA games this season all involve the Fever, including the most-watched game, a July 12th contest between the Las Vegas Aces and Fever that drew 2.64 million viewers on NBC and Peacock in primetime. While Clark is not the best player in the WNBA — that title belongs to Aces centre and four-time MVP A’Ja Wilson — she is a legitimate All-WNBA player and the league’s most recognizable face. To not recognize her staggering economic impact is to not deal in reality. Caitlin Clark on Alyssa Thomas punching her in the throat:

"It seems like there's always a moment like that in every season that I've played so far. It gets exhausting. It gets frustrating... It was a hard foul and it should have been dealt with in the moment and they should… —BrickCenter_ Clark as a political avatar You cannot escape politics in the United States during the Trump Era and Clark has found herself thrust into the endless culture wars. She is an avatar for political motivations far beyond her control and typing her name into a social media outlet often leads to a soufflé of misogyny, racism, toxicity, and homophobia. In July, a group of 11 Republican lawmakers wrote a letter to WNBA commissioner Cathy Englebert saying they were concerned by reports that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated" following Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas receiving a one-game suspension after she made contact with her fist to Clark's throat in a matchup against Indiana. (Thomas and her family received racist abuse and death threats after the incident.) It’s important to note Clark herself is far from a polarizing personality. Quite the opposite, in fact. She generally puts on a clinic when it comes to how to perform in the public sphere and has repeatedly called out harassment and hate of WNBA players. She owes no one a public dissertation of her politics, yet she continually faces criticism from disparate ideologies who want her to be more vociferous on issues they care about. One of women’s basketball most prominent figures — the 12-time NCAA champion UConn coach Geno Auriemma — recently highlighted Clark being used as a vessel in America’s culture wars. "Because the bandwagon and the fandom became so obsessed with the whole thing, it turned into a cause," Auriemma said. "She became the reason why white players get beat up in the WNBA and she became the reason why Black players don't get the endorsements and don't get the adulation that white players get. ... So instead of it becoming Caitlin Clark gets fouled hard … no sh**, every first-round draft pick gets fouled hard. Not every foul is a good foul. Not every foul is a bad foul but there are fouls that are flagrant. But that's all they are. They are not a referendum on America, which is what the whole goddamn thing has become." “She's never said or done anything controversial, yet some people like to project their agendas onto her,” Lobo added. “ It's been an unfair burden dumped onto her — she just wants to hoop.” Clark pursues Toronto Tempo's Tima Pouye during their meeting June 16 in Indiana. The Fever won that game, 113-91. (Andy Lyons/Getty Images) Welcome to Toronto In a season that has gone south record-wise since Tempo star guard Brittney Sykes suffered a left plantar fascia non-contact injury in a June 16 loss to the Fever in Indianapolis, Clark playing in Toronto is one of the remaining highlights of the season for Tempo fans. Even with a losing record, the in-game atmosphere has been fantastic and the franchise is in a strong position having smartly positioned themselves as Canada’s team rather than a Toronto team. Lisa Ferkul, the Tempo’s chief revenue officer, said the goal of the franchise was to be at the top of the WNBA among revenue generation, and the franchise is tracking as one of the highest partnership-revenue-generating teams in the league in its first season. The Tempo opened the season with 17 inaugural sponsors, including Sephora and CIBC, and new partnerships including SiriusXM, Destination Toronto, Lucille’s and MoveU were added as part of the Cross Canada Series (games played in Montreal and Vancouver). “A few of my former UCLA teammates said Toronto is one of their favourite cities they've come to so far,” said Tempo rookie Kiki Rice, the team’s first-round pick in its inaugural draft. “People like coming here. It's obviously a beautiful place, a lot going on. We have great fans, a great atmosphere, a great arena, and that’s really a special thing regardless of the outcome of the game.” When Wilson played in Toronto on July 20, she was struck by how many people were wearing her sneakers and jersey.
