Stopping the pillage of Mexican art and culture

Of course, the nationalization of the Gelman Collection would cause entrepreneurs, art dealers and speculators at firms like Sotheby’s to raise their eyebrows, fearing a market disruption that would jeopardize their secretive business model. But this also presents a reward: an opportunity for Mexico to legitimize its stewardship of culture and send the right signals abroad to put a stop to all forms of pillage, however sophisticated they may be.

No, the history of nationalizations is not a pretty one, whether in Mexico, Venezuela, Iran or Russia. It is always concerning when leaders — vested with power and the national flag — decide that they know better than the market. Yet, there is a right moment for it. Like now.

To President Sheinbaum:

On the day you took office, you paid tribute to Frida Kahlo before your 125 million fellow citizens. Those words will ring hollow if you allow her works to be more acclaimed by others abroad than by those at home.

More recently, in Barcelona — during the so-called “Summit of Progressive Leaders” organized by the Spanish government — you stated: “I come here to acknowledge the courage of Frida Kahlo, who, even amidst physical frailty, knew how to fill the struggle for justice with color.”

It is a time for justice, not for patriotic narratives.

You may, in good faith, accept the Banco Santander Foundation’s plans to return the collection within two years. Yet let us not forget that the art world is rife with unfulfilled guarantees and broken promises. The Banco Santander Foundation assures us that any damage or degradation will be minimal; however, those within the art world know that the deterioration of quality is as certain as the law of gravity. Published financial documents suggest that Banco Santander may hold a lien on a loan that enabled the Zambrano family to acquire the collection. What happens if the Zambrano family defaults? The Spanish bank becomes the owner.

What real guarantee is there that the Gelman Collection will return? Are we to take the word of the very same people, citizens and public servants alike, who have blocked us and denied us information for at least 18 years?

Precedents for action

Use the precedent of the private Remedios Varo collection — safeguarded by the INBAL since it was donated in 2002 by a foreign couple — as a basis to affirm that your administration protects our cultural heritage and historical monuments for the benefit of the people.

Leadership entails persuading, enticing, intimidating, pressuring and appealing to every type of personality under the sun. Nationalizing this collection need not be an adversarial process. Through just a few meetings — and by leveraging your authority — you could swiftly ensure that this works for all the stakeholders involved.

No matter how one views it, the ownership of the Gelman Collection remains murky. You must declare that no private interest stands above the interest of the Nation. Tell us all, right now, that reclaiming these works is genuinely “what the People demand.”

Keith Rosenblum and Jesús Ibarra are contributors to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: El Jalapeño: FIFA allowed Mexico to host 2026 World Cup matches in exchange for Estadio Azteca’s entire revenue stream
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Representatives from world soccer’s governing body FIFA reassured Mexican fans and corporate investors this week that the 2026 World Cup was a deeply collaborative partnership, shortly after finalized financial terms confirmed that host venues were permitted to keep up to 100% of all unpaid operational cleanup costs.

The announcement comes on the heels of financial filings from Grupo Ollamani, owner of the iconic Estadio Azteca, which reported a net loss of 557.2 million pesos (US $32.2 million) during the second quarter, and a US $47 million loss on the World Cup in total. According to internal documents, the losses were directly linked to “standard tournament hosting compliance,” a procedural category that includes retrofitting stadium suites to FIFA specifications and legally surrendering the venue’s real estate and naming rights until mid-2027.

“We were immensely proud to bring the spirit of global football back to Mexico City,” said FIFA Deputy Chief of Global Commercial Extraction Eric Van Houten, speaking to local reporters. “In exchange for providing the sacred privilege of hosting five matches, FIFA asked for very little: total concessions revenue, local tax exemptions, zero corporate liability and temporary power of attorney over the municipal water grid during match days.”

When queried if local venue operators might reasonably expect to break even on their multi-million dollar capital investments, Van Houten expressed visible confusion. “Break even? The stadium received global exposure,” he noted. “When three billion people tuned in to watch a group stage match, they saw an exquisite facility that was entirely renovated to FIFA specifications. That kind of promotional opportunity is simply priceless … unless of course you’re the one paying for it. Then there is definitely a price.”

Local stadium management confirmed that while financial projections remain temporarily negative, internal morale remains high following FIFA’s official confirmation that venue employees will be permitted to keep all uncollected trash left in the upper concourses after each match.

“This is an unprecedented business model, but we are learning to appreciate the efficiency of it,” said an anonymous financial analyst familiar with the venue’s operations. “Usually, a corporate takeover takes months of hostile negotiations. FIFA managed to convince a major media holding company to pay US $47 million for the privilege of letting strangers redecorate their house and take all the furniture when they left. It is truly a lesson in how modern sports management works.”

World.title: Mexican soccer league ends promotion and relegation, sparking protests
World.content:
During the opening kickoff of the Expansión MX season, several teams decided not to play for the first minute of the game. Players passed the ball back and forth while opposing teams stood still. In one of the matches, a referee pleaded with players to resume play, to no avail.

The players, in effect, were protesting a change to the rules that have governed the Liga MX system for more than seven decades — a change they say permanently alters the spirit of the game.

The end of promotion and relegation

The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) announced July 16 that it is doing away with promotion and relegation, known in Mexico as “ascenso y descenso.”

Essentially, the promotion and relegation system paved the way for lesser-known teams from Mexico’s second-tier league, Expansión MX, to move up to Liga MX, creating a pipeline where more players could perform under a bigger and brighter spotlight.

Now, however, Liga MX teams are set in stone, diminishing the tension that came with relegation.

‘Mourning’ the loss of promotion

The news did not sit well with players or fans.

Following the Expansión MX protest on the pitch, the FMF and the Comisión Disciplinaria (Disciplinary Commission) threatened to fine teams more than US $11,000 for any further disruptions.

In response, players have been covering their mouths during team photos, signaling that they will not be silenced. Atlético Morelia went a step further, asking fans to wear black to games as a symbolic gesture mourning the loss of possible promotion.

The controversy came to a head when, during his latest public appearance for the Concacaf U-20 final, FMF President Mikel Arriola was met with boos from the stands as chants of “ascenso” echoed throughout the stadium.

The end of a 75-year-old tradition

While promotion and relegation existed in the broader Mexican soccer system since the early 1930s, it was not until 1950 that a “Second Division” was created and “Liga Mayor” became “Primera,” or “First Division.” With that, a new rule was instituted allowing one team to be promoted to the top league. One team was also relegated to the lower league each year.

The change was a response to the growing popularity of the sport and more teams joining the fold, fostering a more competitive structure and opening a pathway for additional cities across the country to reach the primetime that is Liga MX.

The system held for the next seven decades.

But in April 2020, promotion and relegation were paused for Liga MX over ongoing financial issues that were expected to compound due to the Coronavirus pandemic. At the time, then-Liga MX President Enrique Bonilla said, “Given that the financial crisis expanded the problems for the division, several current projects (clubs) are close to bankruptcy and in danger of disappearing.”

The pause was only supposed to last six seasons, a decision supported by FIFA, which urged Liga MX to bring back the system. In a 2020 interview, then-FMF President Yon de Luisa said, “The comment that FIFA made to us is that promotion and relegation has to return.”

A permanent ‘pause’

With FIFA applying this sort of pressure, it was assumed that the pause would be temporary. However, several decisions made in the intervening years suggested that the league had other plans in mind.

In February 2022, Liga MX released a statement detailing six certification requirements Expansión MX teams needed to meet before they could be promoted to Liga MX. That included new infrastructure and stadium standards, such as field of play, lighting, suites, dressing rooms and security. For many of the teams, the requirements were simply cost-prohibitive.

In response, nine Expansión MX teams released a statement in July 2022, arguing that “the ‘certification to ascend’ is nothing more than a legal simulation to disguise that there is no real commitment to return the promotion and relegation.”

An arbitration battle is lost

In their letter, the clubs stated that they took up their cause with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) because they are “tired of how Mexican football is managed.” They accused the league’s front office of turning the sport into a “business that favors only Liga MX clubs to the detriment of the entire national football ecosystem and where financial profits seem to carry more weight than passion for the sport.”

“The so-called certification process is not a quality filter,” the clubs added. “It is a padlock designed so that promotion to the First Division never opens.”

Another nail in the coffin came in September 2025, when the CAS handed down a ruling that denied the system’s return a year early.

In its ruling, the CAS noted that “after examining the evidence, the CAS Panel concluded that the FMF had always determined to suspend the system until the conclusion of the 2025-2026 season, which was made clear to the clubs when the decision was taken.”

It was a shock to those who expected Liga MX to return to the model that had been in place since the creation of the Segunda División (Second Division) during the 1950-1951 season.

What does the end of promotion and relegation mean for the sport?

Under the previous system, the bottom three teams in Liga MX would face fines upwards of US $4 million for ranking last. That money would then be funneled down to the Expansión MX league. Under the new system, those fines are no longer applicable, leaving Expansión MX teams with even fewer resources.

The new model more closely follows Major League Soccer in the United States, which focuses on commercial investments. “We proved that we can build the most valuable commercial market in the world (for soccer),” MLS Commissioner Don Garber said in a July interview with Front Office Sports.

In the wake of the 2026 World Cup, this money-driven model caused controversy after FIFA President Gianni Infantino proposed a US $20 billion plan to sell the tournament’s commercial rights to private equity investors.

Infantino was forced to scrap the plan after all 55 member associations of UEFA (Union of European Football Associations) threatened to boycott the 2030 World Cup, while all 41 member associations of Concacaf (Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football) unanimously rejected the idea.

On a global scale, getting rid of the promotion and relegation model deviates from soccer tradition and culture, as the English Premier League, Spanish La Liga, German Bundesliga, Italian Serie A and the French Ligue 1 all use it.

‘Many fans have stopped believing’

The cloud currently hanging over Liga MX is a stark contrast to the 2026 World Cup, which saw the national Mexican team, El Tri, bring hope and optimism to the country at large.

Despite those hopes being dashed during a round of 16 defeat to England, Mexico had regained worldwide respect both on and off the pitch, as well as the faith of its loyal fanbase.

However, following the recent developments for Liga MX, that faith is now slowly fading away.

Mexican footballer Diego de Buen Juárez posted a statement to his X account highlighting some of the frustrations with the league’s decision.

“Without the chance to compete for a genuine sporting objective, many fans have stopped believing,” the statement reads. “And when that sense of hope vanishes, the bond connecting a city to its team is broken as well.”

Jesse Foley-Tapia is a writer and photographer living in the Yucatán Peninsula, where he has dedicated his time and energy to shedding light on issues affecting Indigenous communities. His biggest journalistic accomplishment is interviewing Kendrick Lamar in 2010. His work has appeared in The Sun Magazine and BreakThrough News.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Mexico’s biodiversity and honey production
World.content:
Mexico ranks fourth among the world’s most biodiverse countries, hosting more than 10% of the world’s known species on just 1.5% of the planet’s territory. Due to its abundant biodiversity, Mexico is also considered one of the world’s bee diversity hotspots, with nearly 2,000 bee species found in the country.

In this week’s “Mexico in Numbers,” we’ll explore Mexico’s biodiversity and its importance as an apicultural hub and global honey exporter.

Mexico’s forests and bee habitats

A whopping 72.6% of Mexico’s surface is covered by plant life. Within this, the country has around 138 million hectares of forest ecosystems. Of these forest ecosystems, 40.5% are xerophytic scrub, or low-thorn forests found in arid and semi-arid areas capable of withstanding long periods of drought and extreme sun. Coahuila state, located in northern Mexico, boasts the highest abundance of xerophytic scrub.

Roughly a quarter of forest ecosystems are temperate forests, characterized by the dominance of broadleaf trees often found in mountainous regions such as Chihuahua and Durango. Of Durango’s total surface area of 9.1 million hectares, 4.98 million hectares are considered forest, making it Mexico’s top forestry state.

Rainforests make up 21.9% of the country’s forest ecosystems. Part of the rainforest is the dry tropics, which lie below 4,600 feet above sea level and present well-defined dry seasons, or semi-evergreen tropical forests with shorter dry seasons, as in Quintana Roo and Yucatán, and the humid tropical forests that have consistent yearly rainfall and are most abundant in Chiapas.

Mangroves cover 0.7% of Mexico’s forest ecosystems and are present in coastal regions such as the Mexican South Pacific coast and along the Baja California Peninsula. Oaxaca is the state that holds the most categories of forest ecosystems. (11.8% of the remaining ecosystems can be considered as “others.”)

Impact of pollination on food crops

According to a study on global patterns and drivers of bee distribution, xeric areas with arid and semi-arid climates are particularly rich in bee species. It is no surprise that Mexico, with its abundance of xerophytic scrub, is considered such a suitable habitat for bees, with an estimated 1,800 to 2,000 bee species represented, some of them stingless, such as the melipona bee.

Bees provide important ecosystem services because they are key pollinators. The global contribution of pollination services to food crops is estimated at between US $235 billion and US $577 billion annually, with the honeybee serving as the most important managed pollinator. In North America alone, honeybees pollinate more than 100 commercial crops, such as apples, almonds and pumpkins.

Across Mexico — especially in Sinaloa, Chihuahua and Coahuila — honeybees are used for pollination services. In those states, 140,000 beehives are utilized for crop pollination.

In 2025, Mexico had a record year for honey production, with 60,297 tons of honey produced, a 5% increase from the previous year. Yucatán is Mexico’s top producer of honey, followed by Chiapas and Jalisco.

Mesquite honey and other regional varieties

According to the Secretariat of Agriculture and Rural Development, the northern region of Mexico is the top producer of mesquite honey, foraged from the mesquite tree, part of the thorn forest, which has adapted to harsh climates and periods of drought through a deep root system. Mesquite honey is a light-colored, sometimes white honey with mild and smoky notes and rapid crystallization. The northern region produces around 7.4% of national honey production.

The Gulf Coast region of Mexico is especially known for its orange blossom honey, foraged from citrus plantations, with an acidic and tangy taste. Nine percent of all honey is harvested there.

The Pacific Coast region of Mexico produces 21.4% of all honey, with mangrove honey being a specialty due to its sweet and briny notes.

The Mexican Plateau region contributes 29.8% to national honey production, and the Yucatán Peninsula region is Mexico’s top honey producer, responsible for 32.4% of all honey production. The dzidzilché honey, a product of the native Mesoamerican Gymnopodium floribundum tree, is foraged not only by honeybees but also by the stingless melipona bee. It is an emblematic honey of the Yucatán region and, with its amber color and floral and caramel flavor profile, a sought-after delicacy worldwide.

Supporting local beekeepers

Over 47,000 beekeepers work in Mexico, of whom 2,322 are certified organic producers.

Mexico ranks ninth among the world’s honey exporters, with Germany being one of its top buyers. Out of every 10 kilograms of honey consumed in Germany, between 7 and 8 kilograms are of Mexican origin. In Germany, per-capita consumption of honey is around 2 kilograms per year. In Mexico, average per-capita consumption lies around 200 grams per year.

Mexico is not only rich in biodiversity but also rich in honey varieties and flavors. By consuming local honey, consumers can support local beekeepers who look after the health of beehives, which in turn play a significant role in biodiversity.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Disaster diplomacy and a persistent peso
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the weekend before this week began in Puebla, kicking off the 2026 National Reforestation Day from the mountain pass between the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes. There, marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, she declared that the Paso de Cortés — named for the conquistador who marched through it in 1519 — would be a great candidate for a new name.

On Monday morning, the president’s attention had shifted south: a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing hundreds. Sheinbaum immediately pledged Mexico would send Colombia everything it needed, but the country’s military rescue brigade quickly ran into a diplomatic hurdle, part of a tangle of certification disputes and friction that unfolded even as quietly extraordinary Mexican solidarity continued — not just with Colombia, but with wildfire-stricken Canada as well. Colombia’s quake also revived an old question for Mexico, one we explore in more depth here: with Venezuela and now Colombia both rattled by major temblors this year, does Mexico’s own position on the Pacific Ring of Fire mean its odds just went up?

Otherwise, the week of Aug. 10-14 in Mexico brought big economic headlines, athletic glory and advances in the Ayotzinapa criminal case.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico extends a hand abroad

Mexico’s instinct to help its neighbors was on full display this week. More than 300 Mexican firefighters traveled to British Columbia to help battle over 100 active wildfires that have forced tens of thousands to evacuate, drawing an outpouring of gratitude on Canadian social media. Farther south, a 45-member team of Mexico’s famed “Topos” rescue brigade reached Cali, Colombia, on Wednesday to dig through earthquake rubble — but only after Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella initially rejected their help, citing sovereignty concerns.

On Thursday, Sheinbaum confirmed that an official Mexican Army rescue brigade had not been authorized to enter Colombia and therefore remained at home. According to the president, Colombia’s new government demanded a type of certification the Mexican team does not have. Mexico kept sending humanitarian aid regardless — more than 58 tonnes of food, water and medicine by week’s end.

Ex-governor bound over in Ayotzinapa case

In one of the week’s most significant justice developments, former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre was ordered to stand trial over his alleged role in the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students. Prosecutors allege Aguirre ordered the destruction of security footage from Iguala’s Palace of Justice on the night the students vanished, partly to protect a nephew with ties to a local criminal gang. Aguirre, who resigned as governor weeks after the disappearances, remains jailed at the Altiplano maximum-security prison as the case — one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved human rights tragedies — grinds toward trial nearly 12 years later.

The super peso returns

Mexico’s currency briefly broke back below 17 to the US dollar on Friday morning for the first time since 2024, in what analysts are calling the return of the “super peso.”

The peso has now strengthened for four consecutive days and appreciated more than 5% this year, a move Citibanamex attributes largely to global dollar weakness rather than Mexican fundamentals. Still, by the MND Peso Index™, which compares a basket of goods in Mexico and Dallas, the currency looks overvalued by 2.4% — a smaller gap than June’s 2.9%, suggesting the exchange rate isn’t too far removed from what prices on the ground would imply.

Homicides fall, but Sinaloa gets reinforcements

Security officials reported on Wednesday that the daily homicide average has fallen 51% since Sheinbaum took office, with July recording the lowest monthly tally of her administration so far. Even so, nearly half of the country’s murders remain concentrated in just seven states, Sinaloa among them. That reality was underscored by the Navy’s deployment of over 1,700 personnel to Mazatlán after the port city logged its bloodiest month of the year in July, as fighting between rival Sinaloa Cartel factions Los Chapitos and Los Mayos continues to spill beyond Culiacán into the tourist-heavy coastal city.

Visa fights spill into the mañanera

Washington’s campaign against Mexican political figures widened this week.

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador and a former Morena party organization secretary, said the United States had revoked his visa, accusing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his deputy of a politically motivated move. At Friday’s mañanera, Sheinbaum called the decision “essentially political in nature,” urging Washington to produce evidence against anyone it targets while insisting the dispute won’t spiral into a broader conflict with the United States.

Business indicators to know

Peso: Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued.

Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued. Inflation: July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.”

July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.” Jobs: Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high.

Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high. Industry: Industrial activity grew 0.2% month-on-month in June, lifted by mining and construction, while manufacturing logged its 12th straight month of annual decline.

Cyclospora cleared in the Riviera Maya

After British health authorities flagged a spike in cyclosporiasis cases among travelers returning from Mexico, Cofepris tested food and water samples from 16 Riviera Maya hotels — and found no trace of the parasite. All 43 samples, drawn from Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Isla Mujeres, tested negative, and no contamination indicators turned up elsewhere. Mexico’s Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cyclosporiasis cases nationwide this year, a tiny fraction of the population, though the source of the UK cases remains unidentified.

Tourism notes

June brought 4.11 million international tourists to Mexico, up just 1.1% year-on-year — a muted bump given that Mexico hosted 12 of its 13 World Cup matches that month.

Tulum’s airport will regain five international routes this winter to cities in Canada and the United States, part of a state push to reverse a steep decline in international traffic.

Sargassum accumulation, though still tracking toward the second-heaviest year on record, has begun easing across most monitored stretches of the Quintana Roo coast as collection efforts and shifting currents bring relative relief to hard-hit beaches like Tulum and Playa del Carmen.

Mexican athletes seize the moment

It was a banner week for Mexican sport. The under-20 men’s soccer team defended its Concacaf title, beating the United States 2-0 at Mexico City’s Estadio Banorte for a record 15th championship, with defender Cristóbal Alfaro scoring twice.

Meanwhile, Mexico delivered its best-ever medal haul at the Central American and Caribbean Games, where the delegation topped the table with a record 407 medals in Santo Domingo. The government announced every medal — not just an athlete’s best result — will now earn a cash prize, a change Conade chief Rommel Pacheco said was Sheinbaum’s own idea.

World.title: How fragile is Chacahua’s lagoon ecosystem? A conversation with locals on the Oaxaca coast
World.content:
A bus from Puerto Escondido. A minibus, aka colectivo, from Rio Grande. Then a lancha, or small boat, across the water to Zapotalito. One more open-air truck and you’ve made it.

Laguna de Chacahua sits along the western coast of Oaxaca, part of the state’s more than 300 milePacific coastline – a lagoon ecosystem padded with jungle flora, where the network of mangroves roots the island in its gurgling brackish tides.

It is part of the municipality of Villa de Tututepec de Melchor Ocampo and around 100 miles down the coast from the popular beach city of Puerto Escondido. In the daytime, the high sun smelts the soft sand and rocks while hammocks loll idly in the low breeze. After sunset, bioluminescent plankton set the water aglow in a neon blue glacé.

Technically, Chacahua is a barrier island, meaning it is not entirely separate from the mainland but is only accessible by boat. The community is predominantly Black and Afro-Indigenous, partially linking back to the Spanish enslavement of Africans and their forced labor in Mexico in the 16th and 17th centuries. But many residents make their way over from the mainland to surf, fish and enjoy the more relaxed pulse of daily life.

“Here, you can be whatever you want to be,” Augusto, an architect living in Chacahua, tells me. “And nobody is going to look down on you; you’re living in a free place.”

‘The sea is starting to reclaim the land’

But it isn’t all peace in paradise. Coastal environments and their communities are facing increased exposure to natural hazards.

The rainy season from June to September brings storms and natural climate variations, but Oaxaca state’s geography, situated along Mexico’s southwest Pacific coast, leaves it particularly vulnerable to climate change. Pacific hurricanes and Atlantic basin tropical systems pose a dual threat, alongside the increasing reality of heavy rains, droughts, and rising temperatures and sea levels.

While it is difficult to find more localised data for the island, average yearly temperature in Oaxaca City rose by 1.1 degrees Celsius (2 degrees Fahrenheit) between 1994 and 2024. While this figure may seem small, it represents a rapid change over three decades, even at the local level.

Global sea level rise has been affecting the coast of Oaxaca, and Chacahua is no exception. Drawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) 6th Assessment Report, NASA’s Sea Level Projection projects extreme sea level rise along Oaxaca’s Pacific coast, and the lagoon’s low relief offers little defense.

Sitting in a cabana just 100 meters inland, Augusto points towards Playa Chacahua. “The sea is starting to reclaim (the) land. That’s why the houses over there are collapsing.”

It was Hurricane Pauline in 1997 that dramatically shifted the landscape of Chacahua, the lagoon rising to such a level that a new inlet was created and swathes of the beach were eaten away. Today, the beach faces an ever-greater risk due to the damaging erosion.

‘Everyone fishes sooner or later’

Fishing is integral to life in Chacahua, and the catch is diverse – shrimp, puffer fish, oysters, blue crabs, and red snapper by the Bajo Este. “There are all kinds of fish,” Antonio says. “There’s a bit of everything here.”

Antonio started fishing at the age of 8 with his grandfather. At 17, he began fishing for sharks; tiburoneros (shark fishermen) use a simbra, a 14-kilometre-long (9-mile) fishing line with around 300 hooks every 18 meters.

“We’d head out along the Guerrero coast, going out toward the horizon where the sun sets … to where you can’t see a thing anymore,” Antonio tells me. “Transatlantic ships pass through there. We’d stay one night and head back the next day.”

The population is no more than 800 and, according to Antonio, more than half of its residents are fishermen.

“Everyone fishes sooner or later,” he says. But security isn’t promised. “Later, some move onto other jobs because fishing is just a matter of luck.”

Santiago was born on the island and has been a fisherman for 20 years.

“Because of the rains and the storms that come, it’s more dangerous now. It’s more dangerous than compared to before. It used to be a good life.”

The ecocide of the Chacahua-Pastoría Lagoons is a key culprit, with toxic chemical influx from local oil-crop industries, as well as chemical waste from a lime-oil factory beyond Zapatalito. Shrimp and fish populations are declining. Locals have faced the consequences of diminishing catch and have even demanded government action.

In 2013, local fishermen’s collective, supported by the Human Rights Ombudsman of the People of Oaxaca (DDHPO), produced a report regarding violations against the inhabitants of Zapotalito, Chacahua, La Pastoría and El Corral details the public health risks, loss of livelihood and environmental degradation that communities have faced due to federal infrastructure projects, such as Irrigation District 110 and breakwaters in the Boca de Chacahua.

The resilience of mangroves

Part of a roughly 51-square-mile national park designated in 1937, Chacahua Lagoon is surrounded by a network of mangrove corridors, anchoring the island in verdant, woody tresses. Mangroves are trees or bushes that thrive in brackish tidal waters, often where a river meets the sea, offering nesting grounds for a diversity of wildlife.

The red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), black mangrove (Avicennia germinans), white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa), and buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) are also essential to maintaining the health of the local ecosystem.

Their long, complex root systems are adapted to survive in low-lying waters, optimising oxygen absorption and filtering out saline contamination. They endure conditions that are virtually impossible for other plants, and their resilience is recognized by the locals.

Angél runs a grocery shop in the central square. His family has been living on the island for generations. The salinity of the sea is getting worse, he concedes, but “the mangroves are strong. We don’t have to cut them that much.”

“The mangroves are doing well,” Antonio agrees. “They’re tough. When they fall, they land upright,” due to their roots.

The resilience of locals

Perhaps Antonio and Angél aren’t giving themselves enough credit. In reality, mangroves are vulnerable to climate change, specifically increasing salinity, hurricane events, and worsening El Niño patterns. But it’s the locals who demonstrate climate resilience every day, in working as a community to restore the things that Angél says the government is neglecting financially and administratively.

“The effort is made every day; it’s part of life here on the island,” Augusto says. “People engage in what’s called tequio, voluntary community work to help the environment.”

In the same way, the fishermen are taking it upon themselves to try and mitigate the marine pollution, but there is a limit to what can be done without wider support.

Tequio “takes place because people love their land,” Augusto explains, but as Angél marks, the climate is getting hotter, the sea saltier, and the water warmer.

On top of this, the briny waves of gentrification are lapping at the island’s shores. Lavish cabanas with their polished wood walls and hiked-up rent are beginning to rear their haute heads.

Tourism has also been shown to worsen pollution. In Mexico’s Caribbean coast, the tourism sector accounts for one-third of the region’s total waste, and light pollution has been proven to pose threats to turtle populations, of which species such as the Leatherback are populous in Chacahua.

What’s in store for Chacahua?

Oaxaca has been strongly affected by hurricanes Otis, John, Erick, and Boris in the last four years.

While federal budgeting continues to be an issue for Natural Protected Areas across Mexico, local cooperatives, in tandem with the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (CONANP), are taking measures to respond to growing tourism in the state of Oaxaca and have made major steps in wildlife protection and sustainable infrastructure, but the direct effects on Chacahua are yet to be comprehensively reported.

Looking into its climate future, Chacahua is standing at a delta. It goes without saying that the community has demonstrated its climate resilience through supporting mangroves, keeping the waters around the island clean, and reconstructing and relocating seafront buildings.

However, without sufficient government support, the effects of environmental jeopardy and injustice may ultimately uproot the mangrove system and local way of life to an irremediable degree.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: Guatemala growth and TPS: remittances, US aid and what it means
World.content:
Guatemala · Economy

Key Facts The economy is picking up speed: Guatemala’s central bank, known as Banguat, says overall economic activity grew 4.4 percent between January and May 2026. That beats the 3.9 percent it recorded in the same five months of 2025.

Guatemala’s central bank, known as Banguat, says overall economic activity grew 4.4 percent between January and May 2026. That beats the 3.9 percent it recorded in the same five months of 2025. Careful — that is not the GDP number: The 4.4 percent comes from a monthly activity gauge, not from GDP, which means gross domestic product, the total value of everything the country produces. Actual GDP grew 4.5 percent in the first quarter of 2026.

The 4.4 percent comes from a monthly activity gauge, not from GDP, which means gross domestic product, the total value of everything the country produces. Actual GDP grew 4.5 percent in the first quarter of 2026. Money from abroad keeps pouring in: Guatemalans working overseas sent home about Q117.8 billion (~US$15.45 billion) in the first seven months of 2026. That is 6.6 percent more than the same stretch of 2025.

Guatemalans working overseas sent home about Q117.8 billion (~US$15.45 billion) in the first seven months of 2026. That is 6.6 percent more than the same stretch of 2025. That money is one fifth of the economy: Remittances were a record 21 percent of Guatemala’s GDP in 2025, according to the International Monetary Fund. Very little else in the country moves that much cash.

Remittances were a record 21 percent of Guatemala’s GDP in 2025, according to the International Monetary Fund. Very little else in the country moves that much cash. Washington released half the aid: The US State Department signed off on 1 July 2026 that El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras are meeting ten conditions, which frees up 50 percent of their yearly US economic and security aid. The department did not publish what that half is worth in dollars.

The US State Department signed off on 1 July 2026 that El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras are meeting ten conditions, which frees up 50 percent of their yearly US economic and security aid. The department did not publish what that half is worth in dollars. Protected status is nearly gone in the region: TPS, or Temporary Protected Status, is the US permit that lets people from disaster-hit countries live and work legally for a set time. It has already ended for Honduras and Nicaragua, and El Salvador’s expires on 9 September 2026.

TPS, or Temporary Protected Status, is the US permit that lets people from disaster-hit countries live and work legally for a set time. It has already ended for Honduras and Nicaragua, and El Salvador’s expires on 9 September 2026. The 500,000 figure doing the rounds is wrong: Central American holders of that status peaked at roughly a quarter of a million people — about 170,000 Salvadorans, 72,000 Hondurans and a few thousand Nicaraguans. Guatemala has never had the programme at all.

Guatemala is growing faster than last year, Washington has released half its aid to three Central American governments, and the programme that let hundreds of thousands of Central Americans work legally in the US is being wound down.

Guatemala is having a good year. The central bank says the economy grew faster in the first five months of 2026 than it did a year earlier, and the money Guatemalans send home from abroad has never been higher.

Then there is the other half of the story. The US permit that has let hundreds of thousands of Central Americans work legally — and send that money home — is being dismantled country by country, and El Salvador’s runs out in three weeks.

Guatemala’s economy is growing, but its neighbours’ migrants face an uncertain US status. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Guatemala’s economy is picking up speed

Banguat — the Bank of Guatemala, the country’s central bank — publishes a monthly gauge called the IMAE, or Monthly Index of Economic Activity. It is a running read on how much the country is producing, and between January and May 2026 it grew 4.4 percent.

That is genuinely better news than it sounds. The same measure grew 3.9 percent over those months in 2025, so the slowdown of recent years has broken.

The proper GDP figure tells a similar story. Gross domestic product — the total value of everything Guatemala produces — rose 4.5 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with a year before, up from 3.8 percent.

The growth is spread around, which is what you want to see. Shops and vehicle repair grew 4.3 percent, factories 4.5 percent, hotels and restaurants 5.4 percent, and banking and insurance 6.7 percent.

The official forecast for the whole of 2026 is around 4.1 percent, and the government would like to beat it. The International Monetary Fund finished its annual check-up on 29 July 2026 and called the economy stable, while pushing for faster reform.

The money sent home is doing the heavy lifting

Guatemalans working abroad, overwhelmingly in the United States, sent home Q117.8 billion (~US$15.45 billion) between January and July 2026. That is 6.6 percent more than the same seven months of 2025.

July alone brought in Q18.8 billion (~US$2.47 billion), a 4.2 percent rise on July last year. Banguat released those figures on Thursday 6 August 2026.

The full-year picture is bigger still. Remittances reached Q194.6 billion (~US$25.53 billion) in 2025, and the central bank expects about Q204.3 billion (~US$26.81 billion) this year — a rise of 5 percent.

Here is the number that matters most. Those transfers were 21 percent of Guatemala’s GDP in 2025, an all-time record, according to the IMF — meaning roughly one dollar in five circulating in the economy arrives from someone’s relative overseas.

All figures convert at the central bank’s reference rate of Q7.62 to the US dollar, quoted for mid-August 2026.

Washington has unlocked half the aid money

Every year the US Congress writes a condition into its spending law: half the economic and security aid promised to the governments of El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras is frozen until the State Department certifies they are behaving. Ten conditions have to be met, covering good government, corruption, human rights, rule of law and cooperation on migration.

That certification came through on 1 July 2026. Christopher Landau, the Deputy Secretary of State, signed it for all three countries, and it was published in the Federal Register on 6 August.

The legal hook, if you want to look it up, is Section 7045(b)(2)(A) of the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026. The certification also has to be sent to Congress with a written justification.

One caveat worth being straight about: the State Department did not publish a dollar figure for what that 50 percent actually amounts to. Anyone quoting you a number for it is guessing.

It is a vote of confidence in the three governments. It does not, however, touch remittances — that money comes from individuals, not from Washington.

Where protected status actually stands right now

TPS stands for Temporary Protected Status. It is a US permit that lets people from countries wrecked by disaster or conflict live and work legally for a fixed period, and it is worth stressing that it is not a green card and never turns into one.

For El Salvador, it is still in force and expires on 9 September 2026, covering roughly 170,000 people. The US government was legally required to announce by 11 July whether it would extend or end the designation, and that deadline came and went with no announcement.

The Department of Homeland Security says it has not made an official announcement. Some immigration lawyers argue a six-month automatic extension written into the law has now kicked in, but the government has not confirmed that either.

In the meantime US immigration services have extended Salvadoran work permits to 9 September 2026. So nothing has been terminated — the honest description is that the decision is overdue and the outcome is unknown.

For Honduras and Nicaragua the answer is simpler and harder. Their protections ended on 8 September 2025, covering about 72,000 Hondurans and a few thousand Nicaraguans, and although a judge briefly restored them at the end of 2025, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals put that ruling on hold on 9 February 2026.

Haiti’s ended on 27 July 2026, after the Supreme Court ruled in June that courts generally cannot review these decisions at all. A federal judge in Washington confirmed on 5 August that her earlier block was gone.

Two numbers worth getting right

You will see the 4.4 percent reported as Guatemala’s GDP growth. It is not — it is that monthly activity index for January to May, and the quarterly GDP figure is a separate 4.5 percent.

The second one matters more. A figure of 500,000 Central Americans affected by the protected-status changes has been circulating, and it does not hold up.

Add the real country numbers together and Central American holders peaked at roughly a quarter of a million — about 170,000 Salvadorans, 72,000 Hondurans and a few thousand Nicaraguans. Guatemala has never been designated for the programme, so Guatemalans in the US are exposed to general deportation policy rather than to this particular deadline.

Nationwide the programme has shrunk dramatically. It covered 1,297,635 people from 17 countries in March 2025, and by 12 August 2026 the Pew Research Center counted about 273,200 people from just four — El Salvador, Ukraine, Sudan and Lebanon.

Why this matters if you invest here or live here

Remittances are not a footnote in these economies — they are the engine of household spending. They pay for groceries, school fees, cement and the stock on small-shop shelves, which is precisely why commerce, banking and hotels are the sectors growing fastest.

So the arithmetic is uncomfortable. If large numbers of Central Americans lose the right to work legally in the United States, the flow of money home eventually thins, and so does the consumer demand currently driving the growth figures.

There is an honest counterpoint, and it is worth knowing. During past enforcement scares remittances have gone up rather than down, as people rush savings home ahead of trouble — which is part of what powered the 18.7 percent jump Guatemala recorded in 2025.

That makes the timing tricky rather than the risk imaginary. A surge first, a thinner flow later, is the pattern to plan around.

The practical takeaway for anyone holding Guatemalan assets, running a business there or living on a foreign income: the US immigration calendar has become an economic calendar. The 9 September date is the next one to have in your diary.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Guatemala’s economy really grow 4.4 percent? Economic activity did, but that is not the GDP figure. The 4.4 percent is the central bank’s monthly activity index for January to May 2026, while GDP — the total value of everything produced — grew 4.5 percent in the first quarter. What is TPS, in plain English? Temporary Protected Status is a US permit for people from countries hit by disaster or war, letting them live and work legally for a set period. It has to be renewed by the US government, and it does not lead to a green card or citizenship. Is El Salvador’s protected status ending in September? Nobody knows yet, and that is the whole problem. It is valid until 9 September 2026, the US government missed its own 11 July deadline to say what happens next, and no termination has been announced. Does any of this affect Guatemalans in the United States? Not through this programme — Guatemala has never been designated for protected status. Guatemalans in the US are affected by general immigration enforcement instead, which still matters enormously given how much money they send home.

Sources: Prensa Libre: Remittances to Guatemala reach US$15.447 billion through July; Prensa Libre: Government bets on investment and market diversification to beat 4.1% forecast; IMF concludes 2026 Article IV consultation with Guatemala; Guatemala’s economic activity grows 4.4% (IMAE, Banguat); Soy502: Banguat monthly remittance table, record July 2026; Banguat reference exchange rate, mid-August 2026; Federal Register: Certification under Section 7045(b)(2)(A), P.L. 119-75; Infobae: US State Department certifies El Salvador to release cooperation funds; USCIS: Temporary Protected Status designated country — El Salvador; USCIS: Update on termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haiti; Pew Research Center: TPS ended for most immigrants who had it; UCLA Law: Ninth Circuit permits TPS terminations for Honduras, Nepal and Nicaragua

World.title: Bolivia IMF deal: currency, exports, reform
World.content:
Bolivia · Economy

Key Facts The IMF money is agreed but not signed: Bolivia and the International Monetary Fund — the Washington lender that helps countries in financial trouble — shook hands on a US$1.9 billion loan on 29 July 2026. The Fund’s board and Bolivia’s Congress both still have to say yes before a single dollar arrives.

Bolivia and the International Monetary Fund — the Washington lender that helps countries in financial trouble — shook hands on a US$1.9 billion loan on 29 July 2026. The Fund’s board and Bolivia’s Congress both still have to say yes before a single dollar arrives. Bolivia has a new president, and it is not who you might think: Rodrigo Paz Pereira won the runoff vote on 19 October 2025 with 54.53% and was sworn in on 8 November 2025. He beat Jorge “Tuto” Quiroga, who now leads the opposition.

Rodrigo Paz Pereira won the runoff vote on 19 October 2025 with 54.53% and was sworn in on 8 November 2025. He beat Jorge “Tuto” Quiroga, who now leads the opposition. The old fixed exchange rate is gone: On 15 July 2026 the government scrapped the peg of about 6.91 bolivianos to the dollar and let the currency trade freely. The official rate has since firmed from Bs 11.86 on 10 August to Bs 11.58 per dollar for 15–17 August.

On 15 July 2026 the government scrapped the peg of about 6.91 bolivianos to the dollar and let the currency trade freely. The official rate has since firmed from Bs 11.86 on 10 August to Bs 11.58 per dollar for 15–17 August. The black-market dollar is now cheaper than the official one: For years the informal rate sat far above the official peg, but in August it flipped. On 15 August the parallel rate closed near Bs 11.43 per dollar while the official sat at Bs 11.58.

For years the informal rate sat far above the official peg, but in August it flipped. On 15 August the parallel rate closed near Bs 11.43 per dollar while the official sat at Bs 11.58. Exports jumped in value, but Bolivia shipped less stuff: Sales abroad hit US$6,395 million between January and June 2026, up 55% on the year before. The tonnage actually shipped fell about 19% — this is a price story, not a production story.

Sales abroad hit US$6,395 million between January and June 2026, up 55% on the year before. The tonnage actually shipped fell about 19% — this is a price story, not a production story. The old gas money is drying up: Natural gas exports brought in under US$500 million for the whole half-year, a shadow of Bolivia’s boom years. Fuel import bills fell 11.3%, yet queues at petrol stations have not gone away.

Natural gas exports brought in under US$500 million for the whole half-year, a shadow of Bolivia’s boom years. Fuel import bills fell 11.3%, yet queues at petrol stations have not gone away. The opposition wants the constitution rewritten: Quiroga said his Libre bloc would file a constitutional reform bill on Monday 17 August to allow international arbitration and pull in foreign money. No text has been published yet, so treat it as a promise rather than a done thing.

A new IMF loan on the table, a floating currency, a mineral export boom and a constitutional fight over foreign investment — Bolivia is changing fast, and here is what it means for you.

Bolivia is going through a serious economic reset, and it matters well beyond La Paz. President Rodrigo Paz Pereira, who took office on 8 November 2025, is pushing an International Monetary Fund loan, a floating currency and a stack of new investment laws.

Meanwhile the opposition wants to go further and rewrite the constitution itself. Here is the state of play, in plain English, with the numbers that matter.

Bolivia floated its currency in July and has a staff-level IMF deal. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The IMF deal is agreed by the technical team — not by the board

On 29 July 2026 the International Monetary Fund and Bolivia reached what is called a staff-level agreement. That is a technical handshake between negotiators, not final approval.

The deal is a 36-month loan worth about US$1.9 billion under the Fund’s Extended Fund Facility — a long-term programme for countries fixing deep economic problems. The money is meant to steady the economy, rebuild the central bank’s dollar reserves and shore up social safety nets.

Two big hurdles remain. The IMF’s executive board has to vote yes, and so does Bolivia’s Congress — the Plurinational Legislative Assembly — and no cash has moved yet.

The number also came in below what the government hoped. Economy Minister José Gabriel Espinoza had been talking about US$2.5–2.8 billion in late July.

Even so, the deal is expected to unlock more lending from the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank. Together that could add up to a package worth more than US$5 billion.

What happened to the peg — and why the black-market dollar got cheap

For about 15 years Bolivia fixed the boliviano at roughly 6.91 to the dollar. That rate was mostly fiction — hardly anyone could actually buy dollars at that price.

So an informal or parallel market grew up, where a dollar cost far more, at times above 11 bolivianos. On 15 July 2026 the government ended the peg and let the currency float.

Since then the official rate published by the Banco Central de Bolivia, the country’s central bank, has been drifting down — from Bs 11.86 on 10 August to Bs 11.77, then Bs 11.62, and Bs 11.58 for the weekend and Monday. That is the boliviano gaining about 2.4% in a single week.

Here is the strange part. The parallel rate, which used to sit well above the official one, has flipped below it.

On 8 August El Deber put the informal rate at Bs 11.18–11.22 per dollar against an official Bs 11.86 — roughly 5.4% cheaper. By 15 August the parallel had closed near Bs 11.43 while the official stood at Bs 11.58.

Put it in everyday money. Bs 10,000 in your pocket was worth about US$1,447 under the old official peg, while today that same Bs 10,000 is worth roughly US$864.

One caution — those parallel quotes come from peer-to-peer and crypto platforms, not from the central bank. Treat them as a good indication rather than gospel.

Exports are booming in value — but Bolivia is shipping less

The national statistics institute, known by its Spanish initials INE, published preliminary figures showing exports of US$6,395 million for January to June 2026. That is up 55% on the same months of 2025, and it left a trade surplus of US$1,669 million.

It sounds fantastic, and it partly is. But the real driver is prices, not output — the tonnage actually shipped fell about 19%.

The boom is almost all minerals. Traditional exports, meaning mining and hydrocarbons, rose 70%, and minerals alone nearly doubled from US$2,326 million to US$4,452 million on the back of gold and metal prices.

Farm and agro-industrial exports, including soy, did far less dramatically at US$1,433 million, up 18%. Natural gas — once the country’s cash cow — brought in under US$500 million for the whole half-year.

There are smaller bright spots. Electricity sales to northern Argentina nearly quadrupled to US$31.9 million, and China, India and Japan together took 41% of Bolivian exports.

The constitutional fight over foreign investment

Bolivia’s current constitution obliges foreign investors to take their disputes to Bolivian courts and blocks international arbitration — the neutral outside tribunals most global companies insist on. That single rule is what reformers want removed.

On Monday 17 August opposition leader Jorge “Tuto” Quiroga — the man who lost the 2025 runoff to Paz — said his Libre bloc would present a constitutional reform bill. He framed it around legal certainty, foreign investment, international arbitration and avoiding an energy collapse.

It is worth being straight about this. So far it is an announcement, with no published text, no article-by-article list and no confirmed filing.

One partial reform bill has been formally filed, though, by deputy Carlos Alarcón of the Unidad alliance. It would strip about 30 articles of their constitutional rank, end the popular election of judges in favour of merit selection, and allow national and international arbitration in investment disputes.

That bill gives the Assembly one year to pass the follow-up laws, and any partial reform needs a two-thirds vote in Congress.

Instead the president sent a 103-article Investment Law to Congress on 12 August. It aims to normalise private capital, create incentives and set clear rules, with further bills promised on hydrocarbons, mining, electricity and lithium.

Why this matters if you invest in Bolivia or live there

If you send money in or out of Bolivia, or you import anything, the exchange rate is suddenly the whole ballgame. With the boliviano floating and the parallel rate below the official one, the market is quietly signalling the currency may settle stronger than people feared.

For expats on the ground, fuel queues and patchy energy supply are still a daily fact of life. Espinoza says the rate should settle below Bs 11 to the dollar, and markets are not convinced.

If you have a big transfer or a large purchase coming, there is a decent argument for waiting a few weeks. The IMF board vote and the congressional vote could move the picture quickly in either direction.

For investors, the constitutional fight is the one to watch. If international arbitration becomes legal, mining, lithium and infrastructure could finally look investable — but nothing counts until the votes are counted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Bolivia IMF deal final? No, not yet. It is a staff-level agreement, meaning the IMF’s negotiating team and the Bolivian government agreed the terms on 29 July 2026. The IMF’s executive board and Bolivia’s Congress both still have to approve it before any money is paid out. Who is the president of Bolivia right now? Rodrigo Paz Pereira, who was sworn in on 8 November 2025. He won the 19 October 2025 runoff with 54.53% against Jorge “Tuto” Quiroga, ending roughly two decades of MAS rule. Why is the black-market dollar cheaper than the official one? For years the official rate was frozen near 6.91 bolivianos per dollar, but you could not really buy dollars at that price, so an informal market charged far more. When the peg ended in July 2026 the official rate jumped above Bs 11 and the two rates crossed over. The parallel market now prices the dollar slightly below the central bank, which suggests dollar demand has cooled. How good are Bolivia’s export numbers really? Exports were US$6,395 million in the first half of 2026, up 55% on a year earlier, which looks excellent. But the volume shipped fell about 19%, so the gain came from high mineral and gold prices rather than more production. Gas exports stayed weak at under US$500 million.

Sources: IMF Press Release No. 26/268 — Staff-Level Agreement; Reuters — Bolivia IMF deal at US$1.9 billion; Reuters — Bolivia expected US$2.5-2.8 billion, minister said; El Deber — Parallel dollar below official rate; Correo del Sur — Parallel dollar volatility and close at 11.43; Banco Central de Bolivia — Official exchange rate; Ahora Digital — Exports grow 55% to US$6,395 million; La Razon — China, India, Japan take 41% of exports; Los Tiempos — Fuel imports drop 42.9% in June; Straits Times — Paz tests fragile coalition

World.title: Mexico investment resilience: what the May data shows
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts Investment nudged up, and only just: Gross fixed investment — the money companies and government put into buildings, machines and equipment — rose 1.1% in May compared with a year earlier. Measured against April, it actually slipped 0.4%.

Gross fixed investment — the money companies and government put into buildings, machines and equipment — rose 1.1% in May compared with a year earlier. Measured against April, it actually slipped 0.4%. That number is for May, not July: INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, published it on 5 August, because this series always runs about two months behind. There is no July figure yet, and no 6.4% rise anywhere in it.

INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, published it on 5 August, because this series always runs about two months behind. There is no July figure yet, and no 6.4% rise anywhere in it. Greener cars are selling fast: Sales of hybrids, plug-in hybrids and fully electric cars together rose 46.5% between January and July, to 112,313 vehicles. Battery-only cars did even better, up 52.5%.

Sales of hybrids, plug-in hybrids and fully electric cars together rose 46.5% between January and July, to 112,313 vehicles. Battery-only cars did even better, up 52.5%. Roughly one new car in eight is now electrified: Those vehicles made up 12.7% of all light-vehicle sales in the first seven months of 2026. A year earlier the share was 9.1%.

Those vehicles made up 12.7% of all light-vehicle sales in the first seven months of 2026. A year earlier the share was 9.1%. Sinaloa’s China shipment is a taster, not a cargo: The state sent five containers of red sorghum from the port of Topolobampo on 15 August so a Chinese buyer can check the quality. A letter of intent covers up to 1.2 million tonnes, but nothing has been signed.

The state sent five containers of red sorghum from the port of Topolobampo on 15 August so a Chinese buyer can check the quality. A letter of intent covers up to 1.2 million tonnes, but nothing has been signed. The government is doing the heavy lifting: Public investment jumped 19.7% in May from a year earlier, while private investment fell 1.3%. Across January to May, total investment is still down 0.5%.

Investment, greener car sales and a first sorghum shipment to China all point the same way — Mexico’s home market is holding up, while anything pointing north is not.

Three fresh numbers out of Mexico are being stitched together into a Mexico investment resilience story — investment rising, greener cars flying off the lots, and the first sorghum heading to China. The story mostly holds up, but only if you read the fine print.

Start with the dates. The investment figure doing the rounds is for May 2026, not July, and it is a good deal smaller than advertised.

Mexico’s investment numbers are steadier than the tariff headlines suggest. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The investment figure is for May — and it is smaller than you have heard

INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, publishes its gross fixed investment reading about two months after the fact. The latest one landed on 5 August and covers May 2026.

Gross fixed investment is simply spending on buildings, machinery and equipment. It rose 1.1% compared with May last year, or 2.4% once you strip out the usual seasonal ups and downs.

Against April, though, it slipped 0.4%. A 6.4% rise has been doing the rounds online, and it is not in this release — the only 6.4% on the record is a decline reported back in February, for late 2025.

The detail underneath is uneven. Construction rose 2.7% from a year earlier, led by non-residential work up 12.4%, while spending on machinery and equipment dipped 0.7%.

One split is worth pausing on. Spending on imported machinery rose 5.6% from a year earlier, while spending on Mexican-made machinery fell 9.8% — companies are still buying kit, just not from local suppliers.

Greener cars are the genuine bright spot

Sales of electrified cars — hybrids, plug-in hybrids and fully electric models counted together — rose 46.5% between January and July, to 112,313 units. That 46.5% is the combined figure, not fully electric cars on their own.

Battery-only cars actually grew faster, up 52.5% to 16,605. Plug-in hybrids more than tripled, up 222.4%, and ordinary hybrids rose 28.4%.

The figures come from RAIAVL, the vehicle sales register INEGI compiles from 30 companies and 44 brands, and circulated by AMIA, the carmakers’ trade association. In July alone, electrified sales were 61.9% higher than a year earlier.

Electrified models now account for 12.7% of new light-vehicle sales, up from 9.1% a year earlier. That is roughly one new car in eight, in a market where the plug-in segment barely existed five years ago.

The whole market is warm, not just the plug-in end. Mexicans bought 885,353 new light vehicles between January and July, 5.04% more than last year, with newer brands from outside the established club selling 56.46% more.

Sinaloa’s sorghum trip to China is five containers, not a boatload

On 15 August, five containers of red sorghum left the port of Topolobampo, in Ahome, Sinaloa, bound for China. The state government confirmed the shipment and called it historic.

It is a trial batch, sent so the buyer can test the quality before any contract is signed. No tonnage and no value were disclosed, so treat any figure you see with caution.

The buyer is Sichuan Yourong Group, of Chengdu, which wants the grain for baijiu — China’s national liquor. A letter of intent covers up to 1.2 million tonnes, and growers must meet plant-health rules agreed between the two governments.

On the Mexican side the shipper is Gessa Agroservicios, and the send-off was overseen by the Topolobampo port authority and the navy’s Eighth Naval Zone. Governor Yeraldine Bonilla Valverde framed it as a way to give Sinaloa farmers a market that is not the United States.

Officials also say Chihuahua-grown sorghum passed the same tests. It is a real opening for Mexican farmers, but it is an opening, not a harvest.

Now the awkward part

Mexicans are buying more cars, but the world is buying fewer Mexican ones. Light-vehicle exports fell 9.69% in July from a year earlier, to 261,534 units.

Production between January and July slipped 0.65%, even as home-market sales climbed. Around three-quarters of those exports go to the United States, which is exactly where the [tariff dispute and the review of T-MEC](https://www.riotimesonline.com/mexico-ebrard-us-tariffs-tmec/) — the trade pact Mexico shares with the US and Canada — is playing out.

Investment tells the same story from a different angle. Public money rose 19.7% in May while private money fell 1.3%, and the January-to-May total is still down 0.5%.

There is a turn in there, to be fair. April saw the biggest monthly investment jump since January 2019, ending 19 straight months of annual declines.

The wider economy is still growing, just slowly. Preliminary INEGI figures put second-quarter growth at 1.5% compared with a year earlier.

Why this matters if you invest here or live here

The same pattern runs through all three numbers. Mexico’s home market is holding up, while almost anything pointing north is under strain.

For an investor, that argues for domestic consumer, housing and construction exposure over export-facing factories, at least until the trade picture clears. The peso was trading near 17.02 to the US dollar in mid-August, so any peso earnings still convert on familiar terms.

The sorghum trial is the small one to file away. If five containers turn into a real contract, it is early evidence Mexico can sell to somebody other than its northern neighbour.

For an expat, the practical read is simpler. Jobs and prices tied to local demand look steady, while the manufacturing towns that live off American orders are the ones worth watching.

Frequently Asked Questions

So how much did Mexican investment actually grow? It rose 1.1% in May compared with a year earlier, or 2.4% after adjusting for seasonal patterns. Against April it fell 0.4%, and the January-to-May total is still down 0.5%. Why is there no July investment figure? INEGI publishes this series roughly two months late, so the reading released on 5 August covered May. The June figure is due next, not July. Did fully electric car sales really jump 46.5%? Not quite — the 46.5% covers hybrids, plug-in hybrids and fully electric cars added together. Fully electric cars on their own rose 52.5%, to 16,605 units. Is the Sinaloa sorghum deal worth getting excited about? Only cautiously. Five trial containers have shipped and a letter of intent covers up to 1.2 million tonnes, but no contract has been signed and no value was disclosed.

Sources: INEGI — Boletin de Indicador 483/26, RAIAVL, 7 August 2026; INEGI — Registro Administrativo de la Industria Automotriz de Vehiculos Ligeros; La Razon — Inversion fija bruta se contrae 0.4% en mayo; Forbes Mexico — Inversion en Mexico se eleva un 1.1% en mayo; Revista Fortuna — La inversion en mayo cae 0.4% mensual y crece 2.4% anual; Gobierno del Estado de Sinaloa — Sinaloa embarca los primeros 5 contenedores de sorgo a China; La Jornada — Sinaloa abre a China mercado de sorgo; busca vender 1.2 millones de toneladas; La Cronica de Hoy — Sinaloa abre una nueva puerta para su campo con el primer embarque de sorgo a China

World.title: Draft US Letter Tells 35 Partners to Pick an AI Coalition
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

United States · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —Draft State Department letter: Reuters reported on 14 August 2026 that it reviewed an undated State Department draft letter. The unsent draft tells 35 partner countries to pick one artificial intelligence (AI) grouping. —Exclusion threat: The draft says countries joining a rival grouping would be excluded from the US-led AI coalition. It names no chip or cloud penalty. —Brazil’s position: Brazil was a founding member of China’s new AI body, WAICO, on 16 July 2026. It signed no US AI statement. —Telecom dominance: Huawei alone installed about 70% of Africa’s 4G networks. That estimate comes from Berlin’s Mercator Institute for China Studies, published in 2019. —US response: Washington pledged over US$350 million and said it would help arrange over US$450 million more for African digital projects. —Youth demographic: Africa’s youth population is projected to account for about 42% of the world’s youth by 2030.

Reuters says it reviewed an unsent US draft letter telling 35 partner countries to pick a side on AI. The draft threatens exclusion from a US-led AI coalition.

Server racks. The draft letter’s only stated penalty is exclusion from the US-led AI coalition. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Washington’s ultimatum on the AI coalition

Reuters reported on 14 August 2026 that it reviewed an undated State Department draft letter to 35 governments. Those governments signed the US-backed Joint Statement on AI Opportunity on 25 June 2026.

The draft says signing the Pax Silica Declaration is “not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment”. It adds: “To be part of everything is to be part of nothing.”

The draft says the commitment “cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own”. It is undated, unsent, and the State Department declined to comment.

The draft names neither China nor the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO. Reuters reported that the wording points to WAICO, which China launched in Shanghai on 16 July 2026.

The draft’s only stated penalty is exclusion from the US-led AI coalition. It lists no loss of chips, cloud services, models or minerals.

The chip-control architecture behind the AI race with China

In January 2025 Washington issued the Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion, which sorted the world into three chip-access tiers. The Commerce Department rescinded that rule on 13 May 2025.

That rescinded rule would have capped how much AI computing power US cloud firms could install abroad. The limits were 50% outside the United States, 25% outside tier-one allies, and 7% in any single other country.

Its stated goal was to keep advanced chips away from China’s military.

Where Latin America stands

Six Latin American countries signed the June statement: Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Panama and Paraguay. All but Paraguay also signed the Pax Silica Declaration.

Brazil is on the other side of the line. It was a founding member of China’s WAICO on 16 July 2026 and signed neither US document.

That splits Mercosur. Argentina and Chile sit inside the US coalition while Brazil sits inside China’s.

The split bears on data-centre siting, cloud purchases and 5G vendor choice.

Chile, Brazil and Argentina also hold the lithium, copper and rare earths that Pax Silica covers under minerals refining. Kazakhstan is the only country so far in both camps.

Neither Beijing nor any of the 35 governments had responded publicly as of 17 August 2026.

Africa as the new AI battleground

Africa is not a party to the June statement, but it sits at the centre of the wider contest. Its youth, minerals and new networks are the draw.

China has spent two decades building its footprint. Huawei alone installed about 70% of Africa’s 4G networks, Berlin’s Mercator Institute for China Studies found in 2019.

Washington has responded with its own push. Under Digital Transformation with Africa it pledged over US$350 million and promised to help arrange over US$450 million in financing.

This contest over infrastructure, standards and data rules runs through Africa: The New Scramble.

The risk of digital colonisation

In May 2019 Washington blacklisted Huawei, and Google then cut the firm off from Android services. That showed how fast geopolitics can reach consumer devices.

In April 2024 China’s Cyberspace Administration pushed for a China-Africa AI policy at a summit in Xiamen. That same month Gina Raimondo, then US Commerce Secretary, signed a non-binding AI statement with Kenya.

What the AI race with China means for African governments

No African government signed the US statement, so none will receive this draft letter. African states that join WAICO would still sit outside the US-led coalition.

Governments will face pressure to decide which AI governance club they join.

The choices run across cloud partnerships, 5G vendors and regulatory templates. Kenya, South Africa and Mozambique are WAICO founding members.

Local African firms could see new openings as regional hubs for data centres and AI services. That could also lock in dependencies and limit cross-border interoperability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the US asking its allies to do in the AI race with China? Reuters says it reviewed an unsent State Department draft letter to 35 partner countries. It asks them to choose between the US-led AI coalition and China’s rival grouping. Who built Africa’s 4G networks? Huawei alone installed about 70% of Africa’s 4G networks, Berlin’s Mercator Institute for China Studies reported in 2019. Chinese firms also lead many 5G rollouts on the continent. What happens to countries that join China’s AI framework? The draft says they would be excluded from the US-led AI coalition. It sets out no penalty on chips, cloud services or minerals.

World.title: Global Goods Trade Hits US$13.7 Trillion on Higher Prices
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Global · TRADE

Key Facts —Half-year record: Global goods trade reached about US$13.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, up 12.5%. UN Trade and Development says higher prices explain part of the gain. —Annual milestone: Global trade in goods and services hit a record of about US$35 trillion in 2025. Goods contributed about US$1.8 trillion of the US$2.5 trillion rise, UNCTAD says. —Growth drivers: In the first quarter of 2026 critical minerals trade grew 38%, semiconductors 25%, batteries 15% and electric cars 11%. Solar and wind product trade contracted. —Africa’s share: Africa held 2.8% of world merchandise trade in 2025, down from 5% in 1994. The 46 least developed countries hold just 1%. —Value capture gap: Most African critical minerals leave the continent as unprocessed ore. Africa accounts for under 2% of world manufacturing value added, the UN Economic Commission for Africa says. —Trade governance: Export controls on chips, carbon border measures and local-content rules are reshaping trade flows.

Global goods trade reached about US$13.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, up 12.5% on a year earlier. UN Trade and Development says higher prices drove much of that rise.

Africa and Latin America still capture little of the value.

Containers at a Latin American port. Chile and Peru mined about a third of the world’s copper in 2025. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
