We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among the thousands to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. The proportion of children taking Catholic catechism in schools has continued to fall but remains a majority https://t.co/5bu35hzJ7c — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. World.title: Poland seeks to boost investment with new tax-free personal accounts
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) without paying capital gains tax. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. To największa od lat zmiana dla indywidualnych inwestorów i największy projekt budowy krajowego kapitału napędzającego rozwój polskiej gospodarki. 🇵🇱 — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) July 3, 2026 The government estimates the scheme could result in about 74 billion zloty flowing to the Warsaw Stock Exchange by 2040. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. Poland’s WIG20 stock market index has hit its highest ever level, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year, gaining almost 25% https://t.co/CBbv99v2Uk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Poland already has three mechanisms that allow people to accumulate assets with tax advantages: Individual Retirement Accounts (IKE), Individual Pension Schemes (IKZE), and Employee Capital Plans (PPK). However, in all three cases, the capital gains tax exemption is conditional on withdrawing funds after reaching retirement age. Despite the Polish stock market’s strong performance in recent years, Poles’ direct participation remains modest. Shares make up only 2.9% of household assets, the equivalent of 3% of GDP. That is well below the EU average of 8.2%. By contrast, households’ cash holdings are equivalent to 11.5% of GDP, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). World.title: Polish PM confirms he wants his “right-hand man” to be made constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and whom Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. A newly sworn-in @TK_GOV_PL judge says he will not take his seat until four colleagues appointed by parliament are allowed to take theirs. He said their appointments had been blocked "unlawfully", in the latest twist in a long-running disputehttps://t.co/X30rm1Gfzs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 However, there remain major potential stumbling blocks on Berek’s path to the TK, not least doubts over whether Tusk’s coalition partners will support his nomination in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, declared on Tuesday that, if rumours of Berek’s nomination were true, “he won’t get votes from The Left because we promised our voters that politicians wouldn’t end up on the TK”. Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition to oppose Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. On Thursday, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK. Ale IMHO to bardzo krzywdząca dla @MaciejBerek plotka, on by się jako państwowiec w życiu na coś takiego nie… https://t.co/QWFFmdy4V3 — Anna-Maria Żukowska 💁🏻‍♀️ (@AM_Zukowska) August 11, 2026 The next vacancy on the TK’s 15-judge bench is due to open on 18 September, when the nine-year term of Justyn Piskorski, one of the PiS-era judges regarded as illegitimate by the current government, ends. After that, a further vacancy will open in January. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Earlier this week, his chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Radio Zet that Nawrocki would “accept the oath if procedures are followed”. However, he added that he does “not know if [the Sejm] is able to carry out those procedures properly”. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the re-introduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained a Russian national who it says was planning to assassinate a person with joint US and Ukrainian citizenship in Warsaw. The news was first announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a press conference on Thursday afternoon. “Thanks to the truly brilliant action of our security services – the Internal Security Agency (ABW) with the assistance of the police – on 7 August we detained a Russian citizen, recruited by Russian intelligence services, whose task was to execute an American and Ukrainian citizen right here in Warsaw,” he said. “This is the first time someone on Russian orders has decided to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country,” added Tusk. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: 7 sierpnia zatrzymaliśmy obywatela Rosji, którego zadaniem było wykonanie egzekucji w Warszawie na obywatelu amerykańskim i ukraińskim równocześnie. Dzięki akcji ABW i Policji udało się temu zapobiec. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Though the prime minister said he was not allowed to name either the suspect or the target, he revealed that the latter was someone who is “inconvenient for Putin’s regime”. Tusk also gave no details of how the assassination was supposed to have been carried out, but said that it was foiled “at the last minute”. In a subsequent statement, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland’s security services, confirmed Tusk’s announcement and noted that the operation to prevent the attack had taken place in cooperation with the US. Police headquarters in Warsaw later revealed that the 29-year-old suspect had been charged with planning a murder and accepting an order to carry out murder in return for material or personal benefit. Both crimes carry jail terms of between two and 15 years. He has also been placed in court-approved pretrial detention. 7 sierpnia br. ABW we współpracy z policją zatrzymała obywatela Rosji, który na zlecenie obcej służby przygotowywał zabójstwo obywatela USA ukraińskiego pochodzenia. Do zabójstwa miało dojść w Warszawie. Operacja była realizowana we współpracy ze służbami USA. — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) August 13, 2026 Poland has been a major target for hostile operations by agents working on behalf of Russia. In February, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the most frequently targeted country in a campaign of sabotage being orchestrated by Russia across Europe. That included an attempt last year to use explosives to derail a train. In June, a Russian artist whose work criticised Putin was assassinated in Poland. Soon after, the Polish security services detained the suspected killer, who they said was using a Georgian passport. Last month, a Russian missile hit Poland during intensive attacks on Ukraine. That followed an incident last year in which around 20 Russian drones violated Polish airspace. Poland has also been one of Ukraine’s closest allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, providing significant military, humanitarian and diplomatic support, as well as welcoming millions of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom remain in Poland. World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



Tickets will go on sale soon via Ticketportal and Ticketmaster.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: How Much Can a Prague Taxi Driver Really Earn Each Month
World.content:
For passengers, a taxi ride can make the job look straightforward. Pick someone up, drive them across Prague, wait for the next booking and repeat.

But the income of a full-time taxi driver depends on far more than the fare shown on the meter or app.

Drivers working through platforms such as Uber and Bolt can generate more than CZK 60,000 in gross monthly revenue when working around 40 to 50 hours a week. What they actually keep, however, is considerably less.



Gross income can exceed CZK 60,000

Official figures for Prague’s taxi sector put the average gross monthly pay at roughly CZK 38,000. Drivers who work full time through ride-hailing platforms can earn more, particularly when they concentrate on periods of high demand.

According to Ondřej Krátký, founder of the Czech taxi platform Liftago, drivers can typically earn about CZK 250 to CZK 350 per hour. At the lower end of the market, however, some drivers make only around CZK 80 an hour, which is difficult to turn into a sustainable income in Prague.

Official statistics may also underestimate the money generated by some drivers because not every journey is paid through an app. Cash payments remain part of the business.

Fuel and commissions take a large share

Most Prague taxi drivers operate as self-employed contractors and use their own cars. That means they are responsible for almost all of the costs associated with the job.

Fuel is one of the largest expenses. Someone driving every day can spend more than CZK 10,000 a month on petrol or diesel alone.

Ride-hailing platforms also take a percentage of each fare. Depending on the service and other conditions, commissions can account for roughly 20 to 25 percent of the fare. Drivers must also cover vehicle maintenance, repairs, commercial insurance and the mandatory social and health insurance payments required of self-employed workers.

Once these expenses are taken into account, the amount left from gross earnings can fall by a third or more.

For a full-time driver, a realistic monthly amount after operating costs can therefore be somewhere between CZK 22,000 and CZK 35,000. The exact figure depends on the car, fuel consumption, working hours, platform commissions and the number and type of trips completed.

Tips make only a small difference

Tips are unlikely to transform a taxi driver’s income in the Czech Republic.

Unlike in countries where tipping is a major part of service workers’ earnings, Czech passengers generally round up the fare or leave a relatively small amount.

Uber allows passengers to tip through its app for up to 30 days after a journey, with the full tip going to the driver. Bolt offers a similar feature.

For most drivers, however, tips remain a minor addition to their monthly income rather than a significant source of earnings.

Timing can make a bigger difference

Drivers can increase their income by choosing when and where they work.

Friday and Saturday nights are among the busiest periods in Prague, particularly in the city centre. When demand rises sharply, ride-hailing platforms can increase fares, allowing drivers to generate more revenue from the same number of working hours.

Major concerts, festivals and other large events can have a similar effect. Airport journeys can also be attractive because they tend to cover longer distances than short trips within the city.

World.title: Czechia Now Ranks Among the World’s 10 Best Countries to Live In
World.content:
Czechia has placed ninth among 192 countries in the 2026 Rumavi Global Relocation Index, which assesses destinations based on factors including safety, healthcare, taxation, living costs and opportunities for people considering a move abroad.

The country scored 69.9 points in the overall ranking, putting it just outside the top five but ahead of Malta and several larger European economies. Estonia took first place with 72.8 points, followed by Singapore, Malaysia, Portugal and Taiwan.

Czechia performed particularly well in the ranking for families, where it placed third worldwide. The index also gave the country strong scores for safety, property rights and climate risk.



Within Europe, Czechia ranked fourth overall. Estonia, Portugal and Lithuania were the only European countries placed higher in the general ranking.

The results are based on the Rumavi Global Relocation Index 2026, a privately produced ranking designed for people considering relocation as well as investors. Rumavi evaluates 192 countries using 24 indicators grouped into four areas: finance and taxes, livability and health, safety and stability, and settling and opportunity.

Czechia scores particularly well for families

The index uses different weightings for different types of people considering a move. For families, safety, education, cost of living and healthcare carry greater weight than tax considerations.

Czechia’s overall result is less impressive for other groups. It ranked 20th among countries assessed for retirees and 25th for digital nomads.

The index also evaluates destinations for entrepreneurs and people primarily interested in tax efficiency, although the rankings can vary significantly depending on the category.

What the index measures

Rumavi says its ranking is intended to measure the practical conditions faced by someone moving to another country rather than simply assessing tourism or passport access.

The 24 indicators cover issues such as affordability, income tax, foreign-income taxation, banking, healthcare, housing, air quality, climate, digital infrastructure, education, business opportunities, language, visa access, property rights and startup ecosystems.

Each indicator is converted to a score between zero and 100, with higher scores representing more favorable conditions for someone relocating. The same data is then weighted differently for six groups: general applicants, retirees, digital nomads, families, entrepreneurs and people seeking tax advantages.

For the general ranking, the most heavily weighted indicators include street safety, foreign-income taxation, cost of living and climate comfort.

Rumavi’s methodology draws on sources including the World Bank, World Health Organization, OECD, World Justice Project, UNODC and other international datasets. Some indicators, including visa access, property rights for non-citizens and aspects of taxation, are classified as Rumavi assessments rather than direct institutional data.

World.title: Passenger Attacks Four Airport Staff After Being Denied Boarding in Prague
World.content:
A passenger attacked four employees of ground-handling company Menzies Aviation at Prague’s Airport on Thursday evening after being denied boarding on a flight to Rome.

The incident took place at Terminal 2, near Gate C9, shortly after 8 p.m., according to Zdopravy.cz.

The woman arrived late for boarding on a Ryanair flight. After being refused entry to the aircraft, she reportedly became aggressive and attacked members of the ground-handling staff.



One of the employees stepped between the woman and a colleague who was being confronted by her. The passenger then bit him.

Airport police were called to the scene and used restraint equipment to detain the woman. She was subsequently escorted from the boarding area and handed over to the Czech police.

“The woman was late for the boarding gate, and after being denied boarding, she physically attacked an airport employee,” Josef Urban, a spokesperson for the Foreign Police Directorate said.

“Responding officers detained her using restraint equipment, and the case is now being investigated as disorderly conduct,” he added.

The incident was also confirmed by Prague Airport spokesperson Jiří Hánich.

The injured employees required medical treatment following the attack. Four members of the Menzies team were reportedly involved in the incident.

Menzies Aviation has operated at Václav Havel Airport Prague since 1991. The company provides ground-handling services covering passengers, baggage, aircraft and cargo for a significant share of flights at the airport.

World.title: Around 300 Czech Citizens Evacuated Due to Fire in Croatia
World.content:
Some 300 Czech tourists are among the 1,000 evacuees with a Czech police officer sent to coordinate the emergency response.

Croatian prime minister Andrej Plenković is in the town holding a coordination meeting with all emergency services this morning. Croatian president Zoran Milanović is also expected later today.

“All those injured in last night’s fire are being provided with the necessary medical care,” Plenković said in an earlier update on X.

No fatalities have been reported. The spokesman said there were also no reports of serious injuries among Czech citizens.

Some tourists left the area on their own, while others are staying at evacuation centres in Omiš and Split. A Czech consul is on site and is in contact with local authorities and security forces.

Fire spreads across up to 1,000 hectares

Around 160 firefighters, supported by specialised firefighting aircraft, are battling the blaze.

The fire has caused significant material damage, according to eyewitnesses, with dozens of cars and homes reportedly destroyed. Strong winds have helped the flames spread across an area estimated at between 900 and 1,000 hectares.

Witnesses reported hearing gas cylinders exploding inside burning homes, while the streets were filled with the sirens of fire engines, ambulances and police vehicles. Large parts of Omiš have also been left without electricity.

Mass evacuation underway

Hundreds of people have fled the affected area, with some tourists escaping by boat, catamaran and other small vessels.

The organised evacuation is being coordinated through the Ribnjak sports hall in Omiš. From there, evacuees are being transported by bus to the Gripe sports centre in Split.

According to Omiš fire chief Slavko Tucaković, foreigners make up the majority of those evacuated.

World.title: Czech Villages Face Water Shortages as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Residents say they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pool.

Communities across the Czech Republic are struggling with worsening water shortages as wells dry up and small streams disappear after years of increasingly severe drought, according to local media on Thursday.



In the village of Krsy in the Plzen Region, tankers are delivering drinking water daily to a reservoir above the village. Some private wells have already run dry, while others are close to empty.

Residents said they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pools.

Authorities are urging households to connect to public water networks where available.

The shortages are also putting pressure on tourist destinations. In Horni Becva, in the Beskydy Mountains, the population doubles during the summer holidays.

The municipality’s two wells have been operating close to their limits, with firefighters called in to deliver water.

Hotels with wellness facilities are among the largest users, prompting local officials to ask businesses to reduce consumption.

Officials hope conditions will improve when the tourist season ends and autumn rains arrive.

World.title: This Website Tracks How Many Trams Are Still Running Without Air Conditioning
World.content:
A new website is giving Prague residents a live picture of how many trams are operating without air conditioning, highlighting an issue that has become particularly noticeable during the city’s summer heat.

The service, Smrdime.cz, was created by developer Christoph Korb. Its name is a play on the Czech word smrdíme, meaning “we stink,” and refers to the uncomfortable conditions passengers can face inside overheated trams.

The website uses live data to calculate the share of Prague’s trams that are currently running without air conditioning. The figures change throughout the day as new vehicles enter and leave service.

When the service was checked on Thursday, August 13, Prague was experiencing temperatures of around 37 degrees Celsius. At that point, 188 of the 256 trams in operation did not have air conditioning, representing about 71 percent of the fleet being tracked.



Of the 147 air-conditioned trams available, 77 were operating at the same time.

The figures provide a snapshot rather than a fixed daily total. As trams are taken out of service and replaced, the balance between air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned vehicles changes continuously.

The project draws attention to a long-standing issue facing Prague’s public transport system: a substantial part of the city’s tram fleet still lacks air conditioning.

The website is based on data from two publicly available sources. Transport information comes from Golemio, Prague’s open-data platform, while weather information is provided by Open-Meteo. The two data sources are used to calculate the current situation displayed on the site.

Korb built the service with Anthropic’s Claude Code development tool. He has also published the project’s source code on GitHub, allowing other developers to inspect the project and contribute to its development.

World.title: ‘People were shouting, trapped beneath the seats’ – exclusive interview, video and latest developments in Polish bus crash
World.content:
“I, too, am a victim: my shoulder is broken, my ribs are broken and my spine has been seriously injured,” one survivor of Sunday’s early-morning tragedy on Hungary’s M3 motorway told this outlet in an exclusive interview. She said she had literally dug herself out from beneath the overturned coach before help arrived. Below are the latest developments in the disaster.

Exclusive interview with a survivor of the Polish bus crash – she had to claw her way out

Twelve people died and one was left in a life-threatening condition after the Polish-registered bus, carrying 57 passengers and two drivers, left the M3 motorway under circumstances not yet fully established and plunged into a roadside ditch. Authorities are investigating what happened, but suspicion is mounting that the driver may have fallen asleep at the wheel. All 57 passengers and both drivers were Polish citizens, prompting Hungary’s Prime Minister and Speaker of the National Assembly yesterday to express their condolences to their Polish counterparts.

Read our previous articles about the tragic accident:

12 killed in devastating bus crash on Hungary’s M3 motorway

‘It happened in seconds’: Survivor reveals horror of deadly Polish bus crash on Hungary’s motorway

Bus crash tragedy in Hungary: Company owner claims drivers were experienced, Polish PM to send special aircraft

The survivor interviewed by Global News, an elderly woman whose name has not been released, is currently recovering in a Hungarian hospital. She said she was on the phone to a friend back home when she heard a huge crash, felt the bus spin and struck her head. She remained conscious enough to grasp what had happened and, literally, to dig herself out from under the bus. Those trapped inside were shouting; most had been pinned beneath their seats.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

Brigitta Szűcs, spokeswoman for the National Ambulance Service, said 14 ambulance units reached the scene. Twelve people died in the crash; one person was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. Nine suffered serious injuries and are being treated in Nyíregyháza, Miskolc, Eger and Debrecen.

Here is the full video, followed by the latest developments:

Driver may have fallen asleep – charges expected soon

Police have opened an investigation into the driver of the bus involved in Sunday’s crash on the M3 motorway on suspicion of negligently causing a fatal mass accident, the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Police Headquarters press officer told MTI on Monday. Rudolf Varga said the driver had been taken into custody and a court could decide on his remand in the coming days. According to the police’s preliminary data, the driver probably fell asleep, MTI reports.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

Two patients now in life-threatening condition in Miskolc

Of the nine injured taken to Miskolc, two are being treated in serious, life-threatening but currently stable condition in the Central Anaesthesiology and Intensive Therapy Unit of Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Central Hospital and University Teaching Hospital, the hospital’s press officer told MTI on Monday. Csaba Németh said both seriously injured patients require surgical intervention; one was in the operating theatre at the time of the statement. Their care and intensive treatment are ongoing.

He added that five patients are being treated in the hospital’s trauma unit, their care provided according to the nature and severity of their injuries.

One injured person left hospital on Sunday after outpatient treatment, while a patient with a spinal injury is being kept under observation in the neurosurgery unit. He is in a condition suitable for transfer for further hospital treatment.The press officer indicated that the hospital is providing an interpreter for relatives and that a Polish medical team may arrive today to help ease the treatment of the injured.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

Polish hospitals ready to receive the injured – seven dead identified so far

Two Warsaw hospitals and several hospitals in southern Poland are ready to receive patients injured in the M3 motorway bus crash, Teresa Kubas-Hul, head of Poland’s Subcarpathian (Podkarpacie) Voivodeship, said at a Monday press conference. Ms Kubas-Hul added that seven of the dead had so far been identified.

The Polish air ambulance service is on standby and, if possible, will repatriate the seriously injured. That decision will be taken by the Polish medical team dispatched to Hungary, the voivode said.If some of the injured need to be treated in Hungarian hospitals, Poland’s state Strategic Reserves Agency (RARS) will procure and deliver the necessary medicines, Kubas-Hul announced.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

She also said that, in addition to others, six Polish police officers and a team of prosecutors had set off for Hungary and were investigating the incident on site on behalf of the Polish side.Earlier official reports said that on Sunday evening Poland’s Deputy Health Minister Katarzyna Kacperczyk, Deputy Foreign Minister Wojciech Zajączkowski, several Warsaw diplomats and six doctors flew to Hungary on a government aircraft.

In case any of the injured need to be flown home, a CASA military aircraft based in Kraków, two air ambulance planes and ambulances have been placed on standby.

Horror crash on Hungarian motorway: Child thrown from British-registered car

Eger hospital organising repatriation of motorway bus crash patients

The Markhot Ferenc Hospital in Eger, in northern Hungary, has begun organising the repatriation of those injured in a bus crash on the M3 motorway over the weekend, a spokesperson for the hospital said on Monday. Erzsébet Szegedi told MTI that the hospital is treating 10 people injured in the crash. Seven of them are being treated in the trauma unit, two in orthopaedics and one in intensive care.

All are in a stable condition, though some are still awaiting further tests, Szegedi said. Four are in a serious condition, typically with cervical, thoracic, or skull fractures, she added. She said staff from the Polish embassy and consulate have arrived at the hospital to coordinate and arrange the repatriation of the injured. Their work is being assisted by two interpreters.

A bus carrying Polish pilgrims crashed in the early hours of Sunday on the M3 motorway near the Mezokeresztes exit in northern Hungary. Twelve people died in the accident, and rescuers treated one person with life-threatening injuries, nine with serious injuries, and a further 37 with minor injuries.

World.title: Why is Orbán slowly visiting all our southern neighbours? He has just been photographed in the company of a former adversary
World.content:
Many believe Viktor Orbán breathed a sigh of relief after his election defeat, first travelling to the United States for the final matches of the football World Cup, then to Serbia for a festival, and more recently being spotted in Croatia in decidedly illustrious company. Is he truly merely on holiday, or is the former prime minister engaged in vigorous negotiations?

Political, water and energy crisis, yet Orbán is not at home

According to Viktor Orbán, by the Tisza majority accepting the removal of President Tamás Sulyok – elected by Fidesz – via the 17th constitutional amendment, they have driven yet another nail into the coffin of Hungarian democracy. He chose to voice this on his Facebook page while everyone knew he was in the United States, attending the World Cup semi-final and final in person, albeit not from a VIP box.Since then, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has suggested he might secure a vice-presidential role at FIFA, while also reporting that Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei could be engineering a deputy UN secretary-general post for his erstwhile ally. Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz spokesman, dismissed all such speculation as press fabrication. Further background and possible consequences can be read in our earlier coverage.

Have Orbán’s former allies abandoned him? He may be seeking international posts that offer protection

Yet Orbán’s former allies have not forgotten him

While Hungary grappled with a water and energy crisis brought on by unprecedented drought and low water levels, the former prime minister was not at home but in Serbia, at a brass-band festival. He was not alone: he was accompanied by Oszkár Világi, the Slovak-Hungarian billionaire, former head of Slovnaft (owned by MOL) and MOL deputy chief executive, as well as Dániel Taraczky, the architect behind the Orbán family’s Hatvanpuszta estate. According to hvg.hu, Világi, in his capacity as MOL deputy chief, may even have been smoothing the way for the acquisition of NIS, the Serbian energy company sanctioned for its ties to Putin, while in the Balkan state.

Not the first holiday with Mária Schmidt

The former premier was recently spotted in Croatia, near Opatija (Abbázia), walking with his former propaganda minister, Antal Rogán, and Mária Schmidt, director-general of the House of Terror Museum. This is not the first time he has stayed at the holiday villa owned by a company belonging to Anna Ungár: in 2023 we reported that he holidayed there even as Anna Ungár’s brother, Péter Ungár, then co-chair of the opposition LMP, was criticising the Orbán system.The photograph sent to 444.hu by a reader does not reveal what Orbán was doing at the villa, but a later image taken in a restaurant shows him again with the same party, indicating this was no one-off occasion.

Orbán in Croatia before. Photo: FB/Villa Kaliopa

Did the former Hungarian prime minister send a message to PM Magyar and the government? Here’s what he had to say

After the election defeat, he sought to topple Orbán

Mária Schmidt was, in fact, one of the leaders of Viktor Orbán’s internal opposition following his second election defeat in 2006, arguing that the ousted prime minister should hand over the leadership of Fidesz, as elections could not be won with him at the helm. The plot was exposed in January 2007; Schmidt’s position weakened, but Orbán ultimately forgave her in a highly visible manner, and the officially trained historian became one of the Orbán system’s most ardent defenders.Schmidt, a historian by training, arrived in Fiume (Rijeka) on a private jet belonging to one of Anna Ungár’s companies, not far from the villa in Opatija (Abbázia). However, according to a source close to the scene contacted by Blikk, Orbán and Rogán travelled to the location by car, not by plane or helicopter.

World.title: Minister sheds light on future of Paks II upgrade, motorway concession and “crazy mistake” of Orbán era
World.content:
Regarding the upgrade of the Paks nuclear plant, Dávid Vitézy, Hungary’s transport minister, said at a press conference that a comprehensive review of the entire project was under way. The current water level had been identified as an “event not expected to occur for many thousands of years”, and therefore the project documentation would need to be reconsidered, he said.

Government helps farmers

Government spokesperson Vanda Szondi said that so far, farmers have filed 31,000 claims for damages due to drought on 770,000 hectares. She noted that the deadline for filing claims had been extended until Aug 31. Szondi said the number of claims already exceeded that in 2022, another record year for drought. She added that the drought in 2022 had been described as the “drought of the century”. She also said that the yield per hectare of arable crops was 10-20 percent below the average for the past five years.

Paks II upgrade under review

In response to a question on the M6 motorway, Vitézy said the previous government had amended the motorway concession contract three times, including instances where “it is very difficult to identify the Hungarian public interest.” He added that the concessionaire, citing the war in Ukraine, had imposed war-related cost increases, meaning that the Hungarian state had assumed its financial risks.

Vitézy thanked everyone for their cooperation in the construction of the Paks underwater weir. “We do not discriminate on political grounds when it comes to whose stones we accept,” he added. He said authorities had also contacted Duna Aszfalt, and the company had made available the barges used in the construction of the Mohács bridge over the Danube. Regarding the upgrade of the Paks nuclear plant, he said that a comprehensive review of the entire project was under way. The current water level had been identified as an “event not expected to occur for many thousands of years”, and therefore the project documentation would need to be reconsidered, he said.

Photo: MTI

Government determined to develop Hungarian railways

In response to a question on railway development plans, Vitézy said that a lack of rolling stock would not be an obstacle to railway development. “At the same time, a great deal of work is needed to get the investor side in order, as during former minister Lázár’s time in office, the capacity, workforce and team capable of carrying out such projects in Hungary had been dismantled,” he said.

Regarding the review of the Otthon Start Programme, Vitézy said that there is no problem in itself with the government helping young people to buy their first home through subsidised loans, and that the programme’s core objective is worth maintaining. At the same time, he said aspects of the programme had encouraged abuse and property purchases made solely for investment purposes, which made a recently launched review by the finance ministry necessary.

Paks on the brink: Critical days ahead, ‘superhuman work’ underway to keep 2 turbines running

Minister talks about “crazy mistake”

Asked about the revamping of Budapest’s metro line 3, he said the funding secured was a signal of the government’s support for the capital. He said it had been a “crazy mistake” to order the carriages without air conditioning; at the same time, EU sanctions on the Russian manufacturer and lack of cooperation on part of the manufacturer to find a solution were causing “problems”. Vitézy said that members of the public have until early September to complete a questionnaire on transport reforms.

Russian-made metro carriages without AC system. Photo: BKK

Meanwhile, he said that the government was working to pinpoint projects opened under the previous administration to include in those financed with EU funding. “We can’t eye every one of them as suspicious.” The minister said it was a major dilemma as to which of the projects completed or put out to tender during the previous government’s term the cabinet should include in the list of those to be financed under the recovery plan. He said all necessary public procurement audits, “but it cannot be ruled out that some of the previous government’s actions might result in disputes,” the minister said.

Tisza Party launches platform for public consultation – reviving name of old show featuring young Péter Magyar

World.title: Hungary’s housing in crisis: Government plans major push for affordable rentals – here’s how
World.content:
The government must intervene and incentivise rental housing construction, which the Wekerle Sandor Housing Construction Programme aims to address, Dávid Vitézy, the minister of transport and investment, said on Facebook on Sunday.

Vitézy insisted that opposition representatives were “fiercely trying to prevent the government from reforming housing policy”. He insisted they were “clearly representing the interests of companies that hoped for massive extra profits from incentives granted for priority investments.” He added that the government is reviewing these exemptions.

The previous government’s “ineffective” housing policy measures, Vitézy said, had left the current government with a housing deficit necessitating intervention. Last year, only 1,256 new homes were handed over per million people, which is “by far the lowest figure” in regional comparison, he said.

“This rate is about one-fifth of Austria’s or Poland’s housing construction, while Czechia and Romania build more than two to three times as many new homes as Hungary. This has contributed to a significant price increase in the housing market, far outpacing real wage growth,” he said.

Meanwhile, the average time people needed to work to afford a new home has grown to seven years from 5.9 years a decade ago, he added.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The Wekerle Programme, he vowed, would help create “more, easily accessible, and liveable homes” through tax and construction regulation changes, while the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility can also be used to build new, affordable rental housing and dormitories.

Comprehensive programmes must be compiled by the end of the year, with the government involving local authorities, real estate, and construction industry stakeholders in the consultations, he said. The goal is to ensure that young people, career starters, and families have access to housing, he wrote.

World.title: Did the former Hungarian prime minister send a message to PM Magyar and the government? Here’s what he had to say
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Ferenc Gyurcsány has issued an unexpected warning about the dangers of turning public anger and the desire for revenge into government policy, arguing that even legitimate grievances must be handled through the rule of law.

In a Facebook post published on Sunday, Gyurcsány said that wanting retribution after suffering a serious injustice was a natural human reaction. However, he stressed that what may be understandable for an individual cannot become the guiding principle of a state.

“What may legitimately drive an individual cannot serve as the basis of state policy.”

Gyurcsány, who served as prime minister between 2004 and 2009 and founded the Democratic Coalition (DK), withdrew from active politics in 2025.

‘Revenge is human – but the state must be different’

According to the former prime minister, people who have been deeply hurt or treated unjustly naturally want some form of redress, and there is no reason to be ashamed of that feeling. The problem arises, he argued, when personal anger becomes a principle of government.

Revenge is inherently personal: the injured person decides what they consider sufficient retribution. Such an approach, Gyurcsány said, cannot provide a sound basis for governing a country. A democratic state instead needs rules that apply equally to everyone and are proportionate, transparent and subject to scrutiny.

This means that punishment should reflect the seriousness of an offence rather than the intensity of the victim’s anger.

Warning comes amid Hungary’s accountability debate

Although Gyurcsány did not name any political figures, institutions or specific cases in Sunday’s post, his comments come at a time when accountability has become a major issue in Hungarian politics.

The Tisza-led government has made investigating alleged abuses of the previous political era a prominent issue. Parliament established several investigative committees earlier this year, while legislation has also been passed concerning the creation of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office.

Against this backdrop, Gyurcsány argued that there are ultimately two possible paths for a government responding to widespread public anger.

One is to channel that anger into lawful accountability, proportionate punishment and compensation for those who suffered losses. The other is to turn revenge itself into a political strategy and continually search for new enemies.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

‘Revenge never becomes complete’

Gyurcsány argued that revenge is ultimately a dead end because it can never provide a definitive sense of closure. If those who have suffered injustice are denied lawful redress, he warned, private revenge may begin to take its place, as individuals lose faith in the state’s ability to deliver justice.

He also suggested that a political force which encourages demands for revenge while in opposition could lose credibility once it takes power if it fails to deliver what its supporters expect.

For Gyurcsány, the answer is therefore not to suppress or deny the desire for revenge, but to transform it into something compatible with democratic government: justice, accountability and restitution.

The former prime minister previously addressed similar themes, warning that a legitimate desire for justice can easily turn into a demand for retribution if it is not kept within appropriate legal and institutional boundaries.

World.title: Paks on the brink: Critical days ahead, ‘superhuman work’ underway to keep 2 turbines running
World.content:
“Superhuman work” is underway to raise the water levels of the River Danube near the Paks nuclear plant to keep two of its turbines operational, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Sunday.

Tuesday and Wednesday will be critical, as an additional 14-15cm drop is expected in the water level, he said. The Danube currently stands 9 centimetres above the water level that would require the shutdown of the second-to-last turbine, a scenario that can only be avoided if the scuttling of the barges achieves the desired result, he said.

Rainfall is forecast in the Austrian catchment areas from Thursday, which could cause water levels to rise again, he said, adding that the construction of the underwater weir was progressing at “breakneck speed”. Water management experts have decided they will open the Ráckeve-Soroksár Danube branch lock on Monday, which will add 20 cubic metres of water per second to the main Danube branch, gaining an additional 2 centimetres, he said.

Have you read this? 5,000 tonnes of stone delivered to Paks: PM Magyar reveals what would have happened without intervention

Meanwhile, the slow scuttling of the two 80-metre barges is still under way, with the vessels expected to reach a 1-metre sinking level by Sunday evening. Pumping water into the hulls will resume on Monday morning, he said.

Magyar said the barges are already under immense water pressure. The cross-positioned barges are secured to 70-centimetre-diameter piles drilled 8 metres deep with unprecedentedly thick, 500-metre-long steel cables. Magyar concluded by expressing his gratitude to the hundreds of experts working in the heat at Paks.
