According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

On 12 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Fauci could face prison if convicted of contempt, former prosecutor says
World.content:
Medical experts say the persecution of Anthony Fauci is weakening America's health system and preventing the world from learning valuable lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Georges Benjamin, chief executive of the American Public Health Association, says US health professionals are frightened by what has happened to Dr Fauci.

"They're afraid to do their jobs that they know need to get done because they're afraid they'll be criticised," he said.

The US Department of Justice is weighing whether to prosecute Dr Fauci over his refusal to answer the questions of a Congressional Committee.

He appeared last month under subpoena before the US Senate committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, but invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

Dr Fauci was given a pre-emptive pardon by former president Joe Biden in January 2025, covering all actions he took from 2014 to 2025. However, Republican senators argue that doesn't exempt him from answering their questions, and he could still face charges for anything after that date.

Anthony Fauci appearing before the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington DC. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

Former US federal prosecutor Amanda Vaughn has told 7.30 that a contempt charge against Dr Fauci was possible.

"I would not be surprised at all," Ms Vaughn said.

"There's some case law that's on Dr Fauci's side here," she said, "but we're in a little bit of a different environment, so it'll be interesting to see what the Department of Justice does."

If convicted, Ms Vaughn said it was possible Dr Fauci could be sentenced to time in prison.

Dr Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment rights more than 100 times during the Senate committee hearing.

"It was a show trial really," said Gavin Yamey, a professor at Duke University's Global Health Institute.

Donald Trump listens as Anthony Fauci speaks during a news conference at the White House in March, 2020. (Reuters: Al Drago)

" And at that show trial, we heard some of the most ghastly, horrific anti-vaccine disinformation I've ever heard. "

Republican committee members accused Dr Fauci of hiding evidence about the dangers of COVID vaccines, destroying public trust in health institutions, and even of helping to create COVID via US funding of a Chinese lab in Wuhan.

"Oh, just a ridiculous conspiracy theory, with no evidence, data, or proof, that Republicans are just hanging onto," Dr Yamey said.

"We know that the most likely cause of this pandemic is a zoonosis, that it came from an animal source."

Sharon Lewin, one of Australia's top infectious diseases experts, said the treatment of Dr Fauci "does a lot of damage".

Anthony Fauci with Sharon Lewin. (Supplied: Doherty Institute)

"The erosion of trust is something that's very, very significant," she said.

"If we had a big pandemic now we'd be asking the public to do all sorts of things, to work in partnership to respond to it, and we need that trust."

Dr Benjamin warned it could lead people to "not follow the advice that they're getting".

"We're already having a lot more vaccine misinformation happen in the United States," he said.

"And if you actually look at the places that followed good evidence, their morbidity and mortality was much less than in those places where they demonised or politicised the response."

Kindergarten vaccination rates in the US are dropping, and earlier this month the US president signed an executive order calling for American children to be vaccinated against fewer diseases.

'Didn't do anything wrong'

Anthony Fauci was director of the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 to 2022. (AP: Al Drago)

Dr Fauci led the scientific response to COVID-19 in the US and was the key presidential advisor on the pandemic.

He advocated mask-wearing and social distancing and urged Americans to get vaccinated as quickly as possible.

"All of this is going to affect people's trusts in vaccines," Dr Yamey said.

"We know that hundreds of thousands of people died. They'd be alive today if they took a vaccine."

The US Center for Disease Control reports that more than 1.2 million Americans died of COVID-19.

Australia's Professor Lewin led research on the diagnosis and treatment of COVID-19 and liaised closely with Dr Fauci during the early stages of the pandemic.

Sharon Lewin says she's "really alarmed" by what is happening to Anthony Fauci. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"I am really alarmed, largely because of what great contribution Dr Fauci has made over multiple decades in public health, serving under seven presidents with distinction, a person with the highest integrity, commitment to science and truth," she said.

Dr Yamey said Dr Fauci was "a man with over 50 years of really extraordinary public service who got America through previous outbreaks and pandemics, SARS, the anthrax attacks, flu pandemics".

Dr Fauci became director of America's National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in 1984, when another global pandemic was at its height.

"He had a huge role to play in turning HIV from what was an almost-always fatal disease into something that people can live a normal life with," Dr Yamey said.

Donald Trump speaks about COVID-19 in February 2020 with Anthony Fauci by his side. (AP: Carolyn Kaster)

Dr Benjamin said Dr Fauci "didn't do anything wrong" during COVID.

He said people resented the impositions on their lives during the pandemic.

"You quite frequently had an unnamed, unknown bureaucrat, usually a health official, telling you you needed to stay home, wear a mask and take a shot. And for a while people were okay with that," Dr Benjamin said.

"But then when it began to get in the way of what they wanted to do, people turned on it. And we just weren't very good at risk communication. We could have improved that a lot."

Prison a possibility

Anthony Fauci was the key presidential advisor on the pandemic. (AP Photo: Jacquelyn Martin)

Dr Benjamin said the proper way to examine the response to COVID would be via a national commission similar to the 9/11 Commission, not via politicised public examinations of Dr Fauci.

"I'm actually an emergency physician and I understand disasters and emergencies," Dr Benjamin said.

"And this was a new, emerging disease. We made a lot of assumptions early on that turned out not to be true. And as we learned more, we adjusted just like you would in any disaster … but if we didn't do the things that we did, many, many more people would've died."

The Senate committee investigating Dr Fauci voted to hold him in contempt for refusing to answer questions, and Kentucky senator Rand Paul has referred that resolution to the Justice Department.

Ms Vaughn says that resolution would normally be assessed without political considerations.

But this is a different environment, she said.

Anthony Fauci speaks in front of the Senate committee last month. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

"What I would normally expect is that career prosecutors would evaluate the potential charge, the strengths and the weaknesses, and make a recommendation on what should be done. And the political appointees in the department would be pretty deferential to that," the former prosecutor said.

"From what I see on the outside, it's not clear that that's what would happen here."

In 2022, Ms Vaughn prosecuted former Trump advisor Steve Bannon.

Mr Bannon had refused to testify before Congress over the January 6, 2021 riots.

He refused to attend the hearings, was convicted of contempt and sentenced to four months in jail. The Supreme Court later vacated the charges and sent the case back to the lower courts.

Steve Bannon served four months in prison after being found guilty of contempt of Congress. (Reuters: Kent J Edwards)

Ms Vaughn, who is now in private practice, said Dr Fauci could face a similar sentence if convicted.

"Contempt of Congress is a misdemeanour, and typically I think the maximum is only a year for this offence," she said.

"But in the US we have what are called sentencing guidelines, and that tells a judge what the recommended sentence is. And for crimes like this, for someone like Dr Fauci, it would really be zero to six months.

"That was the range that Mr Bannon was in, and the judge gave him four months there. So I can't imagine that Dr Fauci, if he were to be convicted, would face anything more than that."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Alleged NDIS fraud plot accused had one-way ticket to Nigeria, court hears
World.content:
A dual citizen charged over his alleged involvement in a $5 million National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) fraud plot had "cut ties" in Adelaide and was preparing to fly to Nigeria before he was arrested, a court has heard.

Foluso Omole appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court today where he was refused bail, after Australian Federal Police officers arrested him at Adelaide Airport on Friday.

The court heard Mr Omole, 38, a dual Australian and Nigerian citizen, had "purchased a one-way ticket to Nigeria" before he was arrested as he allegedly prepared to leave the country.

A prosecutor told the court it appeared he had "sent, over the course of his offending, significant funds back to Nigeria" where his wife resides.

The court heard Mr Omole was working as a NDIS coordinator and operated two businesses which employed a number of staff at the time of the alleged offending.

The prosecutor said it was alleged Mr Omole had received "information improperly" from a woman who was employed by the National Disability Insurance Agency over the course of six years, and "used that information to obtain benefit fraudulently".

The court heard she has also been charged with offending and was due to appear in court on Thursday.

The matter was heard in the Adelaide Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Omole's defence lawyer, Mark Twiggs, told the court his client had informed him that he had been planning to travel on a "return ticket to London" which was "purchased prior to any raid" on the woman's home.

"The charges are denied. He has no record at all," Mr Twiggs said.

"My client has good reason why he should be given bail."

Mr Omole is yet to enter pleas to one count of person deal with proceeds of indictable crime over $1 million and one count of dealing with money/property valued greater than $1 million that is proceeds of crime.

Magistrate Patrick Hill refused bail on the basis that Mr Omole posed a flight risk.

"Whether it was a one-way ticket to Nigeria or a return ticket to London do make a difference as to the court's assessment of whether or not Mr Omole is a flight risk," Mr Hill said.

"For the other reasons put forward by the prosecution, in any event, I remain concerned that he is a risk of flight and the application for bail is refused."

Mr Omole will return to court next month.

World.title: Court hears boy who died sleeping rough in skip bin was missing for days
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the death of a 13-year-old First Nations boy who died after sleeping rough in an industrial skip bin has heard he was missing for five days before his death.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

The teenager — whose family has requested that he be referred to as Budda Spencer for cultural reasons — died in May 2021 after a garbage truck driver tipped the bin during a usual collection round in Port Lincoln.

The boy was sleeping alongside two other young boys, aged 11 and 12, who were under the Department for Child Protection's care.

They were not harmed in the incident.

Budda Spencer, 13, died in an incident involving an industrial bin at Port Lincoln in 2021. (Supplied)

Today, special counsel assisting the coroner, Rebecca Schell, told the inquest the boys had made a decision, before Budda Spencer's death, to not return to their respective homes that night.

"The trio had not slept in the bin before this night," Ms Schell said.

"The three boys lay down in the bin in a row. They had planned to stay awake at night but they all fell asleep.

"It was a cold night, but it was warm in the bin and they used cardboard to keep themselves warm."

Flowers and teddy bears were among tributes left near the scene following the horrific incident. (ABC News)

The special counsel said all three boys awoke almost immediately before they were being tipped into the back of the truck.

The court heard one of the younger boys managed to scramble out of the bin to warn the driver.

"[Budda] Spencer attempted to climb out in the same way — [his friend] told him to stay down," Ms Schell said.

The coronial inquest is being held in Port Lincoln. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The inquest heard Budda Spencer died in the process of trying to escape the garbage truck.

Ms Schell told the court that upon noticing Budda's friend "frantically waving his arms", the driver stopped immediately.

The inquest, which is expected to focus on whether the boy's family had appropriate agency support, is being heard before deputy state coroner Naomi Kereru in Port Lincoln, and will move to Adelaide next week.

Ms Schell told the court the teenager was a "kind, fantastic storyteller who made his friends laugh".

'Was he appropriately supported?'

The court heard that, in the five days before his death when Budda Spencer was missing from home, the boy was spotted at a youth event, and that he had also slept rough at a football oval grandstand in Port Lincoln.

The court heard the police located Budda Spencer during the five-day period and attempted to take him to his house.

"No-one answered the door … and [Budda] Spencer ran off from the police," Ms Schell said.

The circumstances of the incident caused widespread shock. (ABC News)

The court also heard the boy had a good rapport with an OTR petrol station worker who regularly bought him food.

Ms Schell told the court he confided in her, saying "home life was not good".

She said that the night before the boy's death, his two friends were "listed as missing with the police".

Ms Schell said the inquest would consider whether Budda Spencer's family had appropriate support from various organisations in the lead-up to his death.

Budda Spencer's mother Deborah Betts and maternal grandmother leaving the inquest. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

The court heard Budda Spencer's mother Deborah Betts made multiple reports to various agencies about her concerns relating to her son and that she was having trouble making him stay at home.

The inquest is expected to hear from SA Police, West Coast Youth and Community Services, Youth Justice and the Department for Child Protection.

"Was he appropriately supported by various agencies?" Ms Schell said.

"If not, what intervention should have been initiated by the Department for Child Protection?"

Members of Budda Spencer's family outside the coronial inquest, with lawyer Rachael Shaw (right). (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Ms Betts attended court today with her son's grandmother.

Budda Spencer's aunty also attended, and at times comforted Ms Betts while she heard details about her son's death.

World.title: Qantas A380 flew to US and back with maintenance light left in wing
World.content:
A Qantas A380 was cleared to fly passengers return from Sydney to Dallas with a large maintenance light accidentally left inside its wing.

It follows a 2023 incident in which a large tool was left inside a Qantas A380 engine and was not recovered until multiple international trips had been completed.

An Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation found the 33 centimetre light was left behind after maintenance on the aircraft's air conditioning system in Sydney on January 7.

The aircraft then flew to Dallas-Fort Worth and back before maintenance staff realised the light was missing and recovered it from the wing two days later.

The ATSB's final report into the incident found that although the light did not cause any damage to the wing, foreign objects posed a "significant risk to the safe operation of an aircraft".

The light was found in the wing of the plane during work on the aircraft's air conditioning system. (Supplied: ATSB)

ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said the incident was due to a breakdown in tool accountability processes.

"Even well-established processes can be vulnerable when they rely solely on consistent human performance, particularly during maintenance tasks which are often conducted in challenging environments and under operational pressures," he said.

Angus Mitchell says the light was not found during a "foreign object clearance" inspection. (Supplied: ATSB)

"Tool control systems and procedures must account for this variability with safeguards to detect and recover from errors."

The report said Qantas issued a safety directive to address changes to its tooling control processes and procedures and had also formed a "tooling working group".

Qantas said the light had no impact on the operation of the aircraft and it had voluntarily reported the incident to the ATSB.

"Since the event, we have strengthened our tool-control procedures, including introducing a mandatory pre-clearance check to confirm all tooling is accounted for following maintenance," a spokesperson said.

Second tool left inside Qantas A380

It is the second incident involving a tool being left in one of the airline's super jumbos.

In December 2023, a Qantas A380 flew multiple international trips before a 1.25 metre nylon turning tool was discovered in one of the plane's engines.

Qantas plane grounded in Johannesburg Hundreds of Qantas passengers arrive home after being stranded in Johannesburg for three days due to the A380 scheduled to fly them to Sydney being grounded with mechanical issues.

An ATSB report found maintenance staff "lost" the "turning tool" in an A380's outboard engine, and it was only discovered after it had been cleared for service, flying multiple trips between Australia and the US.

Last week, Qantas passengers in South Africa were left stranded in Johannesberg for three days after a problem with the nose wheel of an A380 saw their flight to Sydney cancelled.

Qantas sent another flight to bring the stranded passengers home.

CQUniversity aviation expert and associate professor Steven Leib said any unaccounted-for objects found inside an aircraft were "a real safety concern".

"It may not seem like a big deal, leaving a light or leaving a tool, but these are things that could move around during flight, which could jeopardise the safety of the flight," Dr Leib said.

However, he said the two incidents were not enough to suggest Qantas had a systemic problem.

"The discovery of the lost object was made by the accountability system," he said.

"They were able to trace when it was last used, when it was meant to have been returned and what work was being carried out."

World.title: Architect of current GST system says it is 'working exactly as intended'
World.content:
One of the architects of the Morrison government GST deal that for years has seen state premiers bait each other with insults over their slice of the fiscal pie says the deal was "working exactly as intended".

Former Western Australian senator Mathias Cormann's comments were the latest in attacks launched by WA's political leaders against the Productivity Commission, which on Friday issued an interim report that described the 2018 deal as a costly mistake and recommended it be scrapped.

Premier Roger Cook has called the report's authors "east-coast clowns" and said he had assurances from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese that the current arrangements would remain.

Meanwhile, South Australian Labor premier Peter Malinauskas described it today as a "dud deal" for the rest of the country that needed to be scrapped.

Loading...

Mr Cormann, who was a WA senator between 2007 and 2020, was federal finance minister in the government of Scott Morrison that approved the deal.

He said "the unbelievable unfairness that Western Australia was on the receiving end of [was] addressed" by his government's changes.

Those changes included adding a "relativity floor" that righted a wrong that had seen WA taken advantage of for its mining industry, he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"The national economy and the national budget benefit from Western Australia, having developed these resources," Mr Cormann said.

"That is why our federal budget is so sensitive to movements in iron ore prices, up or down. Because it has such a massive impact on the revenue of the Commonwealth."

How does GST work? Goods and services tax (GST) is a broad-based tax of 10% on most goods, services and other items sold or consumed in Australia.

The Australian Government helps put state governments in a position to provide their residents with comparable services by distributing revenue from the goods and services tax pool according to need.

It is the job of the Commonwealth Grants Commission to advise the Australian Government on how the GST pool should be distributed. Source: Australian Taxation Office and Commonwealth Grants Commission.

'Appropriate balance'

The 2018 GST deal ensures WA gets a bigger slice of GST revenue every year than it would under the national formula.

That original formula was meant to give states the ability to offer a similar level of services by giving more money per person to states with higher needs or lower financial means.

It had been contentious because it resulted in GST payments falling at the same time Western Australia faced falling iron ore royalties.

The 2018 changes still courted controversy, because they delivered WA rising GST payments at the same time as its mining royalties surged as a result of high iron ore prices.

Mr Malinauskas said the interim report had found that situation a "dud deal for the rest of the country".

“Premier Cook can call other people clowns all he likes but it won’t change the independently-verified report that now says it’s a dud deal for the rest of the country,” he said.

He warned the federal government would be blamed in South Australia if it failed to intervene.

Mr Cook's government, however, has maintained that changing the GST distribution would unfairly punish WA for its success.

Mr Cormann says no other state or territory has been left worse off due to the 2018 changes. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Mr Cormann said he believed in the GST being used to support equal service delivery across the country, but that pursuing it single-mindedly extracted too much from WA.

"There's got to be an appropriate balance," he said.

No state worse off

The Commission's provisional report on the 2018 reforms is part of a review required by the legislation which introduced those changes.

According to the Commission, every state and territory besides WA has 98 per cent of their expenditure met with the addition of GST returns, compared to WA's 113 per cent. For everywhere else, the "no worse-off guarantee" tops up the remaining two per cent.

[ Mr Cormann served as the finance minister in the Morrison government. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

Mr Cormann said other states and territories were fairly accommodated for in the GST deal via this guarantee.

"No other [state or territory] has been left worse off as a result of those reforms," he said.

The Productivity Commission is due to issue its final report in December, and Prime Minister Albanese has said he would decide on the matter then.

Mr Cormann said while the debate over the deal would help "inform the best possible final report", he still stood by the structural changes made to the GST distribution model.

"You can always make refinements to improve things at the margins, but the core architecture of the reform should remain in place."

World.title: Anger in the bush as NSW gun buyback scheme labelled 'like stealing'
World.content:
Farmers, sporting shooters and gun sellers are reacting angrily to the New South Wales government's buyback scheme.

In December, NSW brought in limits of four firearms for most licence holders, and 10 firearms for others, like farmers and sports shooters.

The buyback will see those with excess firearms receive up to $1,000 for each weapon from November 2, with the aim to remove 274,000 guns from circulation.

John Kater says the gun buyback will waste money and disadvantage farmers. (Supplied)

Grazier John Kater, from Gin Gin in western NSW, said the compensation being offered was "like stealing" because many people paid much more for guns they may now be required to hand back.

"The compensation amounts at the moment don't justify the expense of the people who have gone out and bought guns," he said.

"Just taking back firearms from people who are already law-abiding citizens is not going to help prevent another Bondi event.

"Will the criminals and the terrorists hand their guns in just because there's a gun buyback?

Mr Kater said the government should instead look closely at gun categories and licensing.

"The money of a buyback could be better spent going back towards programs to make sure the registrations are above board and making sure there's enough government funding for the bureaucracy to have it sorted," he said.

Chris Minns (centre), Tony Burke and Anthony Albanese speak at a press conference for the gun buyback scheme in NSW. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

NSW Premier Chris Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese formally announced the gun buyback scheme over the weekend, describing it as "bigger than the Howard-era".

"This is a big undertaking, but the principle behind it is simple: fewer dangerous guns in our community means a safer New South Wales," Mr Minns said in a statement.

In the initial stage of the buyback, there will be a fixed price schedule ranging from $450 for an air rifle to $1,000 for a centre-fire rifle or revolver.

Starting early next year, owners of more expensive firearms with an "indicative market value above $3,000" can apply for compensation which will be capped at $10,000 a gun.

There will be a flat fee for associated ammunition handed in.

Grants of up to $25,000 and licence fee relief worth $500 will be available to dealers.

Firearms type Firearms Sub-type Compensation Handgun Revolver $1,000 Semi-auto $850 Shotgun Double barrel $850 Single barrel $650 Rifle Rim-fire $600 Centrefire $1,000 Air rifle $450

Shooters treated with 'contempt'

Doug Alcock, the director of coaching at the NSW Sporting Clays Association, said its members had been treated with contempt.

"This isn't fair value," he said.

"It's a basic copy of the West Australian buyback.

" It's a pretty poor attempt, pretty disingenuous, it shows contempt really. "

Nicky Bourke says the buyback scheme will leave some buyers out of pocket by about $1,000. (Supplied)

Nicky Bourke is a gun shop owner in Dubbo in western NSW.

She said the most popular firearms in her shop sold for more than $1,900.

"What do you tell somebody who bought one just before Bondi, that they're only going to get $850 for it, if that?" she said.

Regional business impact

Ms Bourke said firearm sales at her shop had dropped off significantly over the past six months.

"I would say we're down 90 per cent in firearm sales, just firearms themselves," she said.

"Financially, it's dragged on too long."

In a similar situation, Tamworth gun maker Jeff Bacon said businesses were hurting "really bad".

He said turnover for his shop was down 80 per cent since the Bondi Beach terror attack in December last year.

Jeff Bacon organised a One Nation-led gun forum in Dubbo. (Lucy Thackray: ABC Western Plains.)

"We've already seen businesses close," Mr Bacon said.

While the scheme was brought in to address public-safety concerns in the wake of the Bondi massacre, Mr Bacon does not believe it will achieve that goal.

"Arbitrary caps on firearms, that's not going to make any difference," he said.

"If someone wants to obtain a firearm, they [can] do it illegally."

World.title: Lawyers push for shorter sentence for rapist Ralph Carr
World.content:
Disgraced celebrity agent and convicted rapist Ralph Carr is experiencing "a living hell" in prison and should be entitled to a reduced jail sentence, his lawyers say.

Last month, a jury found Carr guilty of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault over an attack against a woman in March 2023.

While in his bedroom, the woman said Carr groped her and then sexually penetrated her against her consent. The attack ended after she punched him in the face and called him "a f***ing rapist".

On Monday, Carr was brought before the County Court for a pre-sentence hearing, which was largely dominated by legal arguments from the defence.

He sat in the dock without his trademark black wig, sporting a shaved head, black-rimmed glasses and a grey prison tracksuit.

A court sketch of disgraced celebrity agent Ralph Carr during his pre-sentence hearing. (ABC News)

He spoke softly when asked to confirm his personal details. He stated his address and described his occupation as a "manager", before misstating his age as 67. Carr's actual age is 66.

Carr is planning to appeal the jury's verdicts, and in sentencing submissions, defence barrister Dermot Dann KC said the attacks Carr was found guilty of only lasted a matter of seconds.

"This must be the shortest incidents of rape that's come before the courts," he said.

Carr in solitary conditions in prison, court hears

Mr Dann KC said his client had a history of PTSD, anxiety, depression and previous suicide attempts.

He said a jail term would weigh more heavily on Carr than a person in normal health, and that prison would have a significant adverse impact on his mental wellbeing.

After last month's verdict, Mr Dann said, Carr repeatedly bashed his head into a wall, his blood pressure soared, he experienced panic attacks and had trouble sleeping.

Mr Dann said his client described being kept in his protective custody cell for 23 hours a day as "a living hell" and believed his career had been "destroyed" by negative publicity.

"The damage to his career has been done because his career relied on public relations, connections, knowing the right people at the right time, creating opportunities for his clients," Mr Dann said.

Mr Dann argued the sentence should be moderated because of concerns Carr's prison isolation could continue indefinitely, a notion Judge Frank Gucciardo disagreed with.

Ralph Carr's identity was kept secret during his trial because of a suppression order. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

The judge, who stated that he did not agree with solitary confinement in nearly all cases, said he had to trust prison authorities would only keep Carr in those conditions for an "appropriate" time.

Under cross-examination, Carr's psychiatrist Jacqueline Rakov criticised the level of medical care the 66-year-old was receiving in custody.

"I would not say they're well-equipped or well-experienced," she said.

Later Dr Rakov conceded it was possible reports she'd written about Mr Carr contained bias, because she had a dual role of treating him and providing independent expert evidence to the court.

Carr expected to ask to delay sentence

Carr retained the support of his siblings, second wife and three children, Mr Dann said, and clung to hope he would be acquitted on appeal.

His lawyers are also preparing to put forward a rare application to stay — or delay — his sentence, a move that could see Carr freed on bail if successful.

Prosecutors will get the chance to address the court on Tuesday.

The woman Carr attacked was not present on Monday and has not authored a victim impact statement, the court heard.

Defence barrister Dermot Dann KC told the court the rape by Carr only lasted a matter of seconds. (AAP Image: James Ross)

The rape trial centred around events on March 23, 2023 when Carr and the victim spent the evening socialising, drinking and taking drugs.

The pair had known each other for about a year and she had repeatedly rejected his sexual advances, the trial heard.

Carr denied the allegations of rape and improper behaviour, and fought the charges at trial.

The jury found him guilty after hearing testimony from the woman, and witnesses including her mother, police officers who attended the scene and a couple who spent time with Carr and the woman earlier in the night.

Carr's identity now public

The media was unable to name Carr as an alleged rapist for nearly three years because of a suppression order granted on mental health grounds.

Carr was finally unmasked on August 3 when his legal team abandoned a bid to keep the gag order in place.

In the aftermath, Carr's current and former clients distanced themselves from him.

Last week, the Labor state government pledged to amend Victoria's Open Courts Act to limit the use of suppression orders if re-elected, so that "convicted rapists can't hide behind a mechanism intended to protect victim-survivors".

The Liberal Party has also promised legislative reform to tighten how accused criminals can apply for suppression orders.

Neither party has outlined specific wording changes to the Act.

World.title: Superwog, Eddie Woo among YouTubers inducted into film and sound archive
World.content:
Together, these Youtubers have racked up more than 36 billion views and boast 84 million subscribers worldwide.

Now they are being immortalised for their contribution to Australia's cultural heritage.

For the first time, 10 content creators have been inducted into the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NFSA) in a partnership with YouTube.

Among the inductees to be recognised at a Parliament House event today are mathematician Eddie Woo, musician Tash Sultana and independent animation studio GLITCH.

⬇️Jump to see the full list of creators⬇️

Woo, a teacher whose YouTube maths lessons went viral in 2012, said the induction was "really quite bizarre, but wonderful".

Meet the maths teacher you wish you had in high school Eddie Woo is changing the face of mathematics in Australia, reaching students far beyond his Sydney classroom.

"It feels completely surreal to be part of the historical cultural collection that the National Film and Sound Archive is," he said.

"I grew up in Australia at a time where … I internalised that I was not Australian, despite the fact that this is where I was born and raised and this is the only place I have ever lived or known.

"Being part of the National Film and Sound Archive — as someone who has taken a long time to appreciate and own my own identity as an Australian — just feels like an absolute privilege that no-one necessarily deserves, but I feel extremely honoured by."

Eddie Woo has used YouTube to bring maths to the masses. (Supplied: Eddie Woo/NFSA)

Vlogger Wengie (aka Wendy Ayche) never imagined herself entering the annals of Australian history this way either.

The Chinese-Australian grew up consuming Dolly and Girlfriend magazines that she said did not tend to reflect her own identity or features.

Instead she turned to YouTube, dispensing makeup tips and DIY hacks of her own.

"I would have never imagined me being part of an Australian collection, because even though I'm Australian, when you look different, it's hard to feel that way sometimes," Ayche said.

"I think it's a great testament to our diversity and our acceptance of different people and what Australians look like."

She joked that future viewers could be a little confused by some of her videos.

"I'm imagining maybe future generations looking at this and going, 'Wow, wasn't culture weird back then?'" Ayche said.

Loading...

Preserving the whole 'cultural wrapper'

NFSA estimates 91 per cent of Australian adults use an online platform to watch video content weekly.

None were more dominant than YouTube, NFSA chief executive Patrick McIntyre said.

But he also understands some may still be catching up to its cultural impact and just how radically it has changed the game.

"A couple of generations ago, if you wanted to make it big, you had to move to LA or you had to get a record deal. Or you had to get funding to produce a TV series that might take years to make," he said.

"Now people with a story to tell can do it their way and still reach audiences of millions.

"[YouTube] is not only helping to shape and explore Australian culture of now, but the majority of these creators' views are overseas, so it's actually a major cultural export too."

These Adelaide filmmakers started out filming stunts for a YouTube audience With youthful energy and a quintessentially Australian soundtrack, the debut film from the RackaRacka brothers hits all the right notes.

The archive has been collecting individual YouTube videos since 2013, but Mr McIntyre said this capsule would preserve each channel's "cultural wrapper" too.

That means oral histories, fandom content and, in the case of the Outback Boys, budgie smugglers.

"It was really important for us to collect all of that platform activity — the likes, the shares, the comments — because that is really part of the cultural impact of the videos themselves," Mr McIntyre said.

It is also a sign of how the archive has adapted.

"The iPhone came out 20 years ago and now robots have hit singles on Spotify," Mr McIntyre said.

"You just can't wait a generation to decide what's culturally significant or not.

"We've really got to be much more dynamic and responsive to culture as it's happening."

World.title: The LNP wants more police, not MPs. Expert says it’s a ‘false economy’
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a case for democratic improvement, State Development shareholdings, looming teacher pay talks, and the simmering four-day week. People don’t like the idea of more politicians, according to the widely held belief. Some people also dislike vegetables, but the consequences of going without are not ideal. And if your doctor suggested you should eat more vegetables, you’d listen – right? The Clerk of Queensland Parliament, Neil Laurie, during an estimates hearing last month. Queensland Parliament In this metaphor, the doctor is the Clerk of the Parliament of Queensland, Neil Laurie, who has held the top parliamentary service job since 2003.





While proud of the reform he has been part of, and not reflecting on any particular parliament or government, Laurie wrote he is “neither blind nor mute about the institution’s weaknesses”. Laurie said an upper house would need to be designed properly but, ultimately, would be unlikely to occur due to the need for a referendum and bipartisan support. Instead, he floats constitutional entrenchment of safeguards, including super-majority style votes to rush bills or add unrelated last-minute amendments. But he also suggests lifting the number of MPs in parliament to make up for decades of unmatched population growth putting pressure on its ability to properly fulfil its functions.



The usual argument against this on costs is a “false economy”, Laurie says, because an extra $35 million a year – at least – is now being spent supporting strained MPs and their offices. That’s compared with an estimated cost of $1 million a year for a new MP, office and staff. For Laurie, another non-upper house reform would be bolstering the government-controlled committee system, which has changed little in 15 years. The last review of that, a decade ago this year, held its punches to allow the changes to “slowly evolve and develop”. Develop they have, but not all in a positive direction.





More answers – and curiosities – in State Development chief shares The changing of the guards at State Development is complete, as newly minted director-general David Mackie officially gets his knees under the desk for the five-year term. Both former State Development director-general John Sosso and his successor, former public sector commissioner David Mackie, until recently held shares in a uranium mining company with the largest deposits in the state – despite a ban on their extraction. Sosso left still doing so. (Circus is yet to receive a hint of a response from Premier David Crisafulli’s team about the appointment process after numerous nudges.) The news presents an opportunity to share an update to an earlier question we’d asked the government: specifically, the Queensland uranium shareholdings of Mackie’s predecessor John Sosso.



While Mackie has spent this year offloading potentially tricky shares ahead of a sideways move to serve under his marriage celebrant and minister, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, Sosso held on. Sosso, through the department, had previously refused to answer our questions about when he purchased the shares. Through the magic of Right to Information, we can narrow the window. Department bosses have had to declare their interests for decades, though it wasn’t until the Palaszczuk government that such disclosures became public-facing. Through this scheme, we were able to nail down Mackie’s purchase of shares in Paladin Energy to July 2021, while he was leading the Justice Department. (We suggest no wrongdoing by him or Sosso.) Paladin, one of three firms in which Mackie and Sosso held shares, lays claim to the largest uranium reserves in Queensland – although mining the resource remains banned in the state.



Readers will know that before Sosso’s return to the state public sector at the 2024 change of government, he headed up Justice under then attorney-general Bleijie in the Newman era. Related Article Exclusive

Public service ‘Creates a smell’: Top bureaucrat urged to detail shares in uranium miner The goods from Circus’ RTI request for Sosso’s declarations of interests from this time show he held no shares coming into the role, and filed an update adding Commonwealth Bank shares in mid-2014. Speaking of shares, the declaration from (former) acting State Development chief Shaun Ferris had him take the title during his short-lived term atop the department as the only DG with shares in Tesla, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey’s Block Inc, and bitcoin. The more you know.



Teachers’ day in court looms for first pay rise in more than a year We’re now well over a year since the expiry of a workplace deal between state school teachers and the government – which means a year without the pay rise that would come from a renewed one. And the next date in the ensuing industrial court dance between the teachers’ union and the Education Department looms (before your next Circus edition) on Monday, August 24. In it, the parties will hash it out not over the broader deal, but a 3 per cent interim pay case. Negotiations between the state and the Queensland Teachers’ Union (QTU) fell apart in June last year, leading to a statewide strike last August.



In October, the state made what Education Minister John-Paul Langbroek called its “best and final offer” to the union. The offer was summarily rejected by voting members, and by early November, the QTU threatened (and then carried out) a second strike, alongside rolling work bans and industrial action. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images A letter from Education Department director-general Sharon Schimming leaked to media outlined several asks from the union to halt the further strike action in late 2025. Those requests included ditching matters the union considered well-trodden ground, and including the interim wage increase in line with wages policy – which the department rejected.



Langbroek warned at the time it could take months for arbitration of the case to make it to the industrial court, with repeated warnings from the state the process could take up to two years. While teachers across several pay brackets hit the award threshold in late 2025 – triggering minor pay bumps – the state has remained steadfast against any pay increase outside a new EBA. Langbroek reiterated this point during his recent estimates appearance, saying that while the state wasn’t opposed to wage increases in line with wages policy, it was opposed to this one. This was because of, in the minister’s words, “the wide scope of the claim and the likely effect on the employer and employees” with an interim pay rise an “arbitrary figure” while parties waited for an Industrial Relations Commission ruling. Miles pumps brakes on talk of four-day public sector work week



It’s the simmering push that keeps bubbling up: a four-day week in the Queensland public sector. Related Article Public service The official David Crisafulli calls direct (just don’t say he bypasses Dale Last) Fresh from a fuel-price linked approach by the Australian Services Union in March, outlined in Circus and promptly waved away by the Crisafulli government, the idea is back. This time, the idea of a shorter week for the same pay has emerged as an element of the draft policy platform getting around before the state Labor conference at the end of the month. As laid bare by our column comrades Chooks, the draft form of the now ACTU-backed effort would ask a state Labor government to trial a four-day week in sections of the public sector before a progressive expansion push through legislation and lobbying with industries and unions.



While a spinner for Opposition Leader Steven Miles had said the pitch showed his party was the only one concerned about working Queenslanders, the man himself qualified things a tad more. “Let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves,” Miles said, noting it was a draft to be hashed out over two of the annual Labor gatherings before a call was made on what would be taken to the 2028 election. “[It’s] not something that we’d be open to implementing in any kind of statewide fashion.” Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: How takeaway, delivery and ready-made meals are reshaping Melbourne’s dining scene
World.content:
Eating outHospitality culture How takeaway, delivery and ready-made meals are reshaping Melbourne’s dining scene While Smith & Deli has ramped up its ready-made meals and delivery, Umberto Espresso Bar has walked away from that area altogether. They’ll unpack these decisions at the free Good Food Symposium. Erina Starkey August 17, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether it’s a pizza pick-up on Friday night, dumplings delivered mid-week or a ready-made meal to help relieve life’s busy juggle, more than ever convenience is driving how Australians eat. New data shows Aussies are just as likely to get dinner to go as they are to dine in at a restaurant – ordering takeaway three times a month and home delivery twice a month, according to Lightspeed’s 2026 State of the Hospitality Industry Report. And the trend is showing no signs of slowing. A takeaway seasonal market plate from Smith & Deli. Ashley Ludkin Takeaway is driving the fastest growth in Australia’s food service market, projected to expandat nearly 12 per cent annually through to 2031, according to Mordor Intelligence. This has had an effect on the hospitality industry’s dine-in revenue, which has fallen to just 20 per cent, down from 31 per cent the year before.



To make up the difference, many restaurants have introduced takeaway alongside dining room service, while others have branched out into ready-made meals and retail food lines, hosting events, chef partnerships or selling merchandise, not as a side-hustle, but as an essential secondary revenue stream. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Shannon Martinez makes plant-based meals to dine in on or take away. Shannon Martinez, the chef-owner behind pioneering plant-based restaurant Smith & Daughters Social Club and cafe-deli Smith & Deli in Collingwood, has spent the past year adapting her business model to meet the market where it’s at. “In all honesty, I was gearing up to close,” says Martinez of both the deli and the restaurant. “I had been fighting as hard as I could, but we were running on dregs.” She told Good Food in June she was ready to walk away, but an investment from Kelly Jarrett gave her the capital she needed to reshape her business, and grow it.



Smith & Deli’s plant-based McMuffin riff. Ashley Ludkin Martinez has invested heavily in the deli side of the business, which offers ready-made plant-based meals, including hot and cold foods served cafeteria-style, as well as frozen lasagnes, pies and desserts to cook at home. “Takeaway is something we’ve always done, but we’ve definitely seen a rise in the sales of it,” says Martinez. She opened a second Smith & Deli in the Melbourne CBD’s Degraves Street laneway in June, with plans for a third spot on the south side; a fourth in Brisbane; and then, Martinez says, “We hope to hit every other state”. Diners can build their own market plate from a selection of hot and cold dishes at Smith & Deli. Martinez will talk about how she’s adapting at the next Good Food Symposium, a panel discussion that brings together the hospitality industry to talk about challenges and share solutions.



The free event, presented by Lightspeed and supported by SevenRooms, is on September 7 at Hyde Melbourne Place. It’s open to anyone working in hospitality – with registration. This year Martinez also branched out into home delivery nationwide. “Obviously, we’re all broke. I think this ready-meal era – especially coming from hospitality businesses rather than ready-made meal companies – makes people feel like they’re getting that next level up of products, and a taste of say, Smith & Deli or Smith & Daughters at home.” There are plans to also take the Smith & Deli range into retail stores. “There’s just a general lack of people out and about shopping, so we needed to figure out a way to get the product to people,” she says. “It’s been a pretty decent income into the business, which is good.” Marco Finazio from Umberto Espresso Bar is pulling back on takeaway. Not everyone is doubling down on delivery. Marco Finazio, owner of Umberto Espresso Bar and Gigi Rooftop in Thornbury, has spent years in the takeaway game, making family trays of lasagne and parmigiana to heat at home, plus offering delivery on Uber Eats. In March this year, he pulled out of both.



“The reliance on technology and convenience is huge, and it’s growing,” he says. “There is a very real pressure of cost of living, and this kind of thing helps people still have a dining experience where they don’t have to cook for themselves.” Umberto Espresso Bar is all about the dine-in experience. Takeaway was lucrative during COVID, he says, but creeping costs have been eating into margins. “You need to buy visibility on [delivery] platforms, which creates another expense, and ultimately, it’s just become too saturated with costs.” That wasn’t the only problem. “It was actually starting to do damage to our brand as the delivery service severely impacted food quality and dish integrity.” Finazio says he’s come full circle. “Let’s just play to our strengths and focus on what our core business is, which is serving wonderful people in the flesh. It’s not about chasing dollars today; it’s about what’s going to pay us in the long run.”



Panellists from the 2024 Good Food Symposium in Melbourne. Harrison Moss Coskun Uysal, an Istanbul-born chef and co-owner of Balaclava’s Tulum, is also on the panel. Earlier this year he launched Kismet, a Turkish tavern at the back of his restaurant as a more casual revenue stream. Sutinee “Tinee” Suntivatana will also be there. The chef-owner of cafes Tori’s and Humble Rays, two Melbourne brunch fixtures, has built a strong following on social media, leveraging viral trends to draw a younger Gen-Z heavy customer base through the door. Rounding out the panel is Rob Stone, senior director of APAC hospitality at Lightspeed, who will share industry-wide insights. The event is hosted by Good Food writer Dani Valent. The Good Food Symposium, presented by Lightspeed and supported by SevenRooms, is on Monday, September 7, from 5.30pm at Hyde Melbourne Place at 130 Russell Street, Melbourne. Register for free here.

World.title: British PM exchanged messages with Trump chief-of-staff impersonator
World.content:
WorldEuropeWorld politics British PM exchanged messages with Trump chief-of-staff impersonator Dominic Penna August 17, 2026 — 8:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Andy Burnham exchanged messages with somebody impersonating Donald Trump’s chief of staff, it has emerged. The British prime minister messaged a person posing as Susie Wiles, who is considered the most powerful woman in the White House. The incident, first reported by Politico, prompted such concern in the British embassy that officials raised concerns with their White House counterparts. Susie Wiles in the Oval Office with Donald Trump last year. Getty Images Downing Street sources admitted that Burnham had been in contact with the impersonator but claimed the messages were not of significance.



However, the messages will nonetheless raise concerns about national security. British officials are said to have feared that Wiles’ phone had been hacked again, after an impersonator reportedly texted and called her contacts in May 2025 to ask for cash and presidential pardons. Wiles privately told colleagues that her personal cell phone was hacked and mined for executive contacts. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. AP The FBI launched an investigation after the breach in which the impostor supposedly sent a series of text messages and phone calls to Republican politicians using artificial intelligence to mimic her voice. The White House said at the time that it took the cybersecurity of all staff “very seriously”, while the FBI insisted all threats against Trump were treated with the “utmost seriousness”.





‘Malicious’ impersonation campaign Last year American intelligence services warned of an “ongoing malicious text and voice campaign” where actors impersonated senior US officials to target individuals. Related Article US Votes 2024 Donald Trump’s campaign says its emails were hacked US authorities have previously accused hackers acting on behalf of Iran in the final months of Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Information security has been an ongoing concern at the White House, with one hacker managing to breach the communications service used by Mike Waltz, the former national security adviser, in April 2025.





Just weeks after the illegal Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Ben Wallace and Priti Patel – the then defence and foreign secretaries – were fooled by Russian “impostors” who posed as Ukrainian politicians. Related Article US politics ‘Susie, what do you think?’ The woman of power who has Trump’s ear Both Wallace and Patel held video calls, requested in the name of an aide at the Ukrainian embassy, before eventually becoming suspicious and ending the exchanges. Wallace believed that he was talking to Denys Shmyhal, who was then serving as the Ukraine prime minister and is now Volodymyr Zelensky’s energy minister. He said the man looked and sounded like the Ukraine prime minister but became suspicious when the caller – who was posing in front of a Ukrainian flag – began to ask questions relating to UK security.



Patel responded to the incident by revealing that the same thing had happened to her, calling it a “pathetic attempt at such difficult times to divide us”. A Downing Street spokesman said: “We do not comment on national security matters.” The White House declined to comment.
