World.title: Revealed: The Swans players who could be stood down on finals eve amid sexual assault investigation
World.content:
Key Sydney Swans players are at the centre of a Victoria Police sexual assault investigation putting their immediate playing futures under a cloud and plunging the club’s finals campaign into turmoil. The investigation relates to an allegation of sexual assault at an East Melbourne hotel hours after the team’s victory over Essendon at the MCG on Sunday night. Loading This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and one other player after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. This masthead is not suggesting all five players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with enquiries. The group of five were driving home to Sydney in a rental car on Monday night.



A manager representing a fifth player denied his client was one of the players involved. The five players are unlikely to play this week regardless of the police investigation, as the Swans consider potential sanctions for late-night drinking at the team hotel, which is funded by the AFL, after a match. Chad Warner (left), Isaac Heeney (right), James Jordon (middle bottom) and Riley Bice (middle top) of the Swans. Michael Howard Asked whether they were considering standing down the players, the Swans said all options were open as they worked through the facts of what happened. This was confirmed by a senior AFL source. The players were not arrested. Police asked to review CCTV footage from the Pullman East Melbourne as part of their investigation.



Plain clothes officers went inside hotel rooms and left the venue with a number of items in evidence bags, according to a witness to the police visit. They also asked for footage from cameras that cover public areas of the hotel such as the lobby, stairs and lifts. The Swans have been left “shocked and disappointed” amid the investigation, which focuses on the actions of a group of players in the early hours of Monday morning. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich fronts the media on Monday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The team was staying at the Pullman after their victory over Essendon at the nearby MCG. Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich briefly fronted media in Sydney on Monday to address the alleged incident.



“We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing. It’s safe to say that we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation,” Pavlich said. “We understand the level of interest in the matter. There’s going to be lots of speculation, but given it’s a police matter right now, that is all that we can say.” The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Simon Schluter Pavlich did not take questions, and did not respond to a reporter’s question about whether or not arrests had been made. Two industry sources, speaking anonymously because the investigation is ongoing, said the players were driving back to Sydney on Monday evening to avoid media at Melbourne and Sydney airports.



The AFL held discussions with the Swans on Monday about whether the club would identify the players, and about whether they would be available to play in the coming weeks. One photo being shared in chat groups, showing a woman with damaged teeth, does not relate to the incident. It was published by tabloid news sites in the UK earlier this year, months before the incident. Police with clipboards and camera equipment were seen in the lobby of the hotel on Monday morning. Pullman hotel staff would not comment.



Victoria Police confirmed they were “investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne on August 17”. “The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning,” it said in a statement. “The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing.” Swans board member and club great Michael O’Loughlin was spotted at Sydney’s domestic airport on Monday but declined to shed further light on the matter when approached for comment. “No, we’ll wait and see what the findings are, I don’t know,” O’Loughlin said.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Hidden boardrooms, crime threats and nude pics: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit Earlier on Monday the Swans released a statement. “The Sydney Swans can confirm several players were involved in an alleged incident in Melbourne last night,” the club confirmed in a statement on Monday. “The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage.” The AFL confirmed the league had been notified by the Swans and said the matter rested with police.



In cases such as this, the AFL’s integrity unit defers to police. The Swans are second on the ladder and well-placed to contend for the premiership with 17 wins, with one home-and-away round left before finals. They are due to play North Melbourne next Sunday in Sydney. Unlike the NRL, the AFL does not have a no-fault stand down rule for players charged with serious offences. However, Geelong’s Tanner Bruhn did not play for the Cats in 2025 after he was charged with rape and intentional sexual touching. The charges were dropped last November after a key witness admitted to lying, and Bruhn’s name was suppressed until the case was discontinued. St Kilda sacked Andrew Lovett after he was charged with rape in 2010, terminating his contract over “a series of acts and omissions in breach of his employment contract”. He was later found not guilty of the rape charge.



In 2013, St Kilda player Stephen Milne took an indefinite leave of absence from the club after he was charged with three counts of rape. The charges were dropped when Milne instead pleaded guilty to a single charge of indecent assault. The Sydney players have not been arrested or charged with any offence. With Marc McGowan Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Meet baby Miracle: Australia’s most premature newborn to survive
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBabies Meet baby Miracle: Australia’s most premature newborn to survive Abbey Geran August 17, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I took one look at her and I was like, ‘there’s no way she’s going to make it’,” remembers Annrose Tunavasa of the day she met her baby girl. In the living room of their Logan Reserve home, 35 kilometres south of Brisbane, she and her husband Misi cradle their four-month-old daughter in their arms. Loading Makerita Miracle Tanuvasa has already broken records, defied modern medical standards, and left doctors in awe. But her proud parents are just grateful she has survived. “It was just like she was here to fight,” says mum Annrose.



On March 20, Annrose visited her GP. She had just completed a six-week gym challenge, but dropped little weight, and suspected she may be four or five weeks pregnant. Related Article Fertility Brisbane, where have all the babies gone? See how your suburb has changed over time “I went to do an ultrasound and the sonographer told us that we were about 22 weeks pregnant,” she remembers. “I said ‘that’s impossible’.” Annrose explained that she had suffered a miscarriage in December. “She said, ‘Well, maybe you had a twin, and you miscarried the twin … you’ve got to go to the hospital and you’ll be staying there until you give birth.’”



Five days later, Annrose gave birth at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital at 7:08pm. Her middle name says it all. Miracle, as she is now affectionately known, measured 30.5 centimetres upon arrival and weighed just 351 grams, making her the tiniest newborn in Queensland history. Her weight was some 23 grams less than Australia’s Coke Can Kid, Jonathon Heeley, who was born in 1992 and famously drew comparisons to the size of the soft drink. Miracle made the RBWH’s intensive care unit her home for 14 weeks. Father Misi said his daughter was about the size of his palm. “We weren’t able to hold her, but she was very, very small,” he says.



She was so small, clinicians were left perplexed. “A week later the doctor came in to see me, and she said, ‘She’s just not matching the scans that you came in with, she doesn’t match that baby’,” Annrose explains. “I was measuring at 500 grams, measuring at 22 weeks pregnant.” Baby Miracle and family. Nine News Annrose was asked to retrieve the scans she had completed prior to her miscarriage in December, which showed her baby was even more premature than first thought.



“They said, this has got to be the same pregnancy.” Related Article Pregnancy ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first Doctors told the couple Miracle was in fact born at 21 weeks and 3 days – so premature that resuscitation usually is not an option. The revelation means she is not only Queensland’s smallest baby, but also believed to be the most premature in Australia to live. Previously, that was baby Stevie O’Reilly, born at 22 weeks and two days at Townsville University Hospital in July last year.



The Guinness World Records recognises Iowa toddler Nash Keen, born at exactly 21 weeks in July 2024, as the most premature baby to survive worldwide. “Even the doctors couldn’t explain how she was able to survive everything she’s gone through,” says Misi. Annrose nods. “She said, we can’t give you any answers. Everything is actually just a miracle. And I just said, ‘well, let’s keep it like that’.” Staff congratulate mum Annrose and baby Miracle as she leaves hospital. Nine News Following her frantic delivery, Annrose and Misi spent the next month whispering to their daughter from behind the glass facade of a neonatal intensive care incubator.



Miracle was covered head to toe in tubes and cables as a mighty, multidisciplinary team of health care workers kept a watchful eye over her. Related Article Fertility Seven things to know about Australia’s baby bust – and what it means for you Four weeks into her life, the then petrified parents were finally able to hold their precious girl. “It was magical, but it was also very scary, holding such a tiny baby,” says Annrose. Miracle made the RBWH’s intensive care unit her home for 14 weeks.



After six weeks, Annrose moved into Herston’s Ronald McDonald House and she and Misi juggled parenting their two other children, aged 1 and 4, with monitoring their growing newborn. “Every visit, it was like real quiet, like almost like no one wanted to tell us, ‘we don’t know if she’s going to survive or not’,” Annrose recalls. “But I think after one month, it just started to get real bright in the room.” Baby Miracle with proud parents Annrose and Misi. Eventually, Miracle was transferred to Logan Hospital’s special care nursery.



She was discharged in early August, more than four months after she was born and at what would have marked 40 weeks gestation. “I haven’t seen a 21-plus-three-weeker,” says registered nurse Renee Judd. “We’ve had other little babies here, but not that young, and I have been 16 years in the neonatal journey in Logan.” The nurses and midwives who cared for her formed a guard of honour as Annrose carried her daughter from the facility – remarkably, without an oxygen tank. Annrose and Misi teared up as they thanked the healthcare heroes who kept Miracle alive.



“Thank you guys so much for all the love and care you gave our daughter, the nurses, the doctors, the cleaners … social workers, Ronald McDonald House in Herston. Thank you guys so much for everything.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Middle of nowhere’: fears private primary school would overwhelm farming hamlet
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Middle of nowhere’: fears private primary school would overwhelm farming hamlet Caroline Schelle August 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Plans to build a private primary school for more than 300 students have distressed locals in a tiny farming community of 100 people near Geelong. Bacchus Marsh Grammar School has applied to build a private primary school at its Staughton Vale campus, 40 minutes from Geelong, which now teaches agriculture, outdoor education and environmental studies to 150 students. Locals Mark Trengove, Mandy Cocks, Michael Dragt and Kristy Vasils with Kristy’s children Ollie, 11, and Savannah, 9, on Staughton Vale Road at the site of Bacchus Marsh Grammar School’s proposed campus. Penny Stephens If the government approves the school, it would mean there would be 300 extra students commuting to the 83½-hectare property, dwarfing the local community of just 100 people. The private school already has 3800 students at two other campuses at Maddingley, in Bacchus Marsh, and Woodlea, in Melton.



The school wants to expand the Staughton Vale site to create a primary to Year 8 campus, retaining the 150 agriculture students and offering “added capacity and greater choice for families across the wider region”, according to its application to the state government’s planning department. But Staughton Vale and Anakie Action Group member Kristy Vasils said she was shocked to find out through other members of the community that the school planned to build a primary school at the site. “We’re just kind of wondering why they would want to put a school out in the middle of nowhere and plan to bus kids in. “If we were to have an increase in traffic coming past of buses and things like that, especially at 3.30 in the afternoon, that is really concerning for me because it’s already pretty congested at that time of the day,” she said. Vasils, who lives in Anakie, 12 kilometres away, said the local community was happy with the current campus.



“We don’t mind them bringing students out and showing them a beautiful piece of land and doing gardening and different activities with them there,” she said. “The problem is with this particular permit that they’re now applying for … they’re wanting 300 permanent primary school students there, along with 150 high school students as well.” Mark Trengove and Michael Dragt on Staughton Vale Road with the site of Bacchus Marsh Grammar School’s Staughton Vale farm campus driveway behind them. Penny Stephens Bacchus Marsh Grammar principal Debra Ogston said the campus had operated for more than a decade and the school had followed the standard planning process. “As part of this process, members of the community have the opportunity to consider the proposal and make submissions before a decision is made by the responsible authority,” she said.



The principal said hundreds of Bacchus Marsh Grammar students benefited from the agricultural, outdoor and environmental learning at the Staughton Vale property. “The proposed development will broaden these opportunities for students in Melbourne’s west,” she said. Others who lived closer to the property said they were concerned about how it could affect the landscape and environment of the area. Michael Dragt lives opposite the property and said he feared an approval meant the school could continue to expand. “We have no doubt it’s part of their growth plans,” he said.



Dragt said the number of students would overwhelm the area, which was zoned for farming and had four people per kilometre. “It’ll totally change the environment out there,” he said. The area was zoned for farming, and many locals still grew crops or had stock on neighbouring land, he said. “They’re not connected to anyone in the farming community to help, you know, grow those learnings with the kids – that’s what I’d like to see happen.”



Dragt was also concerned that students wouldn’t be able to evacuate quickly if there was a bushfire. “It’s a deep concern to think that they would place the school so far out of context with no resources.” Ecologist Mark Trengove, who also lives nearby, said the plans were outrageous. “It’s just totally inappropriate the way they’ve treated the community and what they’re actually fundamentally trying to do is inappropriate,” he said. He was also concerned the biodiversity report the school commissioned didn’t address impact on threatened species, including the endangered swift parrot and yellow gum trees.



Students would be bused to the location from the existing secondary school and surrounding areas using private bus services, the planning documents say, while staff would drive and use an on-site car park. The documents claim the rural location is essential to the operation of the campus. A Victorian government spokesman said the proposal would be considered on its merits and as it was under assessment it would be inappropriate to comment further. World.title: Natalie loved her Darebin community – until she felt its undercurrent of hostility to Jews
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCity life Natalie loved her Darebin community – until she felt its undercurrent of hostility to Jews Angelica Snowden August 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Natalie James loved going to her local cafe in her progressive and diverse inner north Melbourne neighbourhood. But her feelings changed after graffiti including “F*** Israel”, “Free Palestine” and “Land Back” appeared days after a mass shooting targeting the Jewish community in Bondi last December killed 15 people. James reported the graffiti – which included a crossed-out Star of David – to Darebin City Council, thinking it would be removed swiftly. It was not, and she began to feel that her neighbourhood was turning hostile to Jews like herself. Natalie James, former Fair Work Ombudsman, fought to have anti-Israel graffiti removed from her local council area. Joe Armao It took six months and multiple complaints for Darebin City Council to remove the graffiti that was spray-painted over a mural. The cleanup took less than a day.



In the meantime, James – a former Fair Work Ombudsman and former secretary of the Federal Department of Employment and Workplace Relations – was left confused and distressed at what had happened to her neighbourhood. “It’s a sign that people who wrote it don’t think Jews are welcome in this neighbourhood. It’s a sign that the neighbourhood might not be safe,” James told The Age. Image of graffiti reported to City of Darebin. James has reflected over the past two years on use of terminology like “get out, Zionist”, which she has also observed around Darebin, trying to understand “who do they mean”, she said. “But they mean me. I don’t know who they are trying to get out other than Jewish people in Darebin,” she said.



Related Article City life Palestinian flag to be lowered from city hall after fiery debate James appeared at the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion in late July. She was one of more than 20,000 individuals and organisations to lodge a submission and was asked to prepare a witness statement which focused on the public service. But in her full submission, shared with The Age, James explained how the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 and the Bondi Beach shooting upended her professional and personal life. “I am not religious. But I am unambiguously Jewish: by culture, by family, by history, by DNA,” her submission read. She was profoundly affected by the December 14 killing of 15 people at a Jewish celebration at Bondi Beach, which came at a key point in her professional life.



“On the evening of 14 December 2025, I was preparing to fly to Canberra the next morning for what I knew would be the announcement of my exit from my role. “After watching the event unfold on my television with disbelief, I was almost paralysed. I didn’t want to go to Canberra. I wanted to be with my family.” After the attacks at Bondi, James said a tension between her love of the neighbourhood and her feelings of isolation as a Jew emerged. “I love my progressive, politically engaged, diverse community,” she said in her submission. But “anti-Israel, anti-Zionist and anti-Jew material began to appear on everything from posters to traffic-light stickers”, her submission read.



Natalie James, recently resigned Department of Employment and Workplace Relations secretary, gave evidence to the Royal Commission into Antisemitism. Joe Armao “As the protests became a weekly fixture, stories emerged about Jewish business owners being targeted and hounded out. I began to feel that my neighbourhood had become hostile to me.” In March, Darebin City Council lowered the Palestinian flag it had flown for more than two years above a council building in Preston, after councillors voted on the municipality’s new flag policy. The flag was lowered after a drawn-out and divisive consultation process that attracted 500 submissions, including one from James, and heated debate among councillors. James had noticed other examples of graffiti around the neighbourhood, including swastikas, “Zionists out” and “protect jews, destroy Israel”.



James briefly mentioned the graffiti in her appearance at the Royal Commission on July 28, but in her full submission, she detailed a six-month quest have it removed. Protesters march through Melbourne supporting Palestine. Elke Meitzel James said she first reported the graffiti in mid-December via the Snap, Send, Solve app, used for reporting issues to councils. “[Israeli Prime Minister] Benjamin Netanyahu is not going to see this graffiti. People making decisions about the conflict in the Middle East are not going to see this graffiti. But ordinary people, including Jewish people, who are members of this neighbourhood, are going to see it,” she said. James said she got no response to her initial December report, but in January followed up and was told the Council could not take action unless graffiti is on council or public property, but she could ask the property owner to remove it herself.



James said she felt distressed. “You want me to out myself to a person who runs a coffee shop and then ask them to spend their money removing this offensive piece of graffiti that they didn’t put there,” she said. Darebin City Council was contacted for comment, but did not issue a response before deadline. The council’s graffiti policy states offensive graffiti is deemed to be “priority one”, and efforts should be made to remove it within two days of a report regardless of location. Offensive graffiti is defined as having the “potential to insult members or groups of the community and commonly includes defamatory or degrading remarks about race, religion, sex or personal privacy”. Despite several calls and emails there was again no action until June 30, when James said a different officer called her, apologised and told her the graffiti would be removed that day. It was, James said. James said she understood people have “strong points of view about things they’re seeing and hearing”.



“I’m not naive. Peace is not going to break out because we have some good conversations, but I think people that I speak to observe that the space we might have had for interfaith dialogue, for sitting down and having these conversations that might not be comfortable, but can be respectful, we’re not sure where that space is any more. “I think we need to be working to create those spaces. Frankly, I think local councils are in a prime position to be facilitating that.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The LNP wants more police, not MPs. Expert says it’s a ‘false economy’
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a case for democratic improvement, State Development shareholdings, looming teacher pay talks, and the simmering four-day week. People don’t like the idea of more politicians, according to the widely held belief. Some people also dislike vegetables, but the consequences of going without are not ideal. And if your doctor suggested you should eat more vegetables, you’d listen – right? The Clerk of Queensland Parliament, Neil Laurie, during an estimates hearing last month. Queensland Parliament In this metaphor, the doctor is the Clerk of the Parliament of Queensland, Neil Laurie, who has held the top parliamentary service job since 2003.





While proud of the reform he has been part of, and not reflecting on any particular parliament or government, Laurie wrote he is “neither blind nor mute about the institution’s weaknesses”. Laurie said an upper house would need to be designed properly but, ultimately, would be unlikely to occur due to the need for a referendum and bipartisan support. Instead, he floats constitutional entrenchment of safeguards, including super-majority style votes to rush bills or add unrelated last-minute amendments. But he also suggests lifting the number of MPs in parliament to make up for decades of unmatched population growth putting pressure on its ability to properly fulfil its functions.



The usual argument against this on costs is a “false economy”, Laurie says, because an extra $35 million a year – at least – is now being spent supporting strained MPs and their offices. That’s compared with an estimated cost of $1 million a year for a new MP, office and staff. For Laurie, another non-upper house reform would be bolstering the government-controlled committee system, which has changed little in 15 years. The last review of that, a decade ago this year, held its punches to allow the changes to “slowly evolve and develop”. Develop they have, but not all in a positive direction.





More answers – and curiosities – in State Development chief shares The changing of the guards at State Development is complete, as newly minted director-general David Mackie officially gets his knees under the desk for the five-year term. Both former State Development director-general John Sosso and his successor, former public sector commissioner David Mackie, until recently held shares in a uranium mining company with the largest deposits in the state – despite a ban on their extraction. Sosso left still doing so. (Circus is yet to receive a hint of a response from Premier David Crisafulli’s team about the appointment process after numerous nudges.) The news presents an opportunity to share an update to an earlier question we’d asked the government: specifically, the Queensland uranium shareholdings of Mackie’s predecessor John Sosso.



While Mackie has spent this year offloading potentially tricky shares ahead of a sideways move to serve under his marriage celebrant and minister, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, Sosso held on. Sosso, through the department, had previously refused to answer our questions about when he purchased the shares. Through the magic of Right to Information, we can narrow the window. Department bosses have had to declare their interests for decades, though it wasn’t until the Palaszczuk government that such disclosures became public-facing. Through this scheme, we were able to nail down Mackie’s purchase of shares in Paladin Energy to July 2021, while he was leading the Justice Department. (We suggest no wrongdoing by him or Sosso.) Paladin, one of three firms in which Mackie and Sosso held shares, lays claim to the largest uranium reserves in Queensland – although mining the resource remains banned in the state.



Readers will know that before Sosso’s return to the state public sector at the 2024 change of government, he headed up Justice under then attorney-general Bleijie in the Newman era. Related Article Exclusive

Public service ‘Creates a smell’: Top bureaucrat urged to detail shares in uranium miner The goods from Circus’ RTI request for Sosso’s declarations of interests from this time show he held no shares coming into the role, and filed an update adding Commonwealth Bank shares in mid-2014. Speaking of shares, the declaration from (former) acting State Development chief Shaun Ferris had him take the title during his short-lived term atop the department as the only DG with shares in Tesla, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey’s Block Inc, and bitcoin. The more you know.



Teachers’ day in court looms for first pay rise in more than a year We’re now well over a year since the expiry of a workplace deal between state school teachers and the government – which means a year without the pay rise that would come from a renewed one. And the next date in the ensuing industrial court dance between the teachers’ union and the Education Department looms (before your next Circus edition) on Monday, August 24. In it, the parties will hash it out not over the broader deal, but a 3 per cent interim pay case. Negotiations between the state and the Queensland Teachers’ Union (QTU) fell apart in June last year, leading to a statewide strike last August.



In October, the state made what Education Minister John-Paul Langbroek called its “best and final offer” to the union. The offer was summarily rejected by voting members, and by early November, the QTU threatened (and then carried out) a second strike, alongside rolling work bans and industrial action. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images A letter from Education Department director-general Sharon Schimming leaked to media outlined several asks from the union to halt the further strike action in late 2025. Those requests included ditching matters the union considered well-trodden ground, and including the interim wage increase in line with wages policy – which the department rejected.



Langbroek warned at the time it could take months for arbitration of the case to make it to the industrial court, with repeated warnings from the state the process could take up to two years. While teachers across several pay brackets hit the award threshold in late 2025 – triggering minor pay bumps – the state has remained steadfast against any pay increase outside a new EBA. Langbroek reiterated this point during his recent estimates appearance, saying that while the state wasn’t opposed to wage increases in line with wages policy, it was opposed to this one. This was because of, in the minister’s words, “the wide scope of the claim and the likely effect on the employer and employees” with an interim pay rise an “arbitrary figure” while parties waited for an Industrial Relations Commission ruling. Miles pumps brakes on talk of four-day public sector work week



It’s the simmering push that keeps bubbling up: a four-day week in the Queensland public sector. Related Article Public service The official David Crisafulli calls direct (just don’t say he bypasses Dale Last) Fresh from a fuel-price linked approach by the Australian Services Union in March, outlined in Circus and promptly waved away by the Crisafulli government, the idea is back. This time, the idea of a shorter week for the same pay has emerged as an element of the draft policy platform getting around before the state Labor conference at the end of the month. As laid bare by our column comrades Chooks, the draft form of the now ACTU-backed effort would ask a state Labor government to trial a four-day week in sections of the public sector before a progressive expansion push through legislation and lobbying with industries and unions.



While a spinner for Opposition Leader Steven Miles had said the pitch showed his party was the only one concerned about working Queenslanders, the man himself qualified things a tad more. “Let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves,” Miles said, noting it was a draft to be hashed out over two of the annual Labor gatherings before a call was made on what would be taken to the 2028 election. “[It’s] not something that we’d be open to implementing in any kind of statewide fashion.” Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: How takeaway, delivery and ready-made meals are reshaping Melbourne’s dining scene
World.content:
Eating outHospitality culture How takeaway, delivery and ready-made meals are reshaping Melbourne’s dining scene While Smith & Deli has ramped up its ready-made meals and delivery, Umberto Espresso Bar has walked away from that area altogether. They’ll unpack these decisions at the free Good Food Symposium. Erina Starkey August 17, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether it’s a pizza pick-up on Friday night, dumplings delivered mid-week or a ready-made meal to help relieve life’s busy juggle, more than ever convenience is driving how Australians eat. New data shows Aussies are just as likely to get dinner to go as they are to dine in at a restaurant – ordering takeaway three times a month and home delivery twice a month, according to Lightspeed’s 2026 State of the Hospitality Industry Report. And the trend is showing no signs of slowing. A takeaway seasonal market plate from Smith & Deli. Ashley Ludkin Takeaway is driving the fastest growth in Australia’s food service market, projected to expandat nearly 12 per cent annually through to 2031, according to Mordor Intelligence. This has had an effect on the hospitality industry’s dine-in revenue, which has fallen to just 20 per cent, down from 31 per cent the year before.



To make up the difference, many restaurants have introduced takeaway alongside dining room service, while others have branched out into ready-made meals and retail food lines, hosting events, chef partnerships or selling merchandise, not as a side-hustle, but as an essential secondary revenue stream. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Shannon Martinez makes plant-based meals to dine in on or take away. Shannon Martinez, the chef-owner behind pioneering plant-based restaurant Smith & Daughters Social Club and cafe-deli Smith & Deli in Collingwood, has spent the past year adapting her business model to meet the market where it’s at. “In all honesty, I was gearing up to close,” says Martinez of both the deli and the restaurant. “I had been fighting as hard as I could, but we were running on dregs.” She told Good Food in June she was ready to walk away, but an investment from Kelly Jarrett gave her the capital she needed to reshape her business, and grow it.



Smith & Deli’s plant-based McMuffin riff. Ashley Ludkin Martinez has invested heavily in the deli side of the business, which offers ready-made plant-based meals, including hot and cold foods served cafeteria-style, as well as frozen lasagnes, pies and desserts to cook at home. “Takeaway is something we’ve always done, but we’ve definitely seen a rise in the sales of it,” says Martinez. She opened a second Smith & Deli in the Melbourne CBD’s Degraves Street laneway in June, with plans for a third spot on the south side; a fourth in Brisbane; and then, Martinez says, “We hope to hit every other state”. Diners can build their own market plate from a selection of hot and cold dishes at Smith & Deli. Martinez will talk about how she’s adapting at the next Good Food Symposium, a panel discussion that brings together the hospitality industry to talk about challenges and share solutions.



The free event, presented by Lightspeed and supported by SevenRooms, is on September 7 at Hyde Melbourne Place. It’s open to anyone working in hospitality – with registration. This year Martinez also branched out into home delivery nationwide. “Obviously, we’re all broke. I think this ready-meal era – especially coming from hospitality businesses rather than ready-made meal companies – makes people feel like they’re getting that next level up of products, and a taste of say, Smith & Deli or Smith & Daughters at home.” There are plans to also take the Smith & Deli range into retail stores. “There’s just a general lack of people out and about shopping, so we needed to figure out a way to get the product to people,” she says. “It’s been a pretty decent income into the business, which is good.” Marco Finazio from Umberto Espresso Bar is pulling back on takeaway. Not everyone is doubling down on delivery. Marco Finazio, owner of Umberto Espresso Bar and Gigi Rooftop in Thornbury, has spent years in the takeaway game, making family trays of lasagne and parmigiana to heat at home, plus offering delivery on Uber Eats. In March this year, he pulled out of both.



“The reliance on technology and convenience is huge, and it’s growing,” he says. “There is a very real pressure of cost of living, and this kind of thing helps people still have a dining experience where they don’t have to cook for themselves.” Umberto Espresso Bar is all about the dine-in experience. Takeaway was lucrative during COVID, he says, but creeping costs have been eating into margins. “You need to buy visibility on [delivery] platforms, which creates another expense, and ultimately, it’s just become too saturated with costs.” That wasn’t the only problem. “It was actually starting to do damage to our brand as the delivery service severely impacted food quality and dish integrity.” Finazio says he’s come full circle. “Let’s just play to our strengths and focus on what our core business is, which is serving wonderful people in the flesh. It’s not about chasing dollars today; it’s about what’s going to pay us in the long run.”



Panellists from the 2024 Good Food Symposium in Melbourne. Harrison Moss Coskun Uysal, an Istanbul-born chef and co-owner of Balaclava’s Tulum, is also on the panel. Earlier this year he launched Kismet, a Turkish tavern at the back of his restaurant as a more casual revenue stream. Sutinee “Tinee” Suntivatana will also be there. The chef-owner of cafes Tori’s and Humble Rays, two Melbourne brunch fixtures, has built a strong following on social media, leveraging viral trends to draw a younger Gen-Z heavy customer base through the door. Rounding out the panel is Rob Stone, senior director of APAC hospitality at Lightspeed, who will share industry-wide insights. The event is hosted by Good Food writer Dani Valent. The Good Food Symposium, presented by Lightspeed and supported by SevenRooms, is on Monday, September 7, from 5.30pm at Hyde Melbourne Place at 130 Russell Street, Melbourne. Register for free here.

World.title: British PM exchanged messages with Trump chief-of-staff impersonator
World.content:
WorldEuropeWorld politics British PM exchanged messages with Trump chief-of-staff impersonator Dominic Penna August 17, 2026 — 8:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Andy Burnham exchanged messages with somebody impersonating Donald Trump’s chief of staff, it has emerged. The British prime minister messaged a person posing as Susie Wiles, who is considered the most powerful woman in the White House. The incident, first reported by Politico, prompted such concern in the British embassy that officials raised concerns with their White House counterparts. Susie Wiles in the Oval Office with Donald Trump last year. Getty Images Downing Street sources admitted that Burnham had been in contact with the impersonator but claimed the messages were not of significance.



However, the messages will nonetheless raise concerns about national security. British officials are said to have feared that Wiles’ phone had been hacked again, after an impersonator reportedly texted and called her contacts in May 2025 to ask for cash and presidential pardons. Wiles privately told colleagues that her personal cell phone was hacked and mined for executive contacts. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. AP The FBI launched an investigation after the breach in which the impostor supposedly sent a series of text messages and phone calls to Republican politicians using artificial intelligence to mimic her voice. The White House said at the time that it took the cybersecurity of all staff “very seriously”, while the FBI insisted all threats against Trump were treated with the “utmost seriousness”.





‘Malicious’ impersonation campaign Last year American intelligence services warned of an “ongoing malicious text and voice campaign” where actors impersonated senior US officials to target individuals. Related Article US Votes 2024 Donald Trump’s campaign says its emails were hacked US authorities have previously accused hackers acting on behalf of Iran in the final months of Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Information security has been an ongoing concern at the White House, with one hacker managing to breach the communications service used by Mike Waltz, the former national security adviser, in April 2025.





Just weeks after the illegal Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Ben Wallace and Priti Patel – the then defence and foreign secretaries – were fooled by Russian “impostors” who posed as Ukrainian politicians. Related Article US politics ‘Susie, what do you think?’ The woman of power who has Trump’s ear Both Wallace and Patel held video calls, requested in the name of an aide at the Ukrainian embassy, before eventually becoming suspicious and ending the exchanges. Wallace believed that he was talking to Denys Shmyhal, who was then serving as the Ukraine prime minister and is now Volodymyr Zelensky’s energy minister. He said the man looked and sounded like the Ukraine prime minister but became suspicious when the caller – who was posing in front of a Ukrainian flag – began to ask questions relating to UK security.



Patel responded to the incident by revealing that the same thing had happened to her, calling it a “pathetic attempt at such difficult times to divide us”. A Downing Street spokesman said: “We do not comment on national security matters.” The White House declined to comment. World.title: How will Jess Wilson cut debt without cutting services?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters How will Jess Wilson cut debt without cutting services? August 17, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. STATE ELECTION The Victorian Coalition has now committed to spending $90 million a year to save some of us (predominantly in marginal seats) toll charges (“Road tolls to be capped at $50 weekly under Coalition commuter plan”, 16/7). Rural voters must be ecstatic about paying more taxes to subsidise Melbourne.

It would help if they could now explain how they’ll keep their commitment to reduce the state debt (by an albeit minuscule 1 per cent per annum) by doing that, when they are also spending $250 million extra per year on potholes, cancelling the ESL, lowering payroll tax, getting rid of land tax and employing thousands more police and PSOs (if they can get them) – without cutting services or sacking public servants.

Maybe it explains why their social media posts now talk about “stabilising” debt rather than reducing it, as they have until recently.

Richard Jamonts, Williamstown Pledge gives help to those who don’t need it

Jess Wilson’s cap on toll fees considers, like so much policy, that the cost-of-living crisis is experienced by everyone equally.

Why give a motorist on $800,000 a year the same help as someone on $80,000? Such general applications assist those who don’t need it while reducing the pool of what might be made to those in real need of financial assistance.

Jenny Herbert, Metung



Wilson gives low priority to sustainability

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has made a number of announcements which focus on the the cost of living but indicate the low priority her Coalition give to sustainability.

Bringing back weekly bin collections ignores the benefits of lowering the amount of waste going into landfill and increases costs to councils. The opposition say they will “end the gas ban” but helping switch Victorian households to more efficient electric technology will have economy wide benefits, reduce harmful pollution and increase energy security.

They say they will run coal plants for as long as possible, locking in more pollution and climate harm for our communities and raising insurance costs.

Nature is under increasing pressure and climate risk is rising. Hip-pocket announcements may be popular, but I don’t think these policies will make Victoria “safer or more affordable” in the long run.

David Hudspeth, Burwood Grid costs are a major part of power bills

The good news is that “record-breaking renewable energy generation” has helped many customers, with lower bills. The bad news is that the grid will continue to require major investment (″⁣Energy giants warn big test still to come for power grid″⁣, 17/8).

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) confirms that the cheapest way to maintain grid reliability is with wind and solar, backed up by batteries, hydroelectric and some gas.

LNP energy policy includes building more rooftop solar and battery installations in urban areas. There would be major impacts of Jess Wilson’s promise to protect farmers by “pausing major transmission projects”. Whatever the chosen energy mix, grid costs are a major part of power bills.

John Hughes, Mentone Why does all the money go to one firm?

In the same edition, The Age reports that a private-sector consortium is circling to get the inside running on building the airport rail link (″⁣Private sector weighs bid to help Melbourne’s airport rail link finally take off″⁣, 16/8). We also read that the Coalition will use our taxes to subsidise Transurban tolls. One may have hoped the Coalition would offer a government that would rein in such cosy deals. If cost-of-living pressures are such that commuters require assistance, why should all the money be directed to one firm? .

Eric Keys, retired transport planner, Flemington Tawdry vote grab

What a ridiculous idea of the state Coalition to reimburse tolls of up to $3000 per year. It makes one wonder if the Coalition would be any better at government than the current lot. This is nothing more than a tawdry attempt at vote grabbing, something that we are more than used to in Australia. It means all Victorians will pay, instead of the toll road users.

This considered action has nothing to do with Transurban, and it does not deserve criticism as it only operates the roads and will receive normal payments due. Keep in mind, Melbourne would not have the freeway network we currently have if it was not for the toll operator.

Mike Weiss, Vermont South THE FORUM



Small business lament

The proposed changes to the tax system, especially the changes to trusts will decimate small business. However, this is hardly mentioned in the media or by politicians. Small business accounts for half of all business output in Australia.

Farmers have a strong voice in the National Farmers’ Federation and the Nationals, and have successfully argued for a carve-out from the tax changes. But why do these 400,000 small businesses that operate through trusts not receive the same consideration? Because they don’t have a voice. (When was the last time anyone saw a headline from the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia or even know who COSBOA is?)

And so, democracy fails. The single vote of a coffee shop owner is valued the same as a public servant who wants to retain “work from home” privileges, or a uni student who votes for HECS fee relief, or the salary worker who demands childcare rebates.

None of these voters care about the changes to the tax system. And so the crucial engine of economic growth in our community will pack up and leave. And we will, as a nation, be all the poorer for it.

Wayne Alexander, Eltham COVID not the problem

Neil Mitchell’s article (″⁣There’s a nasty mood festering in this state″⁣, 16/8) describes the negative society in which we live. Various reasons for the anger and resentment are postulated, such as a hangover from the pandemic. The pandemic privations – there were many– finished almost five years ago.

Blaming the pandemic cannot continue: we can and should be over this. Those who lived through WWII, especially those survivors of Japanese POW horrors who came home and got on with it, worked to rebuild their lives without the anger and appalling behaviour demonstrated now.

The negativity of the press – eg. describing Victoria as a ″⁣rust bucket″⁣ – contributes to disaffection, as does the focus on trivia: ″⁣melongate″⁣. General ignorance is a problem – in an age where the wisdom of the world is available with a click of a few buttons, far too many people look to lies and false ″⁣information″⁣, forming opinions which are simply wrong.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Rich and poor divide

As we approach our state election in November, columnist Neil Mitchell seems to skip over the fact that this anger is not just in our state, or our country, but a mood expressed throughout the “free” world.

Among a list of possible reasons, he leans heavily on the aftereffects of Victoria’s onerous COVID lockdowns. This doesn’t explain why populists whipping up anger are rising in most Western nations. How about the huge wealth gap that has opened in these countries? The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare cites several studies showing wealth inequality significantly reduces happiness in a society. We watch as the “so-called” leader of the free world uses his position of power to enrich himself and his cronies and cuts aid to desperate people on or below the breadline.

Closer to home, who wouldn’t be angry to see our taxpayer dollars fed to already wealthy private schools while the schools their children attend are unable to cover even the most basic necessities?

There are many struggling families in Australia, and it is hard to imagine that this anger won’t continue while they see their “well-off” neighbours enjoying many advantages not available to themselves, not to mention the billionaires able to consistently multiply their wealth every year.

The Albanese government’s recent changes to tax breaks for the wealthy and those with investment properties are steps in the right direction to address the wealth gap. Much more needs to be done at state and federal levels, however. Let us start looking for solutions, rather than blame.

Jan Downing, Hawthorn East Elephant in room

I would suggest that Neil Mitchell’s article (16/8) misses the elephant in the room. Is Victoria much different to the US or UK? What do these places have in common? The failed and selfish economic agenda called neo-liberalism. Oh, and then the columnist’s irony to quote the Centre for Independent Studies, a bastion of free-market individualism.

Phil Labrum, Trentham



Saw it coming

On reading “The Emerald Isle has turned yellow as food supply fears rise across Europe” (16/8), I’m reminded of an ABC Radio National report 20 years ago in which Philip Adams interviewed a British climate scientist who said the British Isles and Europe would face a semi-arid climate within a century.

He said people can live in semi-arid climates but that the population supported would be substantially less that at present and that if carbon emissions were stopped immediately, it would take at least a century for the atmosphere to repair. I think that this summer in Europe is illustrating that the prophesies made are coming to pass.

Christopher Jarvis, Point Lonsdale Living in hotboxes

Many years ago, during an intense heatwave, my late mother-in-law came perilously close to death. She was in her post-war weatherboard house with poor insulation, and, by the third day of heat, with her air conditioner malfunctioning, her house was an inferno.

Hearing her weak voice on the phone we rushed to her side with a fan, wet towels and ice cubes and were able to cool her before the excellent ambulance members came. They were surprised she was alive.

There are thousands of homes of the type she lived in still being used in Melbourne today. They are hotboxes in summer and freezing in the winter. There are also a remarkable number of later built houses and units with no trees or eaves for shading.

To hear Coalition shadow ministers suggest we build lower quality houses is madness. Heat waves are raging in Europe and people are dying in their apartments that were designed for a totally different climate.

Houses built now will still be there in 40 years when the climate will be hotter still.

Helen Hook, Black Rock Yielding to idiom

“The reason why” used in journalist Nikki Barrowclough’s first sentence (″⁣There’s no getting around it: We need to talk about this irksome word″⁣, 15/8) is a tautology but nonetheless has become somewhat idiomatic. At what point does prescriptive grammar yield to idiom?

There are many phrases in English whose origins are obscure and which are not capable of grammatical deconstruction. The writer’s use of ″⁣reticent″⁣ rather than ″⁣reluctant″⁣ is indicative of the way in which words whose meaning once clearly delineated are now becoming interchangeable. The word none can mean no-one or not any as one wishes.

Justin Mackenzie, Sassafras Immigration question

Has federal Labor left its run too late on immigration? (“Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches”, 17/8). In the last stages of Joe Biden’s presidency, it finally dawned that his open door immigration policy was failing, and he rushed in measures to change it, but too late. In the US public’s mind, Biden was soft on immigration and he and the Democrats suffered as a result.

Perceptions in politics take a while to develop, but once they do, they are hard to eradicate. Labor needs a bold, plain statement signalling to the electorate that it is taking charge of this mismanaged system with a new policy framework: sustainable, transparent and catering to the interests of all Australians – not just the business class, whose interests in a high immigration intake are clearly self-serving.

Greg Gardiner, Brunswick Punching the ball

Sports journalist Michael Gleeson’s explanation that you can’t punch your own ball through for a score after the siren has not always been upheld by the league (″⁣The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw″⁣, 17/8).

At round 1, 1982, Carlton v Fitzroy at Princes Park, Mario Bortolotto punched the ball through for a score to Carlton and the match resulted in a draw.

The technical ruling was that the trajectory of the ball would have taken it through even if Mario hadn’t punched it, and as such the goal umpire adjudicated the punch had not assisted the score. Goal umpires back then must have had a type of ESP.

Stephen Turner, Quarry Hill



Denton a class act

Thank you to the Logies awards for recognising the extraordinary talent of Andrew Denton whose strength was guiding guests to step away from their protective public personas and being authentic. It made for extraordinary viewing on Denton Unplugged.

It was a masterclass of extensive research to see what others say about them, including many celebrities who hide behind their PR machines and don’t usually go off script. His shows never insulted the intelligence of his TV audience, and for that I am extremely grateful, providing us with so many memorable moments.

Sally Walcock, Toorak AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Accolades

My faith is restored. Muster Dogs won a Logie.

Heather Barker, Albert Park



Andrew Denton’s acceptance speech for his Logie Hall of Fame award was full of grace, humour and humility. Politicians of every ilk should be forced to watch it!

Peter Venn, East Bentleigh Will Pauline Hanson now request an official enquiry into Shane Jacobson’s joke about her at The Logies? If Gina Rinehart gets offended at jokes at her expense, will Pauline follow in the same manner, or do commercial networks get a free pass ?

Jenny Smith, East Melbourne Can I kindly remind Dave Hughes of the infamous speech by Ricky Gervais at the Golden Globes where he called out the hypocrisy of privileged celebrities: ″⁣You’re in no position to lecture the public about anything as you don’t live in the real world ... you’ve spent less time in school than Greta Thunberg″⁣.

Pamela Papadopoulos, South Yarra Cricket

Good to see only whole numbers used on the report card for Australia’s Test cricketers. Food critics and others, please take note (“Australia player ratings after shock Test loss to Bangladesh”, 17/8).

The use of half marks is pretentious and unnecessary when the mark is already out of 5, 10 or 20.

Lindsay Zoch, Mildura Surely, it’s no coincidence that Australia’s capitulation to Bangladesh occurred in Darwin, whereby Bangladesh best adapted to an old-fashioned notion of preparing for a five-day Test match.

The folly of the Aussies was to rely upon hubris, the downfall of many who have come before.

Tim Goddard, Barwon Heads



Finally

Musk has left his prediction re a future without money too late (″⁣Why the richest man on Earth wants you to think money won’t matter″⁣, 16/8).

l have been living without money three days a week for years.

James Lane, Hampton East The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Revealed: The Swans players who could be stood down on finals eve amid sexual assault investigation
World.content:
Key Sydney Swans players are at the centre of a Victoria Police sexual assault investigation putting their immediate playing futures under a cloud and plunging the club’s finals campaign into turmoil. The investigation relates to an allegation of sexual assault at an East Melbourne hotel hours after the team’s victory over Essendon at the MCG on Sunday night. Loading This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and one other player after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. This masthead is not suggesting all five players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with enquiries. The group of five were driving home to Sydney in a rental car on Monday night.



A manager representing a fifth player denied his client was one of the players involved. The five players are unlikely to play this week regardless of the police investigation, as the Swans consider potential sanctions for late-night drinking at the team hotel, which is funded by the AFL, after a match. Chad Warner (left), Isaac Heeney (right), James Jordon (middle bottom) and Riley Bice (middle top) of the Swans. Michael Howard Asked whether they were considering standing down the players, the Swans said all options were open as they worked through the facts of what happened. This was confirmed by a senior AFL source. The players were not arrested. Police asked to review CCTV footage from the Pullman East Melbourne as part of their investigation.



Plain clothes officers went inside hotel rooms and left the venue with a number of items in evidence bags, according to a witness to the police visit. They also asked for footage from cameras that cover public areas of the hotel such as the lobby, stairs and lifts. The Swans have been left “shocked and disappointed” amid the investigation, which focuses on the actions of a group of players in the early hours of Monday morning. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich fronts the media on Monday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The team was staying at the Pullman after their victory over Essendon at the nearby MCG. Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich briefly fronted media in Sydney on Monday to address the alleged incident.



“We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing. It’s safe to say that we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation,” Pavlich said. “We understand the level of interest in the matter. There’s going to be lots of speculation, but given it’s a police matter right now, that is all that we can say.” The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Simon Schluter Pavlich did not take questions, and did not respond to a reporter’s question about whether or not arrests had been made. Two industry sources, speaking anonymously because the investigation is ongoing, said the players were driving back to Sydney on Monday evening to avoid media at Melbourne and Sydney airports.



The AFL held discussions with the Swans on Monday about whether the club would identify the players, and about whether they would be available to play in the coming weeks. One photo being shared in chat groups, showing a woman with damaged teeth, does not relate to the incident. It was published by tabloid news sites in the UK earlier this year, months before the incident. Police with clipboards and camera equipment were seen in the lobby of the hotel on Monday morning. Pullman hotel staff would not comment.



Victoria Police confirmed they were “investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne on August 17”. “The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning,” it said in a statement. “The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing.” Swans board member and club great Michael O’Loughlin was spotted at Sydney’s domestic airport on Monday but declined to shed further light on the matter when approached for comment. “No, we’ll wait and see what the findings are, I don’t know,” O’Loughlin said.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Hidden boardrooms, crime threats and nude pics: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit Earlier on Monday the Swans released a statement. “The Sydney Swans can confirm several players were involved in an alleged incident in Melbourne last night,” the club confirmed in a statement on Monday. “The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage.” The AFL confirmed the league had been notified by the Swans and said the matter rested with police.



In cases such as this, the AFL’s integrity unit defers to police. The Swans are second on the ladder and well-placed to contend for the premiership with 17 wins, with one home-and-away round left before finals. They are due to play North Melbourne next Sunday in Sydney. Unlike the NRL, the AFL does not have a no-fault stand down rule for players charged with serious offences. However, Geelong’s Tanner Bruhn did not play for the Cats in 2025 after he was charged with rape and intentional sexual touching. The charges were dropped last November after a key witness admitted to lying, and Bruhn’s name was suppressed until the case was discontinued. St Kilda sacked Andrew Lovett after he was charged with rape in 2010, terminating his contract over “a series of acts and omissions in breach of his employment contract”. He was later found not guilty of the rape charge.



In 2013, St Kilda player Stephen Milne took an indefinite leave of absence from the club after he was charged with three counts of rape. The charges were dropped when Milne instead pleaded guilty to a single charge of indecent assault. The Sydney players have not been arrested or charged with any offence. With Marc McGowan Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Meet baby Miracle: Australia’s most premature newborn to survive
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBabies Meet baby Miracle: Australia’s most premature newborn to survive Abbey Geran August 17, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I took one look at her and I was like, ‘there’s no way she’s going to make it’,” remembers Annrose Tunavasa of the day she met her baby girl. In the living room of their Logan Reserve home, 35 kilometres south of Brisbane, she and her husband Misi cradle their four-month-old daughter in their arms. Loading Makerita Miracle Tanuvasa has already broken records, defied modern medical standards, and left doctors in awe. But her proud parents are just grateful she has survived. “It was just like she was here to fight,” says mum Annrose.



On March 20, Annrose visited her GP. She had just completed a six-week gym challenge, but dropped little weight, and suspected she may be four or five weeks pregnant. Related Article Fertility Brisbane, where have all the babies gone? See how your suburb has changed over time “I went to do an ultrasound and the sonographer told us that we were about 22 weeks pregnant,” she remembers. “I said ‘that’s impossible’.” Annrose explained that she had suffered a miscarriage in December. “She said, ‘Well, maybe you had a twin, and you miscarried the twin … you’ve got to go to the hospital and you’ll be staying there until you give birth.’”



Five days later, Annrose gave birth at the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital at 7:08pm. Her middle name says it all. Miracle, as she is now affectionately known, measured 30.5 centimetres upon arrival and weighed just 351 grams, making her the tiniest newborn in Queensland history. Her weight was some 23 grams less than Australia’s Coke Can Kid, Jonathon Heeley, who was born in 1992 and famously drew comparisons to the size of the soft drink. Miracle made the RBWH’s intensive care unit her home for 14 weeks. Father Misi said his daughter was about the size of his palm. “We weren’t able to hold her, but she was very, very small,” he says.



She was so small, clinicians were left perplexed. “A week later the doctor came in to see me, and she said, ‘She’s just not matching the scans that you came in with, she doesn’t match that baby’,” Annrose explains. “I was measuring at 500 grams, measuring at 22 weeks pregnant.” Baby Miracle and family. Nine News Annrose was asked to retrieve the scans she had completed prior to her miscarriage in December, which showed her baby was even more premature than first thought.



“They said, this has got to be the same pregnancy.” Related Article Pregnancy ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first Doctors told the couple Miracle was in fact born at 21 weeks and 3 days – so premature that resuscitation usually is not an option. The revelation means she is not only Queensland’s smallest baby, but also believed to be the most premature in Australia to live. Previously, that was baby Stevie O’Reilly, born at 22 weeks and two days at Townsville University Hospital in July last year.



The Guinness World Records recognises Iowa toddler Nash Keen, born at exactly 21 weeks in July 2024, as the most premature baby to survive worldwide. “Even the doctors couldn’t explain how she was able to survive everything she’s gone through,” says Misi. Annrose nods. “She said, we can’t give you any answers. Everything is actually just a miracle. And I just said, ‘well, let’s keep it like that’.” Staff congratulate mum Annrose and baby Miracle as she leaves hospital. Nine News Following her frantic delivery, Annrose and Misi spent the next month whispering to their daughter from behind the glass facade of a neonatal intensive care incubator.



Miracle was covered head to toe in tubes and cables as a mighty, multidisciplinary team of health care workers kept a watchful eye over her. Related Article Fertility Seven things to know about Australia’s baby bust – and what it means for you Four weeks into her life, the then petrified parents were finally able to hold their precious girl. “It was magical, but it was also very scary, holding such a tiny baby,” says Annrose. Miracle made the RBWH’s intensive care unit her home for 14 weeks.



After six weeks, Annrose moved into Herston’s Ronald McDonald House and she and Misi juggled parenting their two other children, aged 1 and 4, with monitoring their growing newborn. “Every visit, it was like real quiet, like almost like no one wanted to tell us, ‘we don’t know if she’s going to survive or not’,” Annrose recalls. “But I think after one month, it just started to get real bright in the room.” Baby Miracle with proud parents Annrose and Misi. Eventually, Miracle was transferred to Logan Hospital’s special care nursery.



She was discharged in early August, more than four months after she was born and at what would have marked 40 weeks gestation. “I haven’t seen a 21-plus-three-weeker,” says registered nurse Renee Judd. “We’ve had other little babies here, but not that young, and I have been 16 years in the neonatal journey in Logan.” The nurses and midwives who cared for her formed a guard of honour as Annrose carried her daughter from the facility – remarkably, without an oxygen tank. Annrose and Misi teared up as they thanked the healthcare heroes who kept Miracle alive.



“Thank you guys so much for all the love and care you gave our daughter, the nurses, the doctors, the cleaners … social workers, Ronald McDonald House in Herston. Thank you guys so much for everything.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Middle of nowhere’: fears private primary school would overwhelm farming hamlet
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Middle of nowhere’: fears private primary school would overwhelm farming hamlet Caroline Schelle August 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Plans to build a private primary school for more than 300 students have distressed locals in a tiny farming community of 100 people near Geelong. Bacchus Marsh Grammar School has applied to build a private primary school at its Staughton Vale campus, 40 minutes from Geelong, which now teaches agriculture, outdoor education and environmental studies to 150 students. Locals Mark Trengove, Mandy Cocks, Michael Dragt and Kristy Vasils with Kristy’s children Ollie, 11, and Savannah, 9, on Staughton Vale Road at the site of Bacchus Marsh Grammar School’s proposed campus. Penny Stephens If the government approves the school, it would mean there would be 300 extra students commuting to the 83½-hectare property, dwarfing the local community of just 100 people. The private school already has 3800 students at two other campuses at Maddingley, in Bacchus Marsh, and Woodlea, in Melton.



The school wants to expand the Staughton Vale site to create a primary to Year 8 campus, retaining the 150 agriculture students and offering “added capacity and greater choice for families across the wider region”, according to its application to the state government’s planning department. But Staughton Vale and Anakie Action Group member Kristy Vasils said she was shocked to find out through other members of the community that the school planned to build a primary school at the site. “We’re just kind of wondering why they would want to put a school out in the middle of nowhere and plan to bus kids in. “If we were to have an increase in traffic coming past of buses and things like that, especially at 3.30 in the afternoon, that is really concerning for me because it’s already pretty congested at that time of the day,” she said. Vasils, who lives in Anakie, 12 kilometres away, said the local community was happy with the current campus.



“We don’t mind them bringing students out and showing them a beautiful piece of land and doing gardening and different activities with them there,” she said. “The problem is with this particular permit that they’re now applying for … they’re wanting 300 permanent primary school students there, along with 150 high school students as well.” Mark Trengove and Michael Dragt on Staughton Vale Road with the site of Bacchus Marsh Grammar School’s Staughton Vale farm campus driveway behind them. Penny Stephens Bacchus Marsh Grammar principal Debra Ogston said the campus had operated for more than a decade and the school had followed the standard planning process. “As part of this process, members of the community have the opportunity to consider the proposal and make submissions before a decision is made by the responsible authority,” she said.



The principal said hundreds of Bacchus Marsh Grammar students benefited from the agricultural, outdoor and environmental learning at the Staughton Vale property. “The proposed development will broaden these opportunities for students in Melbourne’s west,” she said. Others who lived closer to the property said they were concerned about how it could affect the landscape and environment of the area. Michael Dragt lives opposite the property and said he feared an approval meant the school could continue to expand. “We have no doubt it’s part of their growth plans,” he said.



Dragt said the number of students would overwhelm the area, which was zoned for farming and had four people per kilometre. “It’ll totally change the environment out there,” he said. The area was zoned for farming, and many locals still grew crops or had stock on neighbouring land, he said. “They’re not connected to anyone in the farming community to help, you know, grow those learnings with the kids – that’s what I’d like to see happen.”



Dragt was also concerned that students wouldn’t be able to evacuate quickly if there was a bushfire. “It’s a deep concern to think that they would place the school so far out of context with no resources.” Ecologist Mark Trengove, who also lives nearby, said the plans were outrageous. “It’s just totally inappropriate the way they’ve treated the community and what they’re actually fundamentally trying to do is inappropriate,” he said. He was also concerned the biodiversity report the school commissioned didn’t address impact on threatened species, including the endangered swift parrot and yellow gum trees.



Students would be bused to the location from the existing secondary school and surrounding areas using private bus services, the planning documents say, while staff would drive and use an on-site car park. The documents claim the rural location is essential to the operation of the campus. A Victorian government spokesman said the proposal would be considered on its merits and as it was under assessment it would be inappropriate to comment further.
